a380fd3f5684.t: April 1 — "But Government, No." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Tradition Four answers the oldest threat to a group: somebody outside it deciding how

f6ba9e72bab4.t: Tradition Four answers the oldest threat to a group: somebody outside it deciding how it should be run, and one of the first to try was A.A.'s own co-founder. Bill W. wanted to manage the whole movement from New York, and he told what happened (A.A. Comes of Age): "But I soon found that I could do no such thing. Neither could anybody else at A.A.'s Headquarters." The groups answered him plainly: "We are not going to have a personal government in New York, or anywhere else. Services, yes. But government, no." The Long Form wrote their answer down (Big Book, p. 563): "With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." Its own affairs means its own business: when and where it meets, how the meeting runs, who serves, what the basket pays for. No other authority means none at all: not the founder, not the office in New York, not the landlord. If the man who helped start A.A. couldn't run a group from outside, nobody can. Today the outside manager is usually the building: a facility that sets the meeting's time, format and chair, and can end it when its program changes. Test it tonight: ask who decided how your meeting runs, and when the members last voted on it.

0c74be37a86a.t: The groups told A.A.'s own co-founder he could serve them but not govern them. Who outside my group decides how it runs?

ae80adb364e1.t: <0>Read the Long Form (pp. 563–566).</0> The short form on pp. 561–562 is the one everybody quotes — but the <1>Long Form</1> is where the Traditions actually say what they mean. Tradition 3's "no other affiliation" clause, for instance, exists <2>only</2> in the Long Form. That single clause is why no treatment centre can own an A.A. group. Most of what circulates online skips it. <3/><4/> And a distinction worth keeping straight: <5>the Traditions are governance, not theology.</5> They bind A.A. <6>groups</6> and the Fellowship — not individuals, and not outside businesses. They were adopted in 1950 to keep A.A. from being owned or co-opted. They are not a rulebook for your personal life.

cedaf4529725.t: April 10 — "A Center of Service." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. If A.A.'s own head office could never govern a group, no outside office can, and tha

3702c7c79f87.t: If A.A.'s own head office could never govern a group, no outside office can, and that is why a facility's hold on a meeting has no standing in A.A. Bill W. wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 39): "Here at the General Office we have long known that we can merely supply certain indispensable services." Indispensable means the groups couldn't do without them; merely means that is all they are. Then came his list: information, literature, advice to new groups "if asked," help in settling disputes. His conclusion: "even here at the very center of A.A., there can only exist a center of service". The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) leaves each group "responsible to no other authority than its own conscience," and A.A.'s own office accepted that it was not one. Now picture the facility down the road. It has no standing in A.A. at all, yet it decides when the meeting runs, who chairs, and whether it runs at all. It has taken the power that A.A.'s own headquarters refused. The way in is usually service: a room, coffee, a staff member to help. Help that comes with the final say is government. Test it tonight: ask who could cancel your meeting without the members voting, and whether that is a servant or a boss.

bca28f9a2ac0.t: April 11 — "The World Is Waiting." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. The third sentence of Tradition Four is there because one member was ready to speak

a0e43b4c0780.t: The third sentence of Tradition Four is there because one member was ready to speak for all of A.A. on national radio. Bill W. told it (A.A. Comes of Age). A pioneer member had started a group with local radio lectures that mixed A.A. with his own religious ideas. Then a company offered to put them on a national network, under his own name, with a fee for him. The trustees advised against it. His reply: "To hell with the trustees, the world is waiting for my message. I've got the right of free speech, and I'm going on the air whether you like it or not." One man's choice would have told a whole country what A.A. was. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) closes that door: "And no group, regional committee, or individual should ever take any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees of the General Service Board." Conferring means talking it over first. The trustees are the people A.A. made custodians of its Tradition (p. 565). Nobody used force; he was told every group would hear of it, and the broadcast never aired. Today one person on a podcast, or one program's website, tells the world what A.A. is. Test it tonight: ask who in your area speaks publicly for A.A., and who they asked first.

8fb2d6ebed5d.t: One member nearly told a whole country what A.A. was, without asking anyone. Who speaks for A.A. in my town, and who did they ask?

0bf2017a1356.t: April 12 — "Every Group Argument." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Tradition Four was not handed down to the groups; it was written up from them, out

af1f0629786b.t: Tradition Four was not handed down to the groups; it was written up from them, out of years of their own arguments. Bill W. remembered the mid-1940s (A.A. Comes of Age): "It seemed as if every contestant in every group argument wrote us during this confused and exciting period." Headquarters answered without giving orders. Bill said they had to coin sentences that went into half the letters they wrote: "Of course you are at perfect liberty to handle this matter any way you please. But the majority experience in A.A. does seem to suggest" and then the experience followed. Liberty first; experience second, as a suggestion. "The basic ideas for the Twelve Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous came directly out of this vast correspondence." And they were never meant as law: "A code of traditions could not, of course, ever become rule or law. But it might act as a guide for our Trustees, Headquarters people, and especially for A.A. groups with growing pains." The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) sets each group's own conscience over its own affairs because that is how the groups had been living all along. Today the letter a struggling meeting gets is more often a policy from its host, with no liberty in it. Test it tonight: ask where your group goes for advice, and whether it is free to say no.

a7a6b6a7f042.t: The Traditions were written up from the groups' own arguments and offered as a guide, never as law. Is my group being guided or governed?

27cfd30b14e8.t: April 13 — "Paramount." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. The last words of Tradition Four set a limit every group carries: some things belong to A.A. a

a834365adee5.t: The last words of Tradition Four set a limit every group carries: some things belong to A.A. as a whole, and no single group or person gets to decide them. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "On such issues our common welfare is paramount." Paramount means it comes above everything else, above any one group's preference. Such issues are the ones named in the sentence before it: "any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole". When the Traditions were first published in 1946, that sentence named the trustees of The Alcoholic Foundation; a footnote in the pamphlet (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 7) records that in 1954 the name was changed to the General Service Board. Same job, new name. Autonomy covers a group's own meeting. It does not cover changing what A.A. is. Today what A.A. is gets decided, in plenty of towns, by people who never asked anyone: a program prints its own version of the Steps under A.A.'s name, a facility tells a judge what counts as an A.A. meeting. A group that goes along, reading that version or signing those slips, has acted for all of A.A. without asking. Test it tonight: find one thing said about A.A. in your town that A.A. as a whole never agreed to, and ask who said it.

eced5e84bb07.t: Some decisions belong to A.A. as a whole, and no group, program or person gets to make them alone. What has been said about A.A. in my town that A.A. never agreed to?

9e9702743812.t: April 14 — "Full of Wisdom." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. A group gives Tradition Four away most easily to someone it admires. Picture the man who

62a9c3440ebe.t: A group gives Tradition Four away most easily to someone it admires. Picture the man who arrives from another city with twenty years and a voice that fills the room. Within a month he is explaining how his old group did it, which readings are proper, who should be allowed to share. Nobody voted him in. The group just starts doing what he says, because he sounds like A.A. Bill W. described him (A.A. Comes of Age): "Who is less popular than the old-time A.A. full of wisdom, who moves to another area and tries to tell the group there how to run its business?" Bill said such men "meet with stubborn resistance, or worse still, laughter." That resistance is the Tradition working. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) makes the group "responsible to no other authority than its own conscience," and a visitor's experience, however long, is advice, not authority. He can bring it to a business meeting and ask for a vote like anyone else. The group breaks Four when it skips that step and simply obeys. Today the voice from away is often a program graduate's, carrying a treatment centre's house rules into a free group as if they were A.A.'s. Test it tonight: ask whether anything your group does started because one person said so.

237ce9d7410a.t: Long sobriety brings advice to a group, not authority over it; only the group's conscience decides. Does my group do anything just because one person said so?

d5a104109057.t: April 15 — "Improve on Our Methods." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. A group that can't change its own ways can't find better ones, and that freedom i

5134dc5a55eb.t: A group that can't change its own ways can't find better ones, and that freedom is the first thing a captured meeting loses. Defending group autonomy against people who thought it went too far, Bill W. said (A.A. Comes of Age): "If, on the other hand, they found something better than A.A., or if they were able to improve on our methods, then in all probability we would adopt what they discovered for general use everywhere." He meant A.A. groups, answering to no one else. And: "Healthy trial and error always have their day and place in A.A." That is how A.A. was meant to learn: one group tries something, it works, and others take it up. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) protects the trying, because a group answerable only to "its own conscience" can vote to change its format next month. Now look at a meeting run inside a program. Its format is part of the program's curriculum, the same in every room the program runs, approved by people who never attend. The members can't vote it differently, so nothing new ever comes out of that room, and nothing better can travel from it to the rest of A.A. Test it tonight: name one thing your group does differently from the group across town, and ask who decided it.

d754595e3436.t: A.A. was meant to learn from groups free to try things and keep what worked. Is my group free to try something new?

f86237d7043e.t: April 16 — "The Whole of New York State." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. No single body may act for every A.A. group at once, and A.A. learned that f

173968cd432f.t: The Whole of New York State

569151d10f43.t: No single body may act for every A.A. group at once, and A.A. learned that from a lease. The first A.A. club in New York took over rooms on West 24th Street, and a corporation was formed to hold the lease. Bill W. wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 19) that it was titled "Alcoholics Anonymous of New York, Inc." Nobody meant any harm by it. Then: "Only later did we realize we had incorporated the whole of New York State, a mistake recently rectified." Incorporated means set up as a legal company. One clubroom's paperwork had put A.A.'s name over every group in a state, and none of them had been asked. That is why the third sentence of the Long Form exists (Big Book, p. 563): "And no group, regional committee, or individual should ever take any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees of the General Service Board." The trustees look after A.A.'s shared services and its Traditions. Today the same mistake comes with a logo: a program, a website or a local committee using A.A.'s name as if it held the name for a whole city. Test it tonight: ask who decided that anything calling itself A.A. in your town could speak for every group in it.

77850a479b4c.t: April 17 — "Dutiful Children." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Before Tradition Four was written, the groups around New York had settled that no group

40ab7ddb3019.t: Before Tradition Four was written, the groups around New York had settled that no group answers to another, not even the one that started it. Bill W. told the story in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 20). The Manhattan club had nurtured the first suburban groups. As they grew they found their own rooms and their own friends. The club ran a central meeting and paid a secretary who took calls for the whole area, so, Bill admitted, New Yorkers thought "our outlying groups ought financially to support the Manhattan club; dutiful children should look after their" parents. The groups never argued. They simply decided for themselves: "Though many outlying A.A. members personally contributed to the 24th Street Club, nary a cent did their respective groups ever send in." Nary a cent means not one cent. Members gave as they chose; the groups kept their money for their own affairs, and nobody could make them do otherwise. That is the Long Form's first sentence before it was written down (Big Book, p. 563): each group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." Today the parent may be a big meeting, an office or a program that started a group and still expects it to obey. Test it tonight: ask whether any older group, office or person can tell your group what to do with its basket.

89122934682f.t: The Manhattan club called the new groups its children, and the groups answered by running their own affairs. Does my group still answer to whoever started it?

2c93f031671d.t: April 18 — "Who Holds the Link." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. An online meeting is a group's own affair like any other, and whoever holds the link,

e85a30302ffd.t: An online meeting is a group's own affair like any other, and whoever holds the link, the password and the host controls holds the group unless the group decides otherwise. The Big Book's latest foreword notes it (p. xxiv): "A.A. members with computers can participate in meetings online, sharing with fellow alcoholics across the country or around the world." Nothing changed in the Tradition when the room moved onto a screen. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." But an online room has new handles of power. One member pays for the account and can close it. A host can mute, remove or block anyone with a click. A program can run the meeting on its own platform and keep the list of who attended. None of that has to be sinister for it to be authority, and the group never voted any of it in. A group that meets online governs the link the same way a room group governs its key and its basket: by deciding, together, who holds it and for how long. Test it tonight: ask who could end your online meeting tomorrow, and whether the group ever chose them.

b4b71ad43c44.t: Online, the key to the room is the link and the host controls. Did my group choose who holds them?

621e3efa9573.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 4 (Big Book, p. 563); Foreword to the Fourth Edition (Big Book, p. xxiv).

070e5823b07b.t: April 19 — "A Bare Majority." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. A group can run its own affairs by vote and still break itself apart by voting badly. Pi

96f42f8cf5f1.t: A group can run its own affairs by vote and still break itself apart by voting badly. Picture a business meeting about moving the meeting to a new building. Twenty people come; eleven vote yes, nine vote no, and the eleven call it settled and start packing. Nobody asked what the nine needed. Three weeks later the nine are meeting on their own in the old room, and the town has two half-groups where it had one. Bill W. saw this coming (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 29). Writing in 1946 about whether groups should pay for clubs, he set down a principle that reaches every group vote: "But the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority into supporting clubs they do not want or need." Coerce means force. Later, when A.A. built its service structure, it designed elections around the same danger (A.A. Comes of Age): "Another prime cause of grief was the hotly contested close election, which nearly always left behind a large and discontented minority." The Long Form gives each group "no other authority than its own conscience" (Big Book, p. 563), and the whole room is that conscience, not the winning side of a count. Test it tonight: at your next business meeting, before a close vote is called, ask whether the group has talked long enough.

586982abb0f5.t: A group's conscience is the whole room, not the winning side of a count. When my group last voted, what happened to the ones who lost?

60400da1984f.t: April 2 — "That Powerful Minority." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Before there was a Tradition Four, eighteen drunks in a house in Akron already kne

5199f737309a.t: Before there was a Tradition Four, eighteen drunks in a house in Akron already knew that a group settles its own business by vote, and that the losing side can be right. Bill W. and Dr. Bob brought them big plans: paid missionaries, A.A. hospitals, a book. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "The moment we were through, those alcoholics really did work us over!" They argued it out, and then it went to a vote: "By the barest majority, and over the most strenuous objections, the Akron meeting finally decided that we ought to go for the whole works". The founders didn't decide for them; the room did. And Bill later admitted the losers had seen further: "In later years, I came to be very thankful for that powerful minority." Big business and paid missionaries, he wrote, would have destroyed A.A. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) makes that room's way the rule for every group: each is "responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." A group's conscience is its members talking it through and voting, with the minority heard. Today a meeting can run for years without one vote, because its decisions were made somewhere else before anyone sat down. Test it tonight: ask when your group last voted on anything, and who spoke against it.

8efb0a13dd5f.t: Eighteen Akron drunks argued and voted, and the founders lived with the result. When did my group last decide anything by a vote?

9cbfb190e1d0.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 4 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (the Akron meeting's vote on missionaries, hospitals and the book).

2698cc8c6e51.t: April 20 — "Run the A.A. Affairs." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. When the building runs the meeting, the group has another authority, and Tradition

2c69248d4399.t: When the building runs the meeting, the group has another authority, and Tradition Four allows it none. A.A. learned this from its early clubs, separate corporations that rented rooms to groups. Bill W. wrote (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 20): "if an A.A. rotating committee tries to boss the club corporation or if the corporation tries to run the A.A. affairs of those groups who may meet at the club, there is difficulty at once." His answer was to keep the two apart: "If an A.A. group wishes to use a given club, let them pay rent or split the meeting take with the club management." Now look at a recovery centre that houses a dozen meetings. It prints them on its own calendar under its own name, bars people from the building and so from the meetings, and tells the groups what they may put on the wall. It is running the A.A. affairs of whoever meets there. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) says a group answers to "no other authority than its own conscience." A meeting whose rules come from its landlord answers to the landlord, however warm the room. A real group can rent any building that will have it and still run itself. Test it tonight: ask who could change your meeting's format tomorrow without a vote of its members.

db07cb1223cc.t: April 21 — "In Every Group." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. When A.A. grew too fast to be run by anyone, the danger was that someone would try anyway

8c2ce6d72b2c.t: When A.A. grew too fast to be run by anyone, the danger was that someone would try anyway, and the answer was to let each group govern itself under shared principles. By 1941 the Big Book counts 8,000 members, and its foreword asks what everyone feared (p. xviii): "Would there be quarrels over membership, leadership, and money?" It answers on the next page (p. xix): "Soon A.A. was beset by these very problems on every side and in every group." No office could have refereed thousands of group fights by mail, and nobody had the right to. So, the foreword goes on, "we had to evolve principles by which the A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole could survive and function effectively." Notice the two levels: the groups, and A.A. as a whole. That is the shape of Tradition Four. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) gives each group its own affairs, "responsible to no other authority than its own conscience," and keeps for A.A. as a whole only what touches everyone. Today the fear comes back as a demand for a referee: an office, a district or a program asked to settle a group's quarrel for it. Test it tonight: when your group has a fight, ask who it expects to settle it, and whether that someone has any right to.

1516dd8ab2a8.t: A.A. met its fights in every group by letting every group govern itself. Who does my group run to when it can't agree?

4d799c66838a.t: April 22 — "Suggestive Only." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Before any Tradition was written, the first A.A. book had already left each new group to

a7c99e0a3b53.t: Before any Tradition was written, the first A.A. book had already left each new group to run itself. In 1939 there were only a few centres, and the Big Book described what was spreading out from them (p. 162): "Little clusters of twos and threes and fives of us have sprung up in other communities". Nobody was sent to manage them. The book spoke to the reader who might start the next one alone, and handed him no rulebook. About itself it said (p. 164): "Our book is meant to be suggestive only. We realize we know only a little." The people who wrote the book did not claim the right to run what it started. Each new group worked out its own meeting night, its own room and its own ways. Seven years later the Long Form wrote down what those clusters had been doing all along (Big Book, p. 563): "With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." Today a new meeting is often handed a script before its first night: the facility's format, the program's rules, a card to read that nobody voted on. Test it tonight: ask who wrote the rules your meeting reads out, and whether your group ever voted to adopt them.

3bbfb63c8802.t: The book that started A.A. called itself suggestive only and left each group to run itself. Who wrote the rules my meeting follows?

2ff6d0dd2eb6.t: Anything that belongs to every group, the A.A. name, its book, its Steps, can only be changed by asking them all, and today it gets changed without asking anyone. A.A.'s own book was named that way. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "The Akron and New York groups had been voting for months on possible titles." Two groups, one book, both voting, because the book would speak for both. Bill admits he was tempted to settle it himself, with a title he could sign: "I began to forget that this was everybody's book and that I had been mostly the umpire of the discussions that had created it." An umpire calls the game; he does not own it. Friends slapped the idea down, and the groups kept voting. That is the Long Form's third sentence at work (Big Book, p. 563): "And no group, regional committee, or individual should ever take any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees of the General Service Board." Today the Steps get rewritten on a facility's wall, a program prints its own A.A. readings, a website edits the Traditions to suit its point. Each one changes everybody's book without asking. Test it tonight: when you are handed A.A. words, ask whether they match the book, and who changed them.

0e690234d5cf.t: A.A.'s book belonged to every group, so the groups voted on its name. Whose version of A.A.'s words is read in my room?

b421615f64ed.t: April 24 — "The Same Night." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. A group that changes its plans without asking the groups they will hurt has stopped at th

8448adcc8ef0.t: A group that changes its plans without asking the groups they will hurt has stopped at the first sentence of Tradition Four. Picture a small town with two meetings. The big one meets Monday; the small one, eight people who started it so a few women had a room of their own, meets Thursday. The big group's business meeting votes to add a Thursday night, same hour, two blocks away, because the coffee is better there and more people would come. Nobody calls the Thursday group. Within two months the small room is down to three and closes. The big group did nothing outside its own affairs, and it still did harm. The Long Form's second sentence (Big Book, p. 563) was written for exactly this: "But when its plans concern the welfare of neighboring groups also, those groups ought to be consulted." Consulted means asked first, as equals; not permission, not a vote by anyone above them. The Big Book gives the reason the courtesy matters (p. 561): "We alcoholics see that we must work together and hang together, else most of us will finally die alone." The drunk who needed that Thursday room is the one who pays. Test it tonight: before your group changes its time, place or format, ask which other group it will touch, and call them.

d5ebf3743dd1.t: A group can stay inside its own affairs and still close its neighbour's door. Has my group asked the groups nearby before changing anything?

cad486b890c0.t: April 25 — "One Group's Yes." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. One group cannot say yes for A.A., and that is exactly the yes outside programs come loo

bf10a62e4706.t: One group cannot say yes for A.A., and that is exactly the yes outside programs come looking for. A treatment program wants A.A. on its brochure. It asks one friendly group to meet in its building, on its night, and to let it tell families that A.A. is part of its care. One group agrees. Look at what was decided. The public now reads A.A. as a piece of that program. Every other group in town is asked why it won't do the same. That plan greatly affects A.A. as a whole, which the Long Form says no group may take on alone without conferring with A.A.'s trustees, and it ends (Big Book, p. 563): "On such issues our common welfare is paramount." Paramount means first, above everything else. Bill W. had already drawn the line in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A." And: "we cannot link the A.A. name to other enterprises in the alcohol field to the extent that the public gets the impression we have abandoned our sole aim." A group's freedom covers its own meeting, never the name every group shares. Test it tonight: ask whether any brochure or website lists your meeting as part of somebody's program.

dd7832af789c.t: A group may run its own meeting, but it cannot lend out the name every group shares. Has my group said yes to something on behalf of all of A.A.?

806e368f4503.t: April 26 — "Preoccupied With Their Own Affairs." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. A group's freedom has a back door, and A.A. nearly lost its own offic

d5a295e46735.t: A group's freedom has a back door, and A.A. nearly lost its own office through it. As the Fellowship grew in the 1940s, the New York office answered the letters, printed the literature and kept the directory of groups, work done for every group at once. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "Many groups, preoccupied with their own affairs, failed to help us at all. Less than half of them contributed anything." Book sales covered the gap: "Without this book income we would have folded up entirely." Each of those groups was within its rights, because nobody can make a group give. But the Long Form does not end on a group's rights. Its last sentence (Big Book, p. 563): "On such issues our common welfare is paramount." The issues are the ones that touch neighbouring groups and A.A. as a whole, and an office that answers the drunk's letter is one of them. A group that runs its own meeting well while the line that brings the next drunk in goes unpaid has read half of Tradition Four. Today the back door looks the same: a healthy basket that never goes past the group's own rent and coffee, while the phone line, the meeting list and the office are left to someone else. Test it tonight: ask where your group's money goes after the rent.

0b4dd6a544c4.t: The groups had every right to keep their money, and the office that answered the drunks nearly folded. Does any of my group's basket reach past our own room?

640688151027.t: April 27 — "Directly Accountable." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Conferring with the trustees was never meant to be asking a boss, because A.A. went

6ff7a2b6095d.t: Conferring with the trustees was never meant to be asking a boss, because A.A. went on to make its trustees answer to the groups. When the Long Form was first printed in 1946, the trustees were, in Bill's later words, an independent body. The Long Form still told every group, committee and member to confer with them before acting for A.A. as a whole, because someone had to hold the whole in view. Then the groups built a way for their own voice to reach that board: delegates elected out of their own assemblies, meeting as a conference. Bill W. described where it ended (A.A. Comes of Age): "Even our Trustees, once an independent body, are today directly accountable to our fellowship. They are the caretakers and expediters of our world services." Expediters are the people who see that the work gets done. And the line that holds it together: "It is in this spirit of service that we elect the A.A. groups’ informal rotating committees, the Intergroup Associations of the area, and the General Service Conference for A.A. as a whole." The chain runs up from the groups by election and answers back down. Test it tonight: ask whether your group elects someone to carry its voice to the area, and what they last carried.

91dbcc7dc150.t: April 28 — "Never Acts of Government." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. The Traditions bind groups by agreement, not by force, and today they are somet

fdc542597e2a.t: The Traditions bind groups by agreement, not by force, and today they are sometimes used as a rulebook to punish the very groups they protect. The Big Book's foreword says how they took hold (p. xix): "Though none of these principles had the force of rules or laws, they had become so widely accepted by 1950 that they were confirmed by our first International Conference held at Cleveland." Accepted, not imposed. When A.A. built a conference to serve the whole Fellowship, it wrote the same limit into its charter, its founding rules (A.A. Comes of Age): "though the Conference may act for the service of Alcoholics Anonymous, it shall never perform any acts of government". If the conference that speaks for all of A.A. may never govern, nothing smaller may either. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) leaves each group's own affairs to "no other authority than its own conscience." Today the threat comes dressed as the Traditions: a committee that drops a group from the meeting list for reading the wrong thing, a member who threatens a group with A.A. headquarters, a program that tells a group it is breaking a Tradition and must change. Persuasion is welcome. Punishment is government. Test it tonight: if anyone tells your group it will lose something for breaking a Tradition, ask who gave them the power to take it.

a8b5569075a6.t: The Traditions took hold because groups agreed to them, never because anyone could enforce them. Who has threatened my group in the Traditions' name?

15e469ed82e5.t: April 29 — "Voted Away." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. A group can give away its autonomy by its own vote, and it usually does it to be helpful. Pic

7e6133ae0246.t: A group can give away its autonomy by its own vote, and it usually does it to be helpful. Picture a group that meets in a facility's lounge because the rent is free. The staff ask for small things, one at a time. A sign-in sheet, so they know who was in the building. Only the facility's handouts on the table. End ten minutes early for the count. A staff member sits at the back, just to listen. Each time the group votes yes, to keep the room. A year later the facility's rules are the meeting, and nobody remembers deciding that. Every one of those votes was the group's right, and together they spent the right. The Long Form says a group's affairs answer to "no other authority than its own conscience" (Big Book, p. 563), and a group that votes in another authority has made itself a guest. Bill W. listed what A.A. does without (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 37): "no fees, no dues, no rules and regulations, no demand that alcoholics conform to A.A. principles, no one set in personal authority over anyone else." A free room that comes with an authority attached is not free. Test it tonight: list the rules your meeting follows, and mark the ones your members actually chose.

0b8897e488b7.t: April 3 — "No Other Authority." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Tradition Four is about who runs a group's business, and the rumour that it means what

7e3996a981fb.t: Tradition Four is about who runs a group's business, and the rumour that it means what happens in this meeting stays in this meeting hides exactly that. Read the Long Form before anyone explains it to you (Big Book, p. 563): "With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." There is nothing in it about secrets. A group's own affairs are its business: the time, the place, the format, the money, who serves and for how long. The Big Book's own history of the Traditions says it in five words (Big Book, p. xix): "each group was to be autonomous". Autonomous means self-governing: the group makes its own decisions and answers for them. Whatever a room decides about privacy, that is not what this sentence is about. When Four is taught as a rule about keeping quiet, a room learns to keep quiet and never learns that it can vote. Then whoever actually runs the meeting, a facility, its staff or one strong old-timer, never has to face a group conscience at all. Today the slogan is read aloud at the close of meetings that have never once held a business meeting. Test it tonight: ask someone in your room what Tradition Four says, then show them page 563.

5811ab320663.t: Tradition Four gives each group the power to run its own business; it is not a rule about keeping quiet. Does my group know it can vote?

0dfc7ade2097.t: April 30 — "Continuous Effectiveness." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. April ends where Tradition Four starts: each group governs its own business, an

352a7a1cbe6c.t: April ends where Tradition Four starts: each group governs its own business, and whatever takes that away has captured the group, however kindly. The Big Book puts the stakes plainly in its essay on the Traditions (p. 561): "Therefore, no society of men and women ever had a more urgent need for continuous effectiveness and permanent unity." Effectiveness means a group that keeps working; unity means one that stays whole. Read the whole Tradition with that in mind (Big Book, p. 563). A group answers to "no other authority than its own conscience" in its own affairs. It consults its neighbours when its plans touch them. It takes no action for A.A. as a whole alone. And on those issues "our common welfare is paramount." Four sentences, and every one of them is about how groups decide, not how members behave. Capture rarely comes as a takeover. It comes as convenience: a facility that sets the format, a program that supplies the chair, an office that sends instructions, a group that stops meeting to decide anything because someone else always has. Each one quietly ends a group's self-government. May turns to Tradition Five, the one purpose every group's decisions exist for: the drunk still drinking. Test it tonight: ask your group to hold a business meeting this month, and see who comes to decide.

48e40559c444.t: April 4 — "Nobody Was Asked." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. A group can lose Tradition Four without anyone taking it, simply by never using it. Pict

de24461fb2ae.t: A group can lose Tradition Four without anyone taking it, simply by never using it. Picture a Tuesday night meeting that has run the same way for six years. Same opening, same readings, same man at the front, because nobody else put a hand up. Nobody remembers a business meeting. When the coffee money runs short he covers it, and when the format needs changing he changes it. Nobody objects, and nobody was asked. The Long Form gives the group the decision, and the group has stopped making it. A conscience that never meets can't decide anything, so the decisions slide to whoever is willing to make them. Bill W. described how groups were meant to work (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "They prefer rotating committees to handle their simple affairs. These committees are invariably regarded as servants — they have only the authorization to serve, never to command. Each committee carries out what it believes to be the wishes of its group." Rotating means the job passes on. The wishes of the group: someone has to ask the group for them. Today this quiet drift is the most common way a free room ends up run by one person or by one facility, because the members never claimed what was theirs. Test it tonight: ask when your group last held a business meeting, and when anyone last rotated out.

d555fb6c18c9.t: April 5 — "The Sheet on the Table." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. When a facility hands a meeting its rules, the group has a boss, and Tradition Fou

bc1b4964e85a.t: When a facility hands a meeting its rules, the group has a boss, and Tradition Four says a group has none. It happens politely. A sheet is taped to the table: start and end times, no crosstalk, clients sign in, staff choose the chair, no meeting over the holidays. Some of it may even be sensible. But the members never voted on any of it, and none of them can change it. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "With respect to its own affairs, each A.A. group should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience." Its own conscience, not the building's policy manual. Bill W. wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "Nowhere in A.A. is there to be seen any constituted human authority that can compel an A.A. group to do anything." Constituted means officially set up, with power. A.A. has no such authority anywhere, not even at its own headquarters. A facility that writes a meeting's rules has become exactly that authority, from outside. A room that can't change its own format isn't running its own affairs; it is being run. Test it tonight: find any rule read out or posted at your meeting, and ask when the group voted for it.

2609edd46d9a.t: The threat that runs the other way from chaos is hardening: a group, or a whole fellowship, deciding there is only one right way to run a meeting and making it law. Bill W. saw it coming (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 5): "Should we ever harden too much, the letter might crush that spirit. We could victimize ourselves by petty rules and prohibitions; we could imagine that we had said the last word." The letter means the written rule; the spirit is what the rule was for. Tradition Four is the guard against it. Because the Long Form makes each group answer to its own conscience on its own affairs, no group can be forced into another group's format, and no outside body can hand down the approved one. A.A. stays alive because each group can try something, keep what works, and drop what doesn't. Freeze every group into one script and nobody can find a better way again. Today the hardening usually arrives from outside, as a standard format a program uses in all its meetings, read word for word everywhere, with a warning not to change it. Inside, it can look like loyalty: the way we have always done it. Test it tonight: ask whether your group could change one thing about its meeting next week, and who would have to agree.

ea8b02810ede.t: Bill warned that the letter of a rule could crush the spirit it was written for. Could my group change its own format if it wanted to?

56eb65d5c629.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 4 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 5 (Bill W.'s foreword, 1955).

1b6393439047.t: April 7 — "A Town-Meeting Democracy." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Before anyone wrote Tradition Four, the groups had already found out that a room

1024270d1cb1.t: Before anyone wrote Tradition Four, the groups had already found out that a room of drunks has to govern itself, and that it does it by vote. Bill W. told how it happened (A.A. Comes of Age). First came freedom: "We cannot be compelled to do anything. In that sense this society is a benign anarchy." Anarchy means no government; benign means kindly. Then the groups had to act: find a room, pay the rent, open the door on time. Freedom alone didn't get that done. "As the old-timers retired, we began to elect our servants by majority vote. Each group in this sense became a town-meeting democracy." A town meeting is where the people who live there show up, argue and vote, and nobody above them decides. That is what a group conscience looks like in practice: the members in a room, with a motion and a show of hands. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) put it in one sentence: each group is responsible "to no other authority than its own conscience." The old-timers stepping back made room for it. Today the old-timers are often replaced by staff, who never retire from the room, because the room is their job. Test it tonight: ask who your group elected to serve it, and when.

d5424901fd6a.t: The groups learned to govern themselves like a town meeting, by electing their servants. Who did my group elect, and could it elect someone else?

090a283bf74a.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 4 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (benign anarchy and town-meeting democracy).

c6b8078a5766.t: April 8 — "Those Groups Ought to Be Consulted." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. Tradition Four gives a group the run of its own affairs and, in the ne

53bf20028dea.t: Those Groups Ought to Be Consulted

0f46946d9d34.t: Tradition Four gives a group the run of its own affairs and, in the next sentence, draws the edge of them. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "But when its plans concern the welfare of neighboring groups also, those groups ought to be consulted." Neighboring groups are the other A.A. groups in your town. Consulted means asked before, not told after. The rumour says autonomy means a group can do anything it likes. The Book says: anything with its own affairs, and when its plans reach into other groups' affairs, it asks them. Bill W. described how areas learned this (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 22): "Every area, sooner or later, realizes that such concerns as intergroup meetings, hospital arrangements, local public relations, a central office for interviews and information, are things in which every A.A. is interested". An intergroup is a committee the groups of an area set up to handle what they share. Today the edge gets lost when a group moves its hour onto a neighbor's, or opens a meeting across the street from one that is struggling, and nobody calls. And where a program's meetings fill the town, there may be no free groups left nearby to ask. Test it tonight: ask whether your group knows the other groups in your town, and whether anyone asked them before your group's last big change.

9bb03b3292a8.t: A group's own affairs end where another group's begin, and there it asks first. Does my group know the groups around it?

50acf2037a76.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 4 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 22 (Bill W., on clubs and central committees).

c03da763bc0c.t: April 9 — "Rule No. 62." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 4: Each group should be autonomous except in matters affecting other groups or A.A. as a whole. A group's right to run its own affairs includes the right to run them into the ground, and A.

6340c1642f87.t: A group's right to run its own affairs includes the right to run them into the ground, and A.A. kept that right on purpose. Bill W. told the story (A.A. Comes of Age). In one town a newly sober promoter sold his group on a building: a club, a meeting room, a clinic, a loan office upstairs, three corporations and "sixty-one rules, regulations, and by-laws". Members who disagreed wrote to New York. The answer was that "each A.A. group could manage its own affairs as it liked, provided it did not harm surrounding groups." Headquarters warned them anyway, and then: "As it had a right to, this very autonomous group ignored our warnings." It crashed. Afterward the promoter mailed every group a card headed Rule No. 62, which read: "Don't take yourself too damned seriously." Bill's verdict: "Thus, under Tradition Four, an A.A. group had exercised its right to be wrong." The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) leaves a group its own conscience, even a mistaken one. Notice who did not step in: New York. Nobody rescued that group by taking it over, so the group learned. Today a group in trouble is offered rescue by a program that will run it from then on. Test it tonight: if your group made a bad call, ask who would fix it, the members or someone from outside.

3a4c95693564.t: A.A. let a group make a mess of its own affairs rather than take them over. If my group got something badly wrong, who would put it right?

11a22222b752.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 4 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Tradition Four: the right to be wrong).

a3be3e3fa90e.t: August 1 — "The Shingle." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Twelfth Step work is one drunk sitting with another, talking him through

432726fff0ba.t: Twelfth Step work is one drunk sitting with another, talking him through getting sober. It is the engine of the whole program, and it has never cost a nickel. Now imagine a member who is good at it — years sober, dozens of people carried through, a real gift for the work. He rents a small office and hangs out his shingle: the little sign a doctor or a lawyer puts up to announce a practice. Nothing about it is illegal, and the people who come to him get better. Bill W. wrote that sign himself. In <0>A.A. Tradition — How It Developed</0>, he imagined the door and the exact words on it: "Bill W. — Alcoholics Anonymous Therapist. Charges $10.00 per hour." Then he named the thing plainly: "That would be face-to-face treatment of alcoholism for a fee." Then came the verdict this whole month turns on: "It would be quite legal, but hardly ethical." Legal was never the bar. A man with a rate card has a fee schedule, a caseload, a livelihood — he has something to lose. And what A.A. had to give him was a man with nothing to sell.

af5976c3d89f.t: Bill drew the sign himself, priced it, and called it legal but not ethical. What changes in a conversation the moment one person is being paid to have it?

5a654c6fe73d.t: Grounded in: P-17; long form, Tradition 8.

3ab4da54e46c.t: August 10 — "Old Tom Was Right." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. The old clubhouse on Twenty-Fourth Street was a mess. Volunteers p

19631ef4d60a.t: The old clubhouse on Twenty-Fourth Street was a mess. Volunteers painted it, answered the phone, then went home. The place stayed filthy. Drunks slept in it at all hours, in every condition. Bill W. wrote: "Plainly enough we needed a caretaker." So they went after Tom, a retired fireman with a pension — no leverage, they figured. They offered him a nice room. Seven days a week. Make the coffee, walk out the bad ones, sweep the place. Tom listened to the whole pitch and said what you would say: what you guys want is a janitor. They agreed that they did. Then Tom asked whether they were going to pay him anything, and A.A. — young, frightened, and very sure of itself — said no, because "that would make you a professional. This is Alcoholics Anonymous. We must not mix money with spirituality." Tom's reply is one of the most useful sentences in our literature: "no money, no work. I'm doing my Twelfth Step work free, but if you're going to have me here as a janitor, you're going to pay me, see?" There it is — the whole Tradition, from a man with a broom, years before anyone wrote it down. He would carry the message for nothing, forever. He would not sweep the floor for nothing. Bill's verdict, written long after they had haggled the old man down to the last cent: "But old Tom was right. In order for A.A. to function, we had to hire some help."

f89edc2cb51f.t: Tom drew the line himself: the message free, the broom paid. What am I asking someone to do for free that I would never do for free myself?

cb434542f9a5.t: Grounded in: AA Comes of Age (old Tom and the clubhouse); long form, Tradition 8.

dee5250f1d15.t: August 11 — "The Sponsor Who Bills." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Picture a sponsor who starts charging. It begins reasonably —

9ba463acc76c.t: Picture a sponsor who starts charging. It begins reasonably — his time is real, he's been at this twenty years, and the men he takes through the Steps get sober. So there is a monthly figure now, and a schedule, and a message saying he can fit you in Thursday. Watch what it does, because it does not change a single word that gets said. It changes who is sitting in the chair. A sponsee is a man you can tell the truth to; you have nothing to lose by losing him. A client is a man you can lose. And a man you can lose is a man you must control. The harsh truth gets softened. The conversation that belonged to the sponsee starts serving the sponsor. The relationship has acquired an interest, and an interest bends everything it touches — including whether he ever tells you it is there. A.A. drew this line early. Its pamphlet on the Traditions, P-43, says it became clear to the first members that no A.A. should ever ask or accept payment for "carrying this message to somebody else, person to person and face to face." That is what sponsorship is. There is no version of it with an invoice attached: no company the sponsor answers to, no outside organisation with a stake in what he tells you.

67d03283c0af.t: A sponsor has nothing to lose by losing you, which is the only reason he can afford to tell you the truth. Who in my life is free enough to say the thing I do not want to hear?

851f67b641db.t: Grounded in: P-43; long form, Tradition 8; AA Comes of Age.

08b08a2cf403.t: August 12 — "The Certified Audit." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Sooner or later you will hear that somebody, somewhere, is makin

2ac97505964f.t: Sooner or later you will hear that somebody, somewhere, is making money off A.A. This was a real concern before the Traditions existed. Tradition 8 clearly states: A.A. stays "forever nonprofessional." Nobody is ever paid for Twelfth Step work — carrying the message to the drunk still drinking. It breaks the moment the message itself is sold. Even the A.A. founders were once on trial for it. Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers reports: "In 1942, a story got around Cleveland that the New York office and the Big Book were nothing but a racket." After a thinly attended dinner, the local group chairmen led Bill W. and Dr. Bob into a hotel parlor where a lawyer and an accountant waited. The claim: the two founders had split $64,000. Bill wrote (A.A. Comes of Age) that he "happened to have with me a certified audit of all of our affairs from the beginning." The books showed the money ran the office. No alcoholic had ever been charged for help. Dr. Bob was living on thirty dollars a week and had never taken a royalty. The committee apologized. Bill's own verdict: "This was one of the test cases out of which A.A.'s Tradition respecting professionalism and paid workers was evolved."

6e780c164463.t: Somebody first carried the message to me. Was that the Twelfth Step — one drunk, free, wanting nothing — or was somebody being paid to bring me here?

6bc075b89049.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (the Cleveland rumors); AA Comes of Age (the audit; the test cases).

18e461308b08.t: August 13 — "The Bio Line." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Three weeks in, you will meet them online if you have not already: the

74d190e36939.t: Three weeks in, you will meet them online if you have not already: the recovery coach, the sober companion, the mentor with a monthly rate — and, set quietly in the bio like a licence, the years in the rooms. The membership is the marketing, because it works: a frightened family choosing where to send money will choose the one who has been where their son is. A.A. saw this exact sale coming and used its flattest language on it. Bill W. wrote (A.A. pamphlet P-17): "no one ought to advertise himself as an A.A. therapist. As we are strictly amateur there can be no such thing." Not should not — cannot. A.A. licenses nobody and certifies nobody, so an A.A. credential offered for sale is a thing that does not exist, being sold anyway. And what is actually on the price tag is not the coach's skill, which may be real. Bill named it while imagining his own shingle: "And I would surely be trading on the name of Alcoholics Anonymous, a purely amateur organization, to enlarge my professional practice." The name was built over ninety years by people who were paid nothing to build it. Selfishness cloaked as spiritual enlightenment may benefit those doing it, but A.A. pays the price.

6882f6f227fe.t: Being an A.A. member is not a qualification — A.A. says there is no such thing. Have I ever trusted someone, or paid someone, just because they said they were one of us?

c5d0dba1b39f.t: Grounded in: P-17 (no such thing as an A.A. therapist; trading on the name).

cc2c90024e74.t: August 14 — "The Almost-Right Argument." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Some A.A. towns have a small office with one paid worker.

1dbbdade5568.t: Some A.A. towns have a small office with one paid worker. She answers the phone, keeps the meeting list current, and tells a shaky stranger where tonight's meeting is. Now imagine the group's business meeting. Somebody stands up with the Tradition in hand and yells: "She talks to alcoholics all day, that is Twelfth Step work, and Twelfth Step work is never paid!" Nobody is being selfish; the room believes it is protecting A.A. The vote passes, the paid worker is let go, and within a year the phone is a recording. The fight is older than the Tradition. Bill W. wrote down the shout as he heard it (A.A. Comes of Age): "Professionalism! That guy is making money out of A.A.!" And he recorded what nobody checked: not one of the accused had been "hired to do A.A.'s Twelfth Step work." P-43, A.A.'s own pamphlet, asks the question straight and answers it: "but are these A.A.'s then being paid for doing Twelfth Step work? No. In the office, they are just paving the way for this work." Answering the phone is not carrying the message — it is what makes carrying it possible. The group meant to protect the Tradition and broke it instead: a stranger called, and nobody was there.

d8fa1943c512.t: They quoted the Tradition word for word and still broke it, and a stranger got a recording. Where am I defending something in a way that is destroying it?

dece40f6e8d8.t: Grounded in: AA Comes of Age (the cry of professionalism); P-43 (paving the way).

a4744989eadf.t: August 15 — "A Billing Code." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. There is now a version of the conversation that is being invoiced. No

fd4cbeba0811.t: There is now a version of the conversation that is being invoiced. Not inside A.A. — outside it, where the hour a sober alcoholic spends with a struggling alcoholic is given a code and a rate, so that somewhere a third party can be billed for it. Watch what the mechanism does, because it needs no villain. The moment the hour is billable, the payer needs to know what happened in it, so the hour acquires paperwork. The paperwork needs goals, so the hour acquires a curriculum. The rate needs justifying, so the hour acquires outcomes — and the outcomes belong to whoever pays, which is never the drunk. Nothing about the two people in the room has changed, and everything about the hour has: it answers upward now. A.A. put its refusal of all this into one line of P-43, its pamphlet on the Traditions: "The meaning of Twelfth Step work cannot be measured in money" — because what actually changes hands in that hour is "of far greater worth — our very lives." A price does not simply pay for the hour. It measures it, and a measured hour ends up serving whoever holds the ruler. The free hour serves the man who needs it, because it cannot serve anything else.

3fcc3506b2d1.t: The billed hour answers to whoever pays for it; the free hour cannot answer to anything but the drunk in front of it. Which of my hours answer upward?

c24c23941826.t: Grounded in: P-43 (the meaning of Twelfth Step work); long form, Tradition 8.

11413777debd.t: August 16 — "Members Sold It First." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. The first people to sell recovery with A.A.'s name on it were

901ac84aae9a.t: The first people to sell recovery with A.A.'s name on it were A.A. members. That is not an outside accusation; it is the Fellowship's own record of the years after the Saturday Evening Post article of March 1941 made it famous. Membership jumped by thousands within the year, and the pins on the office wall map showed scores of new groups a week — most with no experienced member in them, nothing to steer by but the book and the mail. Into that vacuum came trouble: committees quarreled, orators held forth, groups split wide open, whole groups got drunk. And then the worst of it — Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age) that some members turned professional, "selling A.A. therapy for money to new prospects." His summary of the era: "Such was the beginning of a truly frightening experience that lasted a long time." Hold on to what that means. The threat this Tradition answers was never an invading industry; in 1941 there was no recovery industry to invade. The discovery was simpler and worse: when A.A. spreads faster than its principles, somebody inside will try to sell it — before any outsider ever does. The Tradition is not a wall built against outsiders. It is a mirror, written by people who had watched themselves.

a750a28186b6.t: August 17 — "The Deluge." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. When the Saturday Evening Post told America about A.A. in March 1941, the

0c070289c19e.t: When the Saturday Evening Post told America about A.A. in March 1941, the mail arrived like weather. Pleas for help, first in hundreds, then thousands, hit the little New York office — each one a drunk, or a drunk's wife, asking what to do tonight. The members did what members do: rounded up every A.A. woman and A.A. wife who could type and turned the floor above the Twenty-Fourth Street clubhouse into an emergency headquarters. It was not enough. The volunteers were tempted toward form letters, and the office refused, for a reason Bill W. set down (A.A. Comes of Age): "A warm personal communication must be sent to every prospect and his family." A dying man does not answer a circular. But the flood outlasted every free evening the members had, and Bill recorded the surrender: the correspondence had grown so great that "we saw we would have to have permanent paid help. Volunteers could not handle the situation." The groups were asked for a dollar per member per year, and, Bill wrote, "we were able to add two regular paid workers to the staff." Look hard at what was bought: typing. Two office workers, hired by A.A.'s own office, to answer mail. Basic labor, paid an honest wage — so the message inside the letters could stay free. It still works that way.

b873e9939cc9.t: Help was hired to manage the calls, but a phone answered is not our message carried. Am I soaking up the benefits without carrying them to those still suffering? The still-suffering who don't know there is a way out have no number to call.

dbf08cc43c29.t: Grounded in: AA Comes of Age (the Post deluge; the first paid workers).

5b3af99e8e5e.t: August 18 — "Nothing to Gain." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. The message that reached us was free. Nobody billed us for the conve

a7c66bc87e8f.t: The message that reached us was free. Nobody billed us for the conversation that saved our lives — and that is not a small detail; it is why we could trust it. The one talking had nothing to gain. The Big Book gives every group one purpose (p. 563): "that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Tradition 8 keeps that purpose spiritually clean. If carrying the message could become a living, the program would slowly become a business, and the drunk who still suffers would become a customer. So the Fellowship decided its most valuable work would never have a price. What was given to us free, we keep only by giving free. The moment we look for a return — money, credit, a following, even applause — we have stopped carrying the message and started charging for it, in our own currency. The foundation stays spiritual because the motive stays clean. And the motive stays clean because there is nothing to gain.

edda06c852da.t: August 19 — "It Was Never Complicated." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Tradition 8 says A.A. stays "forever nonprofessional" (Big

37958d63b6b4.t: Tradition 8 says A.A. stays "forever nonprofessional" (Big Book, p. 561). Two words, and both mean exactly what they mean everywhere else. Nonprofessional: not a job. Not a career, not a practice, not a billing code, not a program fee. Nobody in A.A. is ever paid to help you, and nobody who is paid to help you is doing A.A. Forever: not until the field matures, not until licensing improves, not until somebody builds a respectful business model. Forever. That is the whole Tradition, and a newcomer can hold it after one reading. So notice how much work has gone into making it confusing — the essays, the seminars, the professionals explaining that it is more nuanced than it looks. It is not. A line this simple only gets complicated by people standing on the wrong side of it, because a clear rule leaves nothing to hide behind and a muddy one pays. Here is the pocket test, free forever: is anyone being paid for this conversation about my drinking? If yes, whatever this is, it is not A.A. It may be fine. It may even be medicine. But it is not us — and no one may tell you it is.

4dbd2561533e.t: The Tradition fits in two words, and the test fits in one question: is anyone being paid for this conversation? Who benefits when something this simple gets complicated?

fd074628d6c3.t: August 2 — "The Night They Told Him No." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. It is 1937. Bill is broke, Lois is working at the departme

a210879feaef.t: The Night They Told Him No

3fe7ed173cec.t: It is 1937. Bill is broke, Lois is working at the department store, and their house on Clinton Street is full of drunks who are not paying board. Charlie Towns — who owns the hospital where Bill got sober — calls him in and makes him an offer: "I'll give you an office, a decent drawing account, and a very healthy slice of the profits. What I propose is perfectly ethical." Then the closer: "You can become a lay therapist, and more successful than anybody in the business." Bill never pretended he was above it: "There was nothing wrong whatever with becoming a lay therapist." He thought of Lois. He thought of his creditors. On the subway home a verse arrived like guidance — "The laborer is worthy of his hire" — and his mind was made up. Then he told the group. They sat there. Then one of them found his footing: "You tell us that Charlie's proposal is ethical. Sure, it's ethical. But what we've got won't run on ethics only; it has to be better." And finally: "This is a matter of life and death, Bill, and nothing but the very best will do." Someone reminded him of his own line — "sometimes the good is the enemy of the best." Bill wrote afterward that the members deciding together had outranked his own guidance: "Thus spoke the group conscience. The group was right and I was wrong; the voice on the subway was not the voice of God." The office was never rented. Tradition 8 is not an idea somebody had. It is the scar from that living room.

a698c01caa2d.t: The offer was ethical, and the group told him ethical was not the bar. When has the good thing been the enemy of the best thing, in my life?

88e3c94da6ff.t: August 20 — "Included in the Price." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. A.A. looked at owning treatment beds and refused, in writing.

6384100a9e4c.t: A.A. looked at owning treatment beds and refused, in writing. Bill W. put it plainly (A.A. pamphlet P-17): "Years ago we used to think A.A. should have its own hospitals, rest homes and farms. Nowadays we are equally convinced we should have nothing of the sort." Care belongs to doctors; A.A. keeps nothing it could sell. But refusing to own beds did not stop the beds from selling A.A. A facility charges tens of thousands for a stay, and part of what is inside is A.A. itself: the meeting on the schedule, the chairs in a circle, the Steps on the wall — the same thing your town holds for free every night of the week. The invoice never says A.A. It does not have to. Everything inside the walls is included in the price. And hold on to this rule, because it works in every country and under every system: if someone is being paid, then someone is paying. The drunk, his family, an insurer, or every taxpayer at once — even when nobody sees a bill, recovery money is buying what A.A. gives away. So the man discharged after thirty days has learned the price of a meeting, and it is not a dollar. He was sold a free thing. A.A. never saw a cent, and never wanted one.

c22637b7446d.t: August 22 — "Advance Pay." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Here is why no bill has ever followed a Twelfth Step call: the work was

07b28a581787.t: Here is why no bill has ever followed a Twelfth Step call: the work was paid for before it happened. P-43, A.A.'s pamphlet on the Traditions, says we should not tell ourselves how noble we are for working without pay, because "we have received advance pay for it" — and it names the coin: our very lives. Read that twice. The man who sits with you tonight did not waive his fee. He collected it years ago, the night somebody sat with him and he lived. Every call he takes now is him settling up, and the debt only moves one direction — forward, to you, and one day through you. That is why nobody in A.A. can ever charge for carrying the message: it would be billing twice for a life already bought. The Tradition is not asking members for charity. It is keeping their books honest.

eac8aa0ffc34.t: Dr. Bob, co-founder of A.A., gave his sober years to drunks, and in his Big Book story he wrote down exactly why (p. 181): "1. Sense of duty. 2. It is a pleasure. 3. a8b531cc436b.t: The Big Book names recovery's load-bearing wall (p. 97): "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery." 31eae8eea835.t: Before there was a Tradition, there was a phone call. Akron, May 1935: Bill W., months sober, a failed business trip, a hotel lobby with a bar at one end getting louder. He knew what was coming. And his answer was not to find a professional — there were none for this. It was to find a drunk to help, because helping was the only thing that had ever kept the craving off. The calls led to a doctor named Bob who did not want to meet him. Fifteen minutes, Dr. Bob said. They talked for hours, and A.A. began — not with a treatment, with two men who needed each other exactly even. Hold that lobby in mind all month. A.A. was not founded by an expert offering a service. It was founded by a sick man looking for another sick man, for free, to save himself. Tradition 8 protects the founding act. There has never been anything to sell, because the need has always run both ways.

a287ed10358c.t: A.A. Comes of Age reaches for an old line because nothing newer says it as well: "Freely you have received, freely give." 8d6cc1d16b65.t: August 3 — "Nobody Can Charge You." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Nobody in A.A. can charge you. Not for the meeting, not for the

35c7413edc61.t: Nobody in A.A. can charge you. Not for the meeting, not for the coffee, not for the man who drives across town at two in the morning to sit on your bathroom floor. That is not good manners or generosity — it is written down, and Tradition 8 is where. It had to be written because money kept turning up anyway, and A.A. needed to say exactly what it was refusing. The Tradition itself settles it in ten words. It says: "We define professionalism as the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire." Charging a drunk for counsel. That is the whole of what the word means here — and it does not mean paid work in general. A.A. hires people to answer its phones, keep its books and mail literature into prisons, and pays them properly for it. Members mix those two things up constantly, and Bill W. did not pretend otherwise. He said: "On this subject we have all done a pile of fuzzy thinking. And I would be one of the first to plead guilty to that charge." He also said the cause was not greed: "The reason for our fuzzy thinking is the usual one — it is fear." Fear of losing the one thing that finally worked, which is fair enough — but fear without the definition just makes suspects of the people doing the unglamorous jobs.

c655a0cbaab6.t: You will never be charged for help in A.A., and the people who answer its phones are paid a fair wage. Both of those are Tradition 8. Where have I let a word I never checked decide what I think of someone?

47d1a627633a.t: August 30 — "Millions Would Have Ruined Us." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. In 1937 A.A. nearly became an industry on purpose. Eig

ecbc62793b4e.t: In 1937 A.A. nearly became an industry on purpose. Eighteen members met in Akron and voted for paid workers and A.A.-owned hospitals, and Bill W. was sent to New York to raise the money (A.A. pamphlet P-44): "This would require considerable money — millions perhaps." The rich men said no. The hospitals were never built, the missionaries never hired, and the young Fellowship stayed broke, unpaid, and unowned. Years later Bill wrote the verdict: "We didn't know that millions would have ruined us even more than no money at all." Ruined — his word, about getting funded. A paid A.A. would have been an agency with clients, and an agency can die of a budget. A fellowship of unpaid drunks cannot, because there is nothing to cut. Tradition 8 is that lucky escape written down, so luck would never be needed again.

5d4d06b63a1f.t: The best break A.A. ever caught was not getting the money. What no turned out to save me?

258d6568ef9c.t: Grounded in: P-44 (the Akron vote; millions would have ruined us).

0f136da0de9b.t: August 31 — "Read It Again." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. End the month where it started, because the Tradition never needed hel

3ec939f535ca.t: End the month where it started, because the Tradition never needed help — only reading. Alcoholics Anonymous is forever nonprofessional, and the long form closes with a bookend nobody can pry loose: our Twelfth Step "work is never to be paid for." Forever, and never — two absolute words from a Fellowship famously gentle about absolutes. It is not gentle here. A month of history says why: everything carrying the message runs on — the trust, the medicine, the debt, the foundation — dies in the presence of a price. So leave with the test that fits in a pocket: is anyone being paid for this conversation about my drinking? Then it is not A.A. Nobody sober is above that rule, nobody desperate is below it, and nobody anywhere holds a license to bend it, because no license exists. Two words were always enough. Forever. Nonprofessional.

2fc0b0cb8010.t: Forever and never — the Tradition's two absolute words. Do I treat them as absolutes?

cf395d634dc5.t: Grounded in: Big Book, long form, Tradition 8 (pp. 563–566).
