bbd3457b66e5.t: August 4 — "A Definition, Not a Mood." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Almost nothing written about this Tradition does the first t

ede22fb9cd08.t: Almost nothing written about this Tradition does the first thing the Long Form does: define the word. It says: "We define professionalism as the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire." Ten words, doing two jobs. First, they give you a test you can actually run. Take any arrangement and ask one question — is a drunk being charged a fee to be counselled? The paid office secretary, no. The counsellor with a rate card, yes. Second, and this is the part people walk straight past: those same ten words describe every arrangement where a drunk is helped for money — the counsellor's office, the clinic, the treatment centre, the drying-out house with a bill at the end of the week. A.A. wrote down, in plain commercial language, the exact thing it had nearly voted to become, and refused it permanently. That is what "should remain forever nonprofessional" is attached to. And because the definition is precise, it protects the innocent too: anything that is not charging alcoholics for counsel is not professionalism, no matter how much money moves around it. Without a definition, every paid janitor is a suspect. With one, the line can be walked in daylight, by anyone.

b79eb4d65745.t: The Tradition names an occupation — fees, hire — not a mood or a motive. Where would I be freer if I knew exactly where the line was?

87d3dab53630.t: August 5 — "The Going Rate." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Imagine a group that solves its Twelfth Step problem with money. Nobod

3f14afad41b4.t: Imagine a group that solves its Twelfth Step problem with money. Nobody wants the 2 a.m. calls — a drunk on the phone who needs somebody to come — so the group votes to pay forty dollars a call to whoever goes. It works immediately. The calls get answered. Now watch the next year, because this mechanism has nothing to do with anyone's motives. A price now exists, so there is a going rate. Which means the man who goes out at 2 a.m. for nothing is no longer a member doing what members do — he is a man working for free in a room where that job pays. He looks like a mug, or an amateur, or someone angling for something. So he stops. Not out of greed. Out of arithmetic. And the newcomer who would have gone next year never starts, because he has learned that carrying the message is a paid position and he has not been hired. A.A. ran this experiment more than once and wrote down the finding: "Every time we have tried to professionalize our Twelfth Step, the result has been exactly the same; our single purpose has been defeated." Not sometimes. Exactly the same. A Fellowship is nothing but people doing for free the one thing that cannot be bought.

8de5a5f8a759.t: Forty dollars a call got the phone answered and quietly ended the free version. What have I stopped doing freely because someone started getting paid for it?

0bd866ea0e20.t: Grounded in: AA Comes of Age (professionalizing the Twelfth Step); long form, Tradition 8.

e9cc400a767d.t: August 6 — "The Sentence That Only Works If It's True." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. P-43, A.A.'s own pamphlet on the Traditions

eb3a57588755.t: The Sentence That Only Works If It's True

5363ada93859.t: P-43, A.A.'s own pamphlet on the Traditions, sets down the sentence a member can say and nobody else on earth can: "No, I'm not a social worker. I don't get paid for talking with you. I'm doing it because it's the best way to stay sober myself." That sentence is the entire product. It disarms the man on the other side of the kitchen table, and for one reason only — it is true. Take a fee and you can still say the words. They are just not true any more. The Big Book named the conditions before there was a Tradition to protect them: what reaches the new prospect is that there are "no fees to pay, no axes to grind, no people to please, no lectures to be endured." Then, a line later, the finding that should end every argument about scaling this work: "None of us makes a sole vocation of this work, nor do we think its effectiveness would be increased if we did." Not that we shouldn't. That it wouldn't work. The unpaid member is not a budget version of the professional. He is a different instrument, and what gives him his power is exactly what a paycheque would remove. A.A.'s service offices do pay people, properly, for real jobs. But for the newcomer a staff member takes to a meeting that night, P-43 is exact about the wage: "they are paid only with their own continuing sobriety."

4a997a7589c8.t: The sentence works only because it is true, and a fee would make it a lie. What can I offer someone precisely because I am not getting anything for it?

6c337525fa11.t: Grounded in: P-43; Big Book, "There Is a Solution" (p. 19); long form, Tradition 8.

9a2260c8ed6c.t: August 7 — "Scaling the Message." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. A Twelfth Step call is one alcoholic answering the phone line, th

dfa0841c64db.t: A Twelfth Step call is one alcoholic answering the phone line, then going out to meet whoever called and doing the work laid out on pages 89 to 103 of the Big Book. There are rarely enough people to go. The calls come at bad hours, the ones who take them get worn out, and the obvious fix is to hire. So imagine A.A. trains a corps of paid carriers — good people, sober people, properly supervised — and sends them out full time. On paper it is better: more calls answered, consistent quality, nobody burning out. The only problem is that A.A. already ran that experiment. Bill W. wrote: "Early in the game we discovered that under no conditions should an A.A. be paid for taking or carrying this message to somebody else, person to person and face to face." Ruled out, permanently. And he wrote what was at stake if that ever changed: "If professionalism ever invaded us at that level, we were doomed." Not weakened. Doomed. The newcomer feels the difference between a man showing up on the clock, and a man whose own sobriety depends on showing up. Everything A.A. has rests on the second man.

b4f92a41ed77.t: Tradition 8 is what keeps the Twelfth Step free: the person who comes to your door is not being paid to be there, and never can be. What have I tried to make more efficient and accidentally made pointless?

00b0eb5f08e5.t: Grounded in: AA Comes of Age (professionalism at the Twelfth-Step level); Big Book, "Working With Others" (pp. 89–103).

bb95a73aaf8e.t: August 8 — "Not a Verdict on Doctors." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. This is where the Tradition gets misused most often — as a s

d63eb058c1f3.t: This is where the Tradition gets misused most often — as a stick to beat professionals with. It is not that, and it never was. Read what A.A. said about itself in its own history, <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>: "at the point of professionalism money and spirituality do not mix." And then, in the very next breath of the same book, the sentence almost nobody quotes: "We do not decry professionalism in other fields, but we accept the sober fact that it does not work for us." That is not a verdict on counsellors, doctors, nurses or therapists. It is a structural finding about one Fellowship, made by that Fellowship, about the one specific thing it does. Surgeons should be paid. Psychiatrists should be paid. The nurse who sat with us on the worst night of our lives should be paid, and paid well — and A.A. says so out loud rather than sniffing at people who take a wage for healing. A.A.'s claim is narrower and stranger: this particular act, one drunk sitting with another, stops working when it is bought. Not because money is dirty, but because the act was never a service being delivered. It was one man staying alive by helping another, and you cannot pay a man to need something. Get it wrong and Tradition 8 curdles into contempt for anyone with a credential. Get it right and it is a Fellowship being honest about the one thing it cannot sell without destroying.

c1558f23db4b.t: A.A. refused professionalism for itself and declined to judge it in anybody else. Where have I turned a limit on myself into a judgement on someone else?

fb72fa371488.t: Grounded in: AA Comes of Age (money and spirituality; other fields).

c8fd3ce4a5ca.t: August 9 — "Volunteers Only." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 8: Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers. Tradition 8 is one sentence with a hinge in the middle: "Alcoholics A

ee1f534b81fe.t: Tradition 8 is one sentence with a hinge in the middle: "Alcoholics Anonymous should remain forever nonprofessional, but our service centers may employ special workers." Now imagine a group that keeps the first half and throws the second away. Nobody gets paid for anything, ever. No paid secretary, no paid caretaker. Purity, at last — and for about six months it is beautiful. Then the phone at the central office starts ringing at hours when the volunteer is at work. The literature order sits in a box. The meeting list goes stale, and a man who has finally decided to try drives across town to a church basement that has been dark for a year, sits in the parking lot, and drives home. P-43 puts the arithmetic plainly: there is "too great a volume of work to be done in spare hours here and there, and only the rich or the retired could afford to work full-time as volunteers." A.A. pays for the office, and will never pay to carry the message. The office answers phones and keeps the doors findable — driving across town at 4 a.m. to meet a stranger in need is how we stay sober ourselves, the way we always have.

784f96a104f0.t: A phone nobody was paid to answer is how a man ends up sitting in an empty parking lot. Whose unpaid work am I quietly counting on?

63b68bfc4bb8.t: Grounded in: P-43 (the limits of volunteers); short form, Tradition 8.

ef3c77dc9e3b.t: December 1 — "The Thirteenth Way Out." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. The book was finished before its name was. The tit

0d9b6a0d831f.t: The book was finished before its name was. The title members favored in 1939 was "The Way Out" — until Fitz M. went over to the Library of Congress to investigate. He found exactly twelve books already titled "The Way Out." When word was passed around, Bill wrote in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17), the Fellowship "shivered at the possibility of being the" Thirteenth Way Out — and Alcoholics Anonymous became the choice instead. Bill saw what the name carried: "That’s how we got a name for our book of experience, a name for our movement and, as we are now beginning to see, a tradition of the greatest spiritual import." The second-choice name prints the absence of names on the cover. And the book's opening pages made it a request (Big Book, p. xiii): "we urge each of our Fellowship to omit his personal name, designating himself instead as “a member of Alcoholics Anonymous.”" There was no Tradition yet. There was a title, a superstition about thirteen, and a decision that turned out to be doctrine.

fea0fbd1706f.t: A.A.'s name was second choice, and it turned out to hold the whole Tradition. What did I choose almost by accident that has quietly shaped everything since?

9f370d1d851f.t: Grounded in: P-17 (Bill W.'s 1946 anonymity essay); Big Book p. xiii.

2bfbbd833bfc.t: December 10 — "Inflated." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. A.A. had the data before it had the Tradition. Reflecting on th

ef7a7051105a.t: A.A. had the data before it had the Tradition. Reflecting on the Oxford Group years, Bill listed what experience had proved by 1940 (Pass It On): "Alcoholics who talked too much on public platforms were likely to become inflated and get drunk again." Not embarrassed — drunk. Inflation was a relapse mechanism, observed early. Now look at what the platform economy is built to produce. Prominence is the product; the metrics reward the person, not the principle; the more a recovery performs, the more its performer is fed the diet that used to put speakers back in the bottle. Bill's verdict on anonymity's deeper purpose: it exists "actually to keep those fool egos of ours from running hog wild after money and public fame at A.A.'s expense." This capture is not theft of the message. It is the industrialization of inflation. The Tradition is not quaint. It is clinical.

bf55696e17fc.t: Inflation was observed to get alcoholics drunk again, and there is now an economy that produces it on purpose. What is currently feeding mine?

ba0bca288dc2.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (the Oxford Group lessons, c. 1940).

dcdf018b6ea2.t: December 11 — "The Guests of Honor." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. In 1942, word went around Cleveland that Bill and Dr

ab275fe59ec1.t: In 1942, word went around Cleveland that Bill and Dr. Bob were splitting the proceeds — sixty-four thousand dollars in a year, the story went. The response was pure A.A.: a dinner, the co-founders as guests of honor, and beside them a lawyer and an accountant for the investigating committee. Their own members were auditing them (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers). "Bill just “happened” to have brought with him to the dinner a certified audit of all A.A. financial affairs from the beginning." It was read aloud and testified correct. "Records show that Dr. Bob received a total of $1,000 during 1941; evidently, even their weekly $30 was not always forthcoming." A doctor eating bread and milk, suspected of a fortune. "Both Bill and Dr. Bob received apologies." Neither founder claimed the standing to be above the question. In a society allergic to big shots, suspicion is the tax on prominence — the founders paid it with open books.

ba9ae74c35a8.t: The Fellowship investigated its own founders, and the founders answered with an audit instead of indignation. When I am doubted, do I reach for my record or my rank?

d1ec5e48904e.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (the 1942 investigation).

2898a9841039.t: December 12 — "The Plaque on His Desk." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. Dr. Bob kept a definition of humility on his desk

f76665813f8d.t: Dr. Bob kept a definition of humility on his desk, where he would see it between patients (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "Perpetual quietness of heart. It is to have no trouble. It is never to be fretted or vexed, irritable or sore; to wonder at nothing that is done to me, to feel nothing done against me. It is to be at rest when nobody praises me, and when I am blamed or despised, it is to have a blessed home in myself where I can go in and shut the door and kneel to my Father in secret and be at peace, as in a deep sea of calmness, when all around and about is seeming trouble." A co-founder kept that within arm's reach — which tells you he did not believe he had it. He believed he needed it. Spoken, his version was shorter — he didn't believe, he said, that he had "any right to get cocky about getting sober." At rest when nobody praises me. The whole Tradition fits inside that phrase.

0ce0bf93df48.t: He kept the definition on his desk because he expected to keep forgetting it. Am I at rest when nobody praises me?

c1951896f731.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (the desk plaque).

47f2cbe4a6c4.t: December 13 — "Stepping Out of an Office You Love." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. The service structure has a built-in

8e02d66ef5a2.t: Stepping Out of an Office You Love

b98bbefa0e27.t: The service structure has a built-in goodbye. Rotation asks the treasurer whose books balance to the penny, the GSR who finally understands the Conference, to hand the job to somebody who will do it worse — on purpose, on a schedule. The service literature is honest about why (A.A. Service Manual): it can be "a step into the humility that is, for some people, the spiritual essence of anonymity." The office you love is the one that has begun to love you back: it knows your name, returns your effort, tells you who you are on Tuesdays. That is exactly when the Tradition wants it handed over. "With no A.A. “status” at stake, we needn’t compete for titles or praise — we have complete freedom to serve as we are needed." Doing a good job is the best reason anyone ever had for not letting go. Rotation exists so that no job is ever allowed to become a man.

He is a good sponsor — answers at two in the morning, knows the book cold. But listen to the grammar. My fifth. Institutions run on named representatives — it is how accountability works everywhere else. That is precisely the capture. An outside witness saw it at St. Louis in 1955 (A.A. Comes of Age) — Dr. W. W. Bauer of the American Medical Association: "above all anonymity—the insurance that nobody is going to get famous as a leader of Alcoholics Anonymous." a0799f4ef443.t: Anne Smith had a policy before the Fellowship had a name. An early member's wife remembered it verbatim (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "she said, 'Let's you and me stay in the background.'" Not modesty as temperament — a chosen post, held for fifteen years at a kitchen table where drunks and their frightened wives kept arriving. 3c33ccb25d58.t: Frank had thirty-four years and died in October, and the grief was real, so nobody blinked when the anniversary meeting was renamed for him. A framed photograph beside the coffee urn. 7ce576cb916e.t: Before it was a principle, anonymity was a survival instinct. Bill said so at St. Louis (A.A. Comes of Age): "anonymity was not born of confidence; it was the child of our early fears. Our first nameless groups of alcoholics were secret societies. New prospects could find us only through a few trusted friends." They hid because they believed the world despised them — and they were not entirely wrong. The real story is what happened next: the discipline adopted out of shame turned out to hold the spiritual center of everything. Namelessness taught egolessness, and by 1955 Bill could state the stakes without blinking: "If we forget this principle, the lid to Pandora's box will be off and the spirits of Money, Power, and Prestige will be loosed among us." Fear built the wall. Humility moved in.

a30f4b9da584.t: The discipline began as hiding and matured into the spiritual center of the program. What did I start doing out of fear that became something better than its origin?

76ea87a15bff.t: December 20 — "The Story, Priced." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. Every alcoholic owns one asset drinking could not repo

ebe53436da44.t: Every alcoholic owns one asset drinking could not repossess: the story. The market has noticed — a memoir economy, a keynote fee, a bio line — and none of it is malicious; editors and bookers are doing their jobs. But pricing a story changes it. It acquires a hero and an arc; the relapse is repositioned for act two; the parts that don't perform get cut. The teller starts owning a franchise, and franchises need protecting. Bill defined this Tradition's economics in 1946 in one sentence (A.A. pamphlet P-17): "In a spiritual sense, anonymity amounts to the renunciation of personal prestige as an instrument of general policy." The capture is frictionless: nobody forbids anything; the market simply makes the story worth more with the name attached, until renunciation looks like leaving money on the table. It is. That is what makes it a sacrifice instead of a slogan.

c79b511a631e.t: The story is worth more with the name attached, which is exactly the price the Tradition asks us not to collect. What has my story started earning me — and costing?

553addcbd79d.t: Anne Smith died in June 1949, and her obituary did what fifteen years of service never had (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "Through published reports of Anne's death, Dr. Bob's identity as a co-founder of A.A. was disclosed to the general public." The Akron Beacon Journal mourned the anonymity itself — a pity, it wrote, that her "wonderful work could not have received the public's recognition while she still lived". Read the assumption inside that sentence: recognition withheld is payment withheld; Anne died with wages owing. It is kindly meant, and the Tradition disagrees with every word. Her recognition was not deferred — it was declined, by her, repeatedly, on purpose. What the newspaper counted as a debt, she had counted as the working condition of the help: the people at her kitchen table got a helper with no reputation to manage. Two ledgers price the same life differently. Anne knew both prices, and picked.

2ba2ed93be5f.t: The newspaper grieved her anonymity as unpaid wages; she had spent it deliberately, as the working condition of the help she gave. Which ledger am I keeping my accounts in?

0d8fff8c9de9.t: July 3, 1955, St. Louis. The resolution (A.A. Comes of Age) made the General Service Conference "the guardian of the Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous" and — the operative phrase — "the sole successors to its co-founders, Dr. Bob and Bill." Successors, plural and faceless: a rotating conscience of delegates, built so no one would ever again be what the founders had been. He and Dr. Bob had once asked in the Grapevine, "Why can't we join A.A., too?" Now Bill answered from the platform: "Well, this is the day when we do join A.A." The motion carried unanimously. Be honest about the aftermath, because A.A.'s own biography (Pass It On) is: Dennis Manders, longtime controller at the General Service Office, said "Bill would spend the next 15 years stepping down." The letting go took the rest of his life. That is not the resolution failing — it is the resolution working, holding steady while a founder's grip loosened at human speed.

8a73d2d14b7a.t: The founders' last act of leadership was to abolish their own office, and even then the letting go took fifteen years. What have I already, officially, given away — and am still holding?

That warmth is the miracle — and exactly why a room of friends drifts toward its favorites. Principles are affection's correction.

05a338873711.t: December 25 — "The Price Tag." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. The program's vocabulary is everywhere — serenity on kitch

3849e47ed8f0.t: The program's vocabulary is everywhere — serenity on kitchen signs, gratitude in January marketing, one day at a time on anything that holds coffee. The capture is not mockery; it is admiration with the price removed. Bill described where the words came from (A.A. Comes of Age): the new road signs read, "This way to sanity and serenity. The price is self-sacrifice." The copies keep the destination and omit the toll — and the toll is the working part: "The spiritual substance of anonymity is sacrifice." A word that costs nothing teaches nothing; serenity without the surrender underneath it is a font choice. This is how a spiritual language gets hollowed — not banned, not argued with: retailed. The answer is not to chase down every mug. It is to keep paying, quietly, the price the mug leaves off, so the words still mean something on the day a dying drinker reads them.

f7f2041a2e4c.t: A.A.'s biography of him closes it plainly (Pass It On): "It was January 24, and it was Lois and Bill's 53rd wedding anniversary. Bill died at eleven-thirty that night." Two days later the discipline of thirty-six years ended, on schedule: "The Traditions make no reference to posthumous anonymity; Bill's full name and his picture were prominently featured in the page one story." The anonymity had been an arrangement between a living man and the press, and it expired with him — by design, not by failure. The world finally got the name, and what it did with the name was mourn. Then the second artifact, in a Vermont cemetery, cut from the same white marble his father once quarried: a headstone, a footstone, the dates. "There is no mention of A.A." Page one of the Times, and a small stone that keeps the secret forever — both true, and only one of them his. The front page is what the world needed to say about Bill. The stone is what Bill spent thirty-six years saying about himself.

265bfc4f5680.t: Never one dramatic refusal — a policy, applied for years, mostly in private. Bill said he turned down six honorary degrees, with the dryness of a man reporting a diet (Pass It On): "My record respecting public honors is so far very much on the conservative side." The unit of thought was always the precedent, not the honor — not taking such degrees "would be more valuable than the taking of them — from the viewpoint of Alcoholics Anonymous." In 1951 he declined to be listed in Who's Who in America; his mother had refused her own invitation years before. When the Lasker Award came, "Bill's response was to refuse the award for himself personally, but to suggest that it be given to A.A. as a whole" — and at the ceremony he would speak "not as a co-founder, but as an early member." An early member. Every honor redirected became a small constitutional precedent: in this fellowship, credit flows to the whole, or it does not flow.

8cbbf2194d69.t: Success arrived, and Bill treated it as a threat assessment. At St. Louis, with the Fellowship two hundred thousand strong and friends predicting it would spearhead a worldwide spiritual awakening, he weighed the compliment like a chemist (A.A. Comes of Age): "such a tribute and such prophecy could well prove to be a heady drink for most of us". And he forecast the failure point: "it will center about false pride and anger, the two most destructive defects that we alcoholics have." Today the tribute is ambient — courts refer, doctors recommend, the culture speaks the program's vocabulary without knowing where it learned it. The long form had already named the stake (Big Book, p. 566): "that our great blessings may never spoil us". A heady drink — he chose the metaphor, in that room, with intent. Praise is a substance, and this fellowship's whole relationship to substances is the point. Tradition Twelve is how A.A. stays sober about itself.

2501893bfe7d.t: At the year-end meeting the chair does the arithmetic from the front: added together, the room holds two hundred forty-seven years of sobriety tonight. Applause, deserved — it is a true number. At the break, the line forms at the urn around the thirty-year man, warm as a stove. The man with three days stands at the literature rack, holding a styrofoam cup, reading the same pamphlet twice. Nobody reaches him before he leaves at ten past nine. No one was unkind; the room was busy honoring its treasure, and its treasure is not what it is for. Dr. Bob, in his last year, on why he still came (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "I belong at that meeting for the sake of the new man or woman who might walk through that door." And: "I am the living example." The years are proof, not rank. Two hundred forty-seven years of proof stood in that room, and the one person it was proof for went home unmet.

9adf80c2412c.t: The room counted its years and missed its purpose by ten past nine. At my meeting, who gets the line at the break — and who gets the literature rack?

0e56ca9378a2.t: December 3 — "The Big Ego." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. Sobriety does not remove the ego; it relocates it. The pamphl

489aca2b85ca.t: Sobriety does not remove the ego; it relocates it. The pamphlet is cheerfully blunt (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "When we do get sober in A.A., we shed a few small bits of the Big Ego: We admit, “I can’t handle alcohol, and I can’t stay away from it on my own.” Fine so far!" And then, the pamphlet adds, plenty of that Ego stays. The remainder goes looking for new food, and the rooms are full of it — the wisest voice at the table, the most-quoted sponsor, the name that travels between groups. None of it requires a camera. Bill named the counter-instrument (A.A. Comes of Age): "anonymity is real humility at work." And what it protects: "humility, expressed by anonymity, is the greatest safeguard that Alcoholics Anonymous can ever have." The threat was never only fame. It was the daily appetite to be somebody.

bc595ae47c72.t: The Ego survives sobriety and goes looking for smaller stages. On which small stage am I currently performing?

580d50bc27fc.t: Grounded in: P-43 (Tradition One); A.A. Comes of Age (anonymity as humility at work).

ade2e0a25807.t: December 30 — "Him Who Presides." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. The last mechanism is the oldest: the demand that A.A.

63ba29aaefde.t: The last mechanism is the oldest: the demand that A.A. produce a head. Institutions keep needing one — somebody to sign the agreement, sit for the interview, accept the award, answer for the whole. Every other body on earth supplies such a person; the request is reasonable, and it never stops. Capture would not require malice — just an org chart with one box finally filled. The Tradition's answer is its closing sentence, the closing sentence of all Twelve (Big Book, p. 566): that we shall forever live "in thankful contemplation of Him who presides over us all." The position is filled; applications are not being accepted. The pamphlet says it without the theology (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "Our principles come first — and they are not our own invention. They reflect eternal spiritual values." The capture fails not because members are all humble — some are not — but because the office was never created. There is no chair to sit in. There is only the room.

2d4ff0d8bec1.t: The office every institution keeps asking for was deliberately never built, because it is already held. Who presides over what I do — on an ordinary Tuesday, when nobody is checking?

8c0c9b97424e.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 12; P-43 (Tradition Twelve).

30919b3025af.t: A Fine Hour in That Month of July

c3a89844d3c5.t: End where the Traditions began. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "In the summer of 1950 we held our first international convention in Cleveland, Ohio. About 3,000 were in attendance." Dr. Bob was dying and everyone knew it — five of the previous seven months in bed — and he stood up anyway, and chose the smallest words he had (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "Our Twelve Steps, when simmered down to the last, resolve themselves into the words 'love' and 'service.' We understand what love is, and we understand what service is. So let's bear those two things in mind." Then the Convention did what this whole year of readings has been about — Bill called it (A.A. Comes of Age) "the confirmation of our Twelve Traditions by the Convention as the permanent platform of unity and function". A recording preserves "the Convention's unanimous voice of consent." His verdict: "It was a fine hour in that month of July, 1950." Three hundred sixty-six readings end here, on purpose: a dying founder asking for simplicity, and a room of anonymous alcoholics answering with one voice that principles would govern from now on. You can still listen to the yes.

acfe90c4c2da.t: A dying man asked for love and service, and three thousand people made the Traditions permanent with one voice — and the year ends there. Which of the Twelve will I need first in the year ahead?

f7506e8c225a.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Cleveland, July 1950); Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (his last talk).

6a03bef319ec.t: December 4 — "The Thursday Meeting Had a Star." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. He is eleven years sober, funny in the wa

2833987d0e82.t: The Thursday Meeting Had a Star

1f4969d29d24.t: He is eleven years sober, funny in the way that keeps a room warm. Nobody decides anything — it accumulates. Visitors ask whether he's on this week. The group, sensibly, schedules him: first Thursday of the month. On his Thursdays, sixty chairs; other weeks, twenty-five. It runs three years and helps a great many people — which is the difficulty, because in March his firm moves him two provinces away, and by June the Thursday meeting votes to fold itself into Tuesday's. No one did anything wrong. He never asked for the crowd and often looked uneasy in it. The meeting had simply stopped being a group with a speaker and become an audience with a habit, and an audience goes where the show goes. A group organized around a principle can lose any member and hold. A group organized around a person is one job transfer from the end.

1e91c875193e.t: The meeting was an audience before anyone noticed, and it closed when its star moved away. Which room am I in for the principle, and which for a person?

b25fe47181cf.t: December 5 — "Renamed as Shame." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. The argument arrives sounding like liberation: anonymity

bc1d6114f192.t: The argument arrives sounding like liberation: anonymity is stigma in a virtue's clothes, and people should recover out loud. The mechanism is renaming — take a spiritual discipline, call it a symptom, and every act of humility reads as evidence of the disease. Once the frame sets, publicity becomes the prescription and the Tradition becomes the problem. But the definition was written first (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "Anonymity, as we observe it in A.A., is at root a simple expression of humility." And the program's stated aim runs dead against the shame reading: "to put our self-respect on a solid base of truth, rather than on fantasies about ourselves." A member practicing this Tradition is not hiding in disgrace. He is declining to be enlarged. Different acts, different engines — and only one of them has anything to do with shame.

7c910c57231a.t: The capture renames humility as a symptom, so publicity can be prescribed as the cure. Where have I let someone rename a thing I do — and then treated the new name as true?

b2ce692d9930.t: December 6 — "The Stark Fact." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. Around 1949 Bill put it to Dr. Bob in writing, unsoftened

a0cb24e7e9f8.t: Around 1949 Bill put it to Dr. Bob in writing, unsoftened (Pass It On): "The stark fact is that you and I still head Alcoholics Anonymous. By common consent, we remain the only two individuals in A.A. actually entitled and expected to speak for the whole." Fifteen years in, the fellowship of no names had two heads. The cost ran both ways. Bill's psychiatrist had a thesis about it, and Bill repeated it with approval: "So we have the person of Mr. Anonymous in conflict with Bill Wilson." The shelter every other drunk enjoyed was closed to its architects: "Wherever he went, he was sooner or later spotted, named, and asked to lead." Dr. Bob's first reply was doubt — "Maybe I am wrong, but that is the way I feel. Love, Smithy." The founders were the Tradition's last exception, and both men had begun to see that the exception was the threat.

0070ffa46820.t: The fellowship of no names still had two, and the two knew it was unsound. What am I the standing exception to — and who consented to that?

abface542cbf.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (Bill's letter to Dr. Bob; "Mr. Anonymous").

d1a7e3c86b5c.t: December 7 — "The Back of His Head." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. A.A.'s biography of Bill records the offer (Pass It

245412244853.t: A.A.'s biography of Bill records the offer (Pass It On): "When Time magazine wanted to put Bill on its cover — that is, put the back of his head on the front of the magazine — Bill declined, and declined the cover story as well." Read the offer again: it already conceded his anonymity. No face, no name, technically inside the letter of the Tradition. He refused anyway, and his accounting is the hardest arithmetic in A.A.'s history: "I denied recovery to an awful lot of alcoholics — some of these may already be dead." What he weighed against those lives was what the piece would manufacture: "a clear and colorful public image of me as a person." One image, then a precedent, then every power-driver holding a clipping that proves it's allowed. "Therefore, I declined the publicity, and I must confess it wasn't easy." The Tradition was not kept by men who found it painless. It was kept by a man who counted the cost and paid it.

6ad4757e60f5.t: The offer already protected his anonymity, and he refused it for what it would build. What have I kept technically inside the rules while constructing what the rules exist to prevent?

a392cd08705f.t: December 8 — "Faceless Automatons." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 12: Anonymity is the spiritual foundation of all our Traditions, ever reminding us to place principles before personalities. This Tradition has a failure mode, and Bill named it.

05afa71ac95b.t: This Tradition has a failure mode, and Bill named it. Writing on leadership in 1959 (A.A. Service Manual), he watched the phrase become a muzzle: "We are apt to warp the traditional idea of “principles before personalities” around to such a point that there would be no “personality” in leadership whatever. This would imply rather faceless automatons trying to please everybody, regardless." You have seen the warp: the capable member who won't stand for a position because standing looks like ego; the strong proposal withdrawn at the first frown; a group mistaking the absence of initiative for the presence of humility. That is the Tradition inverted — ego managed by hiding instead of by service. Bill's corrective sits in the same essay: "Our leaders do not drive by mandate, they lead by example." Personalities are not the enemy; personalities enthroned are.

ddae86b9a132.t: Bill himself warned that this Tradition can be warped into a demand for facelessness. Where am I calling it humility when it is actually hiding?

87dc7bdd9574.t: Grounded in: A.A. Service Manual (Bill W., "Leadership in A.A.: Ever a Vital Need," 1959).

60845d0ea900.t: Nine Years in the Same Chair

736916f13a92.t: He started the meeting nine years ago — found the church basement, paid the first month's rent himself, carried the literature box in his trunk. He hasn't held a position in six years, which is the elegant part: he doesn't need one. New secretaries check with him before changing the format. The treasurer asks him, not the group, about the rent. The group conscience votes with his eyebrows. Then in February he lands in hospital for six weeks, and the group discovers what it is: nobody else knows the landlord's number, which key opens the cupboard, or why the rent has stayed forty dollars under market. The meeting doesn't die. It finds out it was never quite a group — it was a man with attendees. To his credit, when he comes back he sits in the fourth row and lets them keep it. That is the day it becomes a group.

3311af94259e.t: For nine years the group conscience voted with one man's eyebrows, and it took his hospital bed to prove it. What runs only because I am standing next to it?

3361a17cd03d.t: February 1 — "Never Personal Authority." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do no

50b3f9051389.t: Tradition Two answers one question for every A.A. group: who decides? The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Ultimate authority means the last word, and in a group's business no person holds it. The threat it answers is a boss. Bill W. wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 37): "Time out of mind, families, friends, employers, doctors, clergymen, and judges have tried their hand at disciplining alcoholics. Almost without exception the failure to accomplish anything by coercion has been complete." Coercion means forcing. Every drunk who walks in has already been bossed by experts, and it didn't work. Put a boss over the group and he meets one more person trying to run him, and he leaves. So Bill drew the line: "the only real authority to be found in A.A. is that of spiritual principle. It is never personal authority." That tells no one what to believe. It takes power away from whoever wants it. Today the boss often comes built in: a counsellor at the front of the room, a program that sets the rules, a court that wants a signature. Test it tonight: ask who has the last word in your room, and whether the answer is a person.

621eefcca50a.t: Tradition Two gives the last word in a group's business to no person at all. Who has the last word in my group?

a0d6f9327b6a.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 37 (Bill W., "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

f182d19ccf45.t: February 10 — "No Orders." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern. When

64f8a5486bd6.t: When a facility supplies the person who runs the meeting, the group loses what Tradition Two guarantees it: the power to say who serves and on what terms. Bill W. described an A.A. group's committee once the members have taken charge of their own affairs (A.A. Comes of Age): "This committee can only make the necessary service arrangements by which the group can function. It can give no spiritual advice, judge no one's conduct, issue no orders." Its members, he wrote, are "servants, not senators." And: "Thus throughout our fellowship does the group conscience decree the terms upon which its leaders shall serve." Decree means sets by ruling. Now look at a meeting run on a program's schedule. The person in the chair is staff. She was hired, not elected. She may hand out advice, judge who has been compliant, and sign attendance sheets for the court. No vote put her there and no vote can remove her; her boss can. That room may read the Traditions aloud every week, but the authority the Long Form names (Big Book, p. 563), "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience," has no group conscience to speak through. Test it tonight: ask who chose the person chairing your meeting, and who could replace them.

e72ab9dd0262.t: In A.A. the group sets the terms its leaders serve on, and a hired chair answers to someone else. Who chose the person chairing my meeting?

29cdb5a92305.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy — Tradition Nine).

8afee09e3c41.t: February 11 — "Caretakers Only." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern

c85f44421995.t: The danger Tradition Two closes at the top of A.A. is a headquarters that starts to rule, and Bill W. shut that door from inside the headquarters itself. Writing in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 39): "Here at the General Office we have long known that we can merely supply certain indispensable services." Then the line: "It is most clearly apparent that, even here at the very center of A.A., there can only exist a center of service — custodians, editors, secretaries and the like — each, to be sure, with a special vital function, but none of them with any authority to govern Alcoholics Anonymous." A custodian looks after something that belongs to someone else. On the next page he named the threat (p. 40): "So long as we avoid any menacing accumulation of wealth or the growth of personal government at these centers, we cannot go astray." Menacing means threatening. So the Long Form keeps the authority with the groups (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Today the claim to rule from above comes as an office or a facility telling a group what it must do. Test it tonight: ask what your group was last told it had to do, and who told it.

89cdecc69488.t: An election is a group's brake on a leader who starts to boss, and a group breaks Tradition Two when it stops using it. Bill W. wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "Nowhere in A.A. is there to be seen any constituted human authority that can compel an A.A. group to do anything." Constituted means officially set up. Then he explained why a leader can't become one: "Some A.A. groups, for example, elect their leaders. But even with such a mandate each leader soon discovers that while he can always guide by example or persuasion he can never boss, else at election time he may find himself passed by." A mandate is the permission a vote gives. Notice what that depends on: an election time. Picture a group whose secretary has held the job six years because nobody else ran and nobody called the vote. She now picks the readings, the speakers and who signs at the bank. She wasn't a boss when the group elected her. The group made her one by never voting again. The Long Form keeps the decision with the members (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Test it tonight: ask when your group last elected its secretary, and when it will next.

986c8bcb0f3d.t: Tradition Two takes the last word in a group away from every person, and a facility-run meeting quietly hands it back to staff. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Group conscience means the members of the group deciding together, at their own business meeting. Bill W. explained how A.A. could live without bosses (A.A. Comes of Age): "Other societies have to have law and force and sanction and punishment, administered by authorized people. Happily for us, we found we need no human authority whatever." cb53dd1712c3.t: Before Tradition Two was written, the people around the table overruled the man writing A.A.'s book, and the Twelve Steps are better for it. Just before the manuscript was finished, four of them sat in an office in Newark, still arguing over the Steps. Bill W. remembered (A.A. Comes of Age): "All this time I had refused to budge on these steps. I would not change a word of the original draft". His draft used the word God throughout, and in one place had alcoholics praying on their knees. Henry, who had worked on the book with him, fought it hard, sure it would scare drinkers away by the thousands. Little by little the others came around to Henry's side. The words that came out of that fight are the ones in the Steps today: a Power greater than ourselves, and God as we understood Him, with the Steps offered as suggestions. Bill called it "the great contribution of our atheists and agnostics." Nobody pulled rank. The writer held the pen, and the room still decided. That is Tradition Two before it had a number: no single person, however much they have done, holds the last word for the group. Test it tonight: when your group next decides something, ask whether the member who disagreed most was actually heard, or only outnumbered.

01769f5386ce.t: Tradition Two opens with four words that limit everything after them: for our group purpose. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." The authority it names settles the group's business: where it meets, what happens to the basket money, how the meeting runs, who holds which job. It is not a ruling on what any member has to believe. The rumour runs the other way. A newcomer hears that the Second Tradition means he must believe in God before he belongs, or that a group gets a say over his faith. The Big Book says the opposite, in the chapter on carrying the message to the man still drinking (p. 95): "If he thinks he can do the job in some other way, or prefers some other spiritual approach, encourage him to follow his own conscience. We have no monopoly on God; we merely have an approach that worked with us." A monopoly is sole ownership. So the group's conscience runs the group's affairs, and each member's conscience stays his own. Test it tonight: if anyone in your room has told a newcomer what he has to believe to stay, ask them where the Long Form gives a group that power.

7d6a85dec44a.t: A group can lose Tradition Two without anyone taking it, simply by never meeting to decide anything. Picture a meeting that has run on Tuesday nights for years. The secretary has held the job so long that nobody remembers electing her. She picks the readings, the format, and who leads each week. The basket money goes into an envelope she keeps at home. Nobody objects, because she is kind and reliable and does all the work. But there has not been a business meeting in three years, and when a newer member asks for one, the answer is that it isn't needed. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." 29ed3e762efc.t: Years before Tradition Two was written, Bill W. heard what he took for God's voice, and his group overruled it. It was 1937. Bill was broke, and a hospital owner offered him an office, money to live on and a share of the profits to work there as a lay therapist, a paid counsellor without a medical degree. Bill wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "Going back to Brooklyn on the subway, I had a flash of seeming divine guidance." He told the meeting in his own parlour that night, sure of the answer. The members heard him out in silence, then said no: A.A. could never have a professional, and they could not tie it to that hospital or any other. His verdict: "Thus spoke the group conscience. The group was right and I was wrong; the voice on the subway was not the voice of God." Read it slowly. The co-founder had a private sense of what God wanted, and the room's decision outranked it. From nights like that came the principle he put this way: "God, speaking in the group conscience, is to be our final authority." The Long Form kept it (Big Book, p. 563): the one authority speaks "in our group conscience," not through one member, however sure. Test it tonight: ask when your group last overruled the person who was surest.

e7a0a5ad72c1.t: Bill's private guidance lost to his group's decision, and he said the group was right. Who in my room is too sure to be overruled?

59eaccfeecca.t: When a program pays someone to run a meeting, the person at the front works for the program, not for the group. The Big Book's foreword sums up what the early groups settled on (p. xix): "that our leaders might serve but never govern; that each group was to be autonomous and there was to be no professional class of therapy." Autonomous means self-governing. A professional class of therapy means people paid to treat alcoholics inside A.A. The Long Form puts the authority in the group (Big Book, p. 563): "one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Now watch the capture. A recovery program sends a paid coach to chair the meeting. The coach takes attendance for the program, steers the sharing toward the program's lessons, and reports back to the office. The members can't remove the coach, because the members never chose the coach. A leader the group can't replace isn't serving the group. That leader is governing it, on someone else's payroll. Nothing about the room has to look different for this to happen; the chairs, the readings and the basket all stay. Only the answer to who decides has changed. Test it tonight: ask who chose the person chairing your meeting, who pays them if anyone does, and whether the members could replace them next week.

7948fed575a4.t: The danger Tradition Two answers did not only rise from the groups; for years it sat at the top of A.A., and Bill W. said so. At St. Louis in 1955, as the old-timers handed A.A.'s world services over to the groups, he described the old arrangement (A.A. Comes of Age): "When we first put our world services into effect, Dr. Bob and I and our old-time friends were self-appointed guardians and custodians of this society." Self-appointed means nobody chose them. He went further: "our setup of those days was a sort of a double-headed papacy and a college of cardinals." A papacy is rule from one head, and the cardinals are the circle around it. They did good work, but answered to no one below them. The fix was to make the top answer downward. The new Conference, Bill said, "will represent the conscience of A.A. world-wide, to which our Trustees will in this very hour become directly accountable." That is the Long Form carried all the way up (Big Book, p. 563): the "one ultimate authority" speaks "in our group conscience," and no office outranks it. Today the papacy can be any office, committee or intergroup that starts telling groups what they must do. Test it tonight: if any office or committee has sent your group an instruction, ask who elected it and who it answers to.

c7a166100105.t: As the first groups grew, every job they needed could breed a boss, and the members had to keep the jobholders in their place. Somebody had to collect the money and bank it, so there was a treasurer; then a secretary, sometimes a chairman. Bill W. described what came with them (A.A. Comes of Age): "Absolutely necessary arrangements had to be made and people had to be appointed or elected to do the jobs. This often brought friction and power-driving". A power-driver is someone pushing to be in charge. Then: "Means had to be found to keep friction-makers and power-drivers down to their right size." What worked, he wrote, was a service committee, a good deal of pressure from the members, and much love and understanding. Nobody was made boss to fix the bosses. The group handled them itself, and the jobs stayed jobs. The Long Form later wrote down where the last word had been all along (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Today the drift is the same: whoever holds the bank card, the keys or the meeting list starts making the decisions. Test it tonight: ask whether each job in your group still answers to the members, and when the members last said so.

d9cfa84d0cec.t: A title in an A.A. group gives no power over anyone, and the rumour that it does is how rooms end up with bosses. The Long Form of Tradition Two puts the only authority in the group (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority". The Long Form of Tradition Nine says what the people holding the titles get instead (p. 565): "Universal respect is the key to their usefulness." Universal means from everyone. So a secretary, a chairperson or a treasurer is useful because the members trust them, and only for as long as the members do. Today the rumour runs the other way. Some rooms have a facilitator, a group leader or a coordinator who acts as if the title came with rights: to cut a share short, to pick who reads, to decide who is welcome and who is a problem. Respect that has to be demanded is already gone, and what is left is a boss with a name tag. The group never has to put up with that. It can hold an election and hand the job to someone else. Test it tonight: ask your group's officers when they were elected, how long they serve, and when the next election is.

14c769ad417a.t: February 24 — "The Close Vote." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern.

928fedecf060.t: A group can keep the letter of Tradition Two, take a vote, and still break itself, by forcing a split decision through on one count. Picture a business meeting with thirteen members there. The motion is to move the meeting to a new night. Six want it, six don't, one shrugs, and it passes seven to six. By spring the six have stopped coming, and two of them have started a meeting across town. Nobody broke a rule. But the group's conscience is the members together, and half of them just walked out. A.A. learned this the hard way. When Bill W. and the old-timers planned the elections for A.A.'s first General Service Conference, they named the danger (A.A. Comes of Age): "Another prime cause of grief was the hotly contested close election, which nearly always left behind a large and discontented minority." So they asked for a two-thirds vote, a margin big enough that the losing side could live with it. The Long Form names where a group's authority lives (Big Book, p. 563): "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." A seven-to-six split is a room that hasn't finished deciding. Test it tonight: when your group divides nearly in half, ask whether the question can wait a month for more talk instead of a vote.

d16854ba5d7b.t: A close vote can win a motion and lose half the group. When my group splits down the middle, do we push it through or keep talking?

8f36ad8ef286.t: February 25 — "Nothing Can Compel a Group." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do

d2325b4e37ff.t: No one outside an A.A. group can order it to do anything, and the capture starts when a group forgets that and obeys. Bill W. put the rule for all of A.A. in two sentences (A.A. Comes of Age): "Therefore it is now clear that we ought never to name boards to govern us. It is equally clear, however, that we shall always need to authorize workers to serve us." To authorize is to give someone permission to act. If A.A. itself has nobody who can give a group orders, a landlord certainly doesn't. Here is how it goes. A group rents a room in a facility. The facility starts adding conditions: its clients speak first, a staff member sits in, the meeting ends early to fit the facility's schedule, and the facility's handouts go on the table. Each request is small and the rent is cheap, so the group says yes, and one day the facility's policy is the meeting's format. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." A group that can't say no to its landlord can always vote to find another room. Test it tonight: ask whether any rule in your meeting came from the building, rather than from a vote of the members.

42ecfff3bccb.t: A.A. never names anyone to govern a group, and no building can do it either, unless the group lets it. Did any rule in my meeting come from the landlord?

5d39863df455.t: February 26 — "Righteous Indignation." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not

aa715203a8bd.t: The most dangerous grab for power in a group comes from the member who is sure he's right. Bill W. named the forces the Traditions hold back (A.A. Comes of Age): "These were the desires for power, for domination, for glory, and for money. They were all the more dangerous because they were invariably powered by self-righteousness, self-justification, and the destructive power of anger, usually masquerading as righteous indignation." Masquerading means wearing a disguise. Righteous indignation is anger that feels holy. Nobody takes over a group by saying they want control. They say the group is going wrong and somebody has to fix it. Then they fix it themselves: change the format without a vote, swap the readings, decide who is really A.A. and who isn't. Every step feels like protecting the program. The Long Form shuts that door by naming the only authority there is (Big Book, p. 563): "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." That leaves no room for one member's certainty, however sincere. A member who is right can bring it to the business meeting and persuade the others. A member who won't wait for the vote has stopped serving the group and started ruling it. Test it tonight: the next time someone says the group has to be saved from itself, ask them to put it to a vote.

87b68d620fb5.t: The urge to run a group usually arrives dressed as saving it. Who in my room is fixing the group without asking the group?

68fb6abc57bc.t: February 27 — "We Ought, Not You Must." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not

6f700f630cf6.t: Before there was a Tradition Two, A.A.'s first book had its orders taken out wherever possible, so that nobody in it would stand over the reader. When copies of the manuscript went out for comment in 1939, a psychiatrist in Montclair, New Jersey, Dr. Howard, sent back a criticism: the text was full of you and must. Bill W. remembered (A.A. Comes of Age): "His idea was to remove all forms of coercion". Coercion means forcing someone. Bill argued against it at first, then gave in: "it was perfectly apparent that the doctor was dead right." So the book mostly speaks as we, telling what we did and what we found, and leaves the reader free to take it or leave it. The Traditions grew from the same root. The Long Form gives a group one authority (Big Book, p. 563): "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." No member, chairperson or old-timer gets a you-must over anyone. Yet in some rooms today, must is everywhere: you must get a home group, you must do ninety meetings, you must check in every day, or you're out. Those are orders, and the book itself had them edited out. Test it tonight: count how many times you hear "you must" in your meeting, and ask who gave the speaker the authority to say it.

771f64e4f4ed.t: A.A.'s book took out the you-musts so nobody would stand over the reader. Who in my room hands out orders that the book itself refused to give?

35faf151646a.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Service: the Third Legacy — the mimeograph copies and Dr. Howard).

a41feafeecdd.t: Tradition 2 — February 28: Through the Group | Daily Traditions | Recovery Starts

0e31c4110b9f.t: February 28 — "Through the Group." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not gove

0e97fe4145d4.t: Tradition Two does not let any one person speak for God to a group, and that is the part most often turned around. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Read where the voice comes from: the group conscience, the members deciding together. Not the chairperson. Not the oldest member. Not a counselor telling a room what God wants from it. The Tradition is about who decides for a group, not what anyone believes, and it works the same for the member who prays, the one who doubts and the one who doesn't believe at all. The Big Book is plain about that in its chapter on carrying the message (p. 93): "If the man be agnostic or atheist, make it emphatic that he does not have to agree with your conception of God." Emphatic means said strongly and clearly. Today the twist sounds like this: someone says God has shown them what the group should do, so anyone who argues is arguing with God. That is personal authority in religious clothes, and the Long Form gives it nothing. Test it tonight: when anyone in your room claims to know God's will for the group, ask them to bring it to the business meeting and let the members decide.

9d3f11df64c3.t: No one member speaks for God to the group; the group decides together. Has anyone in my room used God's name to end an argument?

dc48ab8659c0.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); Big Book p. 93 ("Working With Others").

f99b53d191f7.t: Tradition 2 — February 29: The Sole Authority | Daily Traditions | Recovery Starts

68b951e94257.t: February 29 — "The Sole Authority." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not gov

101156821267.t: The month ends with the oldest way a group gives Tradition Two away: it gets comfortable and lets one person decide. Nobody plans it. One member always knows what to do, so the others stop coming to business meetings. The literature order, the rent, the format, the anniversary cakes: one person handles it all, and the group is grateful. Years go by, and the group has a conscience on paper and an owner in fact. A.A. as a whole once faced the same question: could the members really be trusted to run their own affairs? At the first General Service Conference in 1951, delegates chosen by the groups took on hard questions the headquarters people had been unsure about. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "Though their advice was sometimes contrary to our own views, we saw they were frequently right." And then: "Our group conscience could safely act as the sole authority and sure guide for Alcoholics Anonymous." Sole means only. That line is the whole month, and the Long Form said it first (Big Book, p. 563): "one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." It only works when the members show up and decide. Test it tonight: go to your group's next business meeting, and if there isn't one, ask for it.

b3ba9b75b7fa.t: A.A. found its group conscience could safely be the sole authority, but only because the members showed up. Will I be at my group's next business meeting?

ef1be10fbd67.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Service: the Third Legacy — the first General Service Conference, 1951).

1b98cb1435ba.t: February 3 — "Not One Word About Leaders." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do

58818af25ed2.t: Read Tradition Two in its Long Form and you will find not one word about leaders, because the Tradition is about where authority sits, not whom to trust. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) is a single sentence: "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." The line about leaders appears only in the short form (p. 562). Its full version is in the Long Form of Tradition Nine (p. 565): "true leaders in A.A. are but trusted and experienced servants of the whole. They derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern." Servants of the whole means they work for the members. The rumour runs the other way: that a trusted servant is someone you should trust to decide for you. Today the phrase gets printed on a lanyard. A program calls its staff member the meeting's trusted servant, and the room assumes the title came with authority. It came with none. In an A.A. group, the members hand out a job by vote and can take it back the same way, and the title adds nothing to the person holding it. Test it tonight: ask who gave your meeting's leader the job, and whether the group could take it back next month.

bb2c6ceb649e.t: The Long Form of Tradition Two names an authority and no leaders, and Tradition Nine says titles carry no real authority. Who gave the person at the front of my room the job?

cc60d7c745b5.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); short form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 562); long form, Tradition 9 (Big Book, p. 565).

dd5b016ec84f.t: February 4 — "Who Could Know Better." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not g

1ae1ca021aae.t: A group breaks Tradition Two the quiet way when it lets one long-sober member's say-so stand in for its own vote. Picture the business meeting. Someone proposes moving the meeting to a night when more people could come. Heads nod. Then the man with twenty years says that isn't how this group does things, and the motion dies without a vote. Nobody gave him a veto. The room handed it over. Bill W. admitted the old-timers' habit (A.A. Comes of Age): "We oldsters often construed our longer experience as a sort of vested right, even an unlimited license, to run A.A. indefinitely." A vested right is one you believe you own. They even thought they should pick their own successors, he wrote, and asked, "Who could know better than we?" The groups said no. Of the old-timer he concluded: "With all his experience and good works, there was still nothing infallible about him at all." Infallible means unable to be wrong. Long sobriety earns a hearing. It does not earn the decision. The Long Form puts the decision in one place (Big Book, p. 563): "our group conscience," the members deciding together. Today the same veto goes to whoever has run the room longest, from a member's chair or a staff desk. Test it tonight: ask what your group last dropped without a vote because somebody senior said no.

05d37a8ab2ae.t: Long sobriety earns a hearing, not the group's decision. What has my group dropped because one senior voice said no?

8d3469e66a39.t: February 5 — "Places of Service." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not gover

a8bfabf1fb44.t: A.A.'s own service offices cannot govern the groups, because the groups pay for them and can stop. Bill W. wrote about A.A.'s clubs, local offices and the New York office in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 28): "These are places of service; they cannot really control or govern A.A. If any of them were to become inefficient or overbearing the remedy is simple enough. The average A.A. would stop his financial support until conditions were changed." Overbearing means bossy. The members hold the purse, so the office answers to them. That is the Long Form at work (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Now turn it around. A room inside a treatment facility runs on the facility's budget. Nobody in the chairs pays for it, so nobody in the chairs can stop paying. The program decides the night, the format and who may come, and it calls the hour an A.A. meeting. Bill's remedy can't reach it, because the members never held the purse in the first place. A room like that has been captured before anyone in it says a word. Test it tonight: ask who pays for your room, and what would happen if the members stopped.

295ddced5dca.t: A.A.'s offices answer to the groups because the groups pay for them. Who pays for my room, and so who does it answer to?

ff951893e5f0.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 28 (Bill W., "Money", 1946).

fea1bc6203f5.t: February 6 — "A Servant Only." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern.

925be45db72c.t: If the man who started A.A. could not govern it, nobody can, and that is the danger Tradition Two closes. Bill W. co-founded A.A., and in 1947 he described trying to run it anyway (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 39): "After struggling a few years to run the A.A. movement I had to give it up — it simply didn't work. Heavy-handed assertion of my personal authority always created confusion and resistance." Then four words: "Personal power always failed." And the lesson he drew for every member: "In such fashion each of us learns that, in A.A., one can be a servant only." The threat was never a bad man. It was a founder, meaning well, holding a power the drunks would not accept. A fellowship that rested on one man's rule would have split the day he was wrong, or died with him. So the Long Form hands the authority to something no member can hold alone (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Today the founder figure is the program director whose name is on the meeting, or the member who started the group years ago and still runs it. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your room is treated as the one it can't do without.

104d4fc6b6c4.t: Even A.A.'s co-founder found that personal power always failed and that a member can be a servant only. Is anyone in my group treated as the one it can't do without?

44ed86ac97a2.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 39 (Bill W., "Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?", 1947).

4ac1c5ac1ee3.t: February 7 — "Eighteen in Akron." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not gover

9f787257fab1.t: Before A.A. had a single Tradition, its two founders could not move without a vote of the members. In the fall of 1937 Bill W. and Dr. Bob wanted paid missionaries, a chain of hospitals and a book. Dr. Bob suggested trying the ideas on the Akron members first. Eighteen of them sat in a living room and heard the plan. Bill remembered (A.A. Comes of Age): "Paid workers, they said, would kill our good will with alcoholics: this would be sheer ruin. If we went into the hospital business, everybody would say it was a racket." The founders pushed back, and a vote was taken. The plan passed by the barest majority. Years later Bill admitted the minority had been right about the paid missionaries and the big business, and wrote: "Though I did not see it then, the group conscience of Alcoholics Anonymous was already at work hammering out right decisions for A.A.'s future." Notice the order. The founders proposed. The members decided, and the losing side was heard all the same. Nine years later the Long Form wrote it down (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Test it tonight: ask whether your group's members, not its founders or its hosts, decided the last big change in your room.

7d47ef81cf22.t: In 1937 the founders proposed and eighteen Akron members decided. Who decided the last big change in my room?

5fed51c59ecc.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Service: the Third Legacy — the Akron meeting, 1937).

e1b7aca329be.t: February 8 — "Another's Conception." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not go

0dbf74037d67.t: The words "a loving God" in Tradition Two give no member the right to tell the group what God wants, and they ask no member what he believes. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Where does that authority show up? In the group conscience: the members deciding together. Not in one person's prayer or one person's certainty. The Big Book had already refused to make anyone's faith the measure (p. 46): "Much to our relief, we discovered we did not need to consider another's conception of God." A conception is an idea of something. A believer, a doubter and someone who believes nothing can sit at the same business meeting, and each one's vote counts the same. The rumour turns this upside down. It says Tradition Two is about your private faith, or that whoever sounds most spiritual should settle the room's business. Today it shows up as a chair who ends a debate by announcing what God wants, or a program that dresses its rules in spiritual words so nobody argues. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your room has ever closed a vote by claiming to know God's will.

7e3c5980cd2e.t: Tradition Two puts the authority in the group's decision, not in any one person's idea of God. Has anyone in my room used God's name to end a vote?

d3c0a73076f0.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 2 (Big Book, p. 563); Big Book p. 46 (We Agnostics).
