9b6f95ea796e.t: Tradition 2 — February 9: A Brand-New Committee | Daily Traditions | Recovery Starts

d4361c0238fd.t: February 9 — "A Brand-New Committee." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 2: For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience. Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not g

a5cd3bd025a3.t: A group committee that starts making rules for members has stopped serving the group and started governing it. Bill W. described what an A.A. committee is (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "they have only the authorization to serve, never to command. Each committee carries out what it believes to be the wishes of its group. That is all." Then what happened when committees forgot: "Though A.A. committees used to try to discipline wayward members, though they have sometimes composed minute rules and regulations and now and then have set themselves up as judges of other people's personal morals, I know of no case where any of these seemingly worthy strivings had any lasting effect — except, perhaps, the election of a brand-new committee!" Minute rules means tiny ones. Picture it. The steering committee posts a list: shares capped at three minutes, phones in a basket at the door, latecomers at the back. Nobody voted on it. Each rule sounds sensible, which is exactly how a committee drifts from serving to governing. The remedy is the one Bill named, and it belongs to the group: a new committee. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) puts the decision in "our group conscience," not with whoever holds the clipboard. Test it tonight: ask which of the rules in your room the group actually voted on.

2dd85398bc28.t: An A.A. committee has the authority to serve and never to command. Which rules in my room did the group itself vote on?

f2cfbc27c037.t: Twelve months. Twelve Traditions. October is Tradition 10.

d14ccd076d8b.t: A way out for half a million alcoholics died because it took sides in public fights, and the first thing it lost was the drunk. Bill W. told the story of the Washingtonians, a movement a century older than A.A. (A.A. Comes of Age): "At first the society was composed entirely of alcoholics trying to help one another." Their membership "passed the five hundred thousand mark." Then they "permitted politicians and reformers, both alcoholic and nonalcoholic, to use the society for their own purposes." Speakers took sides on slavery. Some became temperance crusaders, out to dry up the whole country. "Within a very few years they had completely lost their effectiveness in helping alcoholics, and the society collapsed." That is why the long form of Tradition 10 names "alcohol reform" by name (Big Book, p. 565). A drinker who hears that the rooms are for or against his party, his church or his bar has one more reason never to walk in. Today the pull comes as a campaign: a drinking law, a funding fight, and somebody speaking for "the recovery community" as if the people in the rooms had signed on. Test it tonight: ask whether your meeting's name appears anywhere outside the room, on anybody's side.

b3fb748fcc62.t: Half a million sober alcoholics lost their power to help the next drunk once their society took sides in public. Is there a drinker who would stay out of my room because of a side it has taken?

3ef28c10fd3c.t: <0>Short form: pp. 561–562. Long form: pp. 563–566.</0> If you only ever read one, read the long one.

595857dafcc4.t: The Twelve Traditions were adopted in 1950 for one reason: to stop A.A. from being <0>owned</0>. Not owned by a benefactor, not by a treatment centre, not by whoever happened to be paying the rent. They are the Fellowship's constitution — written out of near-misses A.A. actually lived through.

4ebe53edf3ef.t: Most of what circulates online quotes only the short form (pp. 561–562) and quietly drops the rest. So we front-load <0>the Long Form, pp. 563–566</0> — where the Traditions actually say what they mean. Tradition 3's clause that a group is A.A. only if "as a group, they have no other affiliation"? That exists <1>only</1> in the Long Form. It's the clause that says no treatment centre can own an A.A. group. It's also the clause the internet forgot.

6403ca028b80.t: One more thing, because it gets blurred constantly: <0>the Traditions are governance, not theology.</0> They bind A.A. groups and the Fellowship — not individuals. They are not a rulebook for your personal life.

0603f72e2225.t: <0>How August reads.</0> The month opens day-by-day — one angle on the Tradition at a time, where groups go wrong with it and the reason it was written — then settles into five questions, run straight through: <1>what specifically threatened A.A.</1> · <2>how the founders solved it before there was a Tradition</2> · <3>where that same danger lives now</3> · <4>how a group drifts off it on its own</4> · <5>how it gets hollowed out from outside</5>. Anything inside quotation marks is A.A.'s own wording, printed exactly, with the source named at the foot of the reading. The explaining around it is ours — plain modern English, and scenes drawn to show how the Tradition actually plays out. You should always be able to tell which is which.

f20a717fb6fc.t: January 1 — "Emotional Dynamite." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. A fellowship of drunks was supposed to blow itself apart, and Tradition One is the reason it did

e0159af49084.t: A fellowship of drunks was supposed to blow itself apart, and Tradition One is the reason it didn't. Bill W. remembered what the experts said when A.A. was new (A.A. Comes of Age): "This fellowship of alcoholics is emotional dynamite. Its neurotic content can blow it to bits." Neurotic means ruled by fear and nerves. The early members were asking the same thing: "would we blow up or could we stay together?" The Long Form gives the answer they found (Big Book, p. 563): "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole. A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die. Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward." Read the order. The group first, because the drunk who calls tonight needs a room that is still standing. The member close behind, never thrown away. The danger was never one person with an opinion. It was a room splitting into camps until nobody was left to answer the phone. Today the charge is often lit from outside: a program wants the meeting, and the members split over whether to let it have it. Test it tonight: if your group blew apart tomorrow, which piece would the next drunk still find with its doors open?

5d53dc206cd3.t: The experts said a fellowship of drunks would blow itself to bits, and Tradition One is how it held. Is anything in my group pulling the room into camps right now?

6342d51eb263.t: January 10 — "Glory and Money." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. The forces that take over an A.A. room from outside are the same four Bill W. found inside, and th

162d00987e3c.t: The forces that take over an A.A. room from outside are the same four Bill W. found inside, and they always arrive looking righteous. He said early A.A. met threats worse than alcohol (A.A. Comes of Age): "These were the desires for power, for domination, for glory, and for money. They were all the more dangerous because they were invariably powered by self-righteousness, self-justification, and the destructive power of anger, usually masquerading as righteous indignation." Masquerading means wearing a disguise. Now look at a room taken over from outside. A facility gets power: its staff decide who chairs. It gets domination: the format is the program's. It gets glory: the brochure says it hosts A.A. And it gets money: the meeting is part of what a client's insurer or the government pays for. Every piece is explained as helping more alcoholics, and that explanation is the self-righteousness. The Long Form keeps the whole above any part of it (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence our common welfare comes first." A.A.'s welfare, not a facility's. A program can mean well and still want all four. Test it tonight: name who gains power, glory or money from your meeting existing, and ask whether any of them is a member of the group.

c7cf9db8c31b.t: Power, domination, glory and money are the four that split A.A., and they come in from outside dressed as help. Who gains any of the four from my meeting?

77e1b870c297.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 1 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy, Tradition One: power, domination, glory, money).

7f0ff3e611a3.t: January 11 — "Ominous Foretaste." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. The first great test of A.A. unity came from success, when a magazine article sent thousands of

0ddd9d354439.t: The first great test of A.A. unity came from success, when a magazine article sent thousands of drunks looking for groups that barely existed. March 1941: Jack Alexander's piece in the Saturday Evening Post. Bill W. (A.A. Comes of Age): "A real Niagara then broke loose, and we were deluged with letters and with alcoholics by the thousands." Then the strain on the groups: "There had already been an ominous foretaste of the problems of mushrooming groups; quarrels over leadership, money, membership, clubs, exploitation of A.A.'s name, panhandling, and even romancing." Ominous means threatening; mushrooming means springing up fast. And as hundreds of new groups tried to form, "the specters of disunity and collapse grew to frightening proportions." A specter is a ghost. Every quarrel on that list is about a group's own affairs, and every one of them could split a room. The Long Form answers all of them with one order (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence our common welfare comes first." Not my leadership, my money, my club, my name. Today the same list comes back whenever a meeting grows fast or gets noticed: who runs it, who holds the money, whose name is on the door. Test it tonight: pick one word from Bill's list and ask whether it is a fight in your group right now.

1930d61927ac.t: A.A.'s first big test of unity was a flood of new drunks and a list of quarrels that could split any group. Which quarrel on that list is alive in my group?

4705c8e123b5.t: January 12 — "Wrecked in the Same Vessel." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. Before any Tradition was written, the first groups held together because the next man i

72ad6fd00744.t: Before any Tradition was written, the first groups held together because the next man in the door mattered more than anyone's rank. The Big Book, written in 1939, describes the early fellowship (Big Book, p. 161): "No one is too discredited or has sunk too low to be welcomed cordially—if he means business. Social distinctions, petty rivalries and jealousies—these are laughed out of countenance." Countenance here means approval: rivalries got laughed out of the room. Then the reason, in two pieces: "Being wrecked in the same vessel" and "with hearts and minds attuned to the welfare of others". Attuned means tuned in, like a radio. The welfare of others came first because the newcomer was the whole point of meeting. Seven years later the Long Form wrote down the same order (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward." Nobody had to vote on it then. They were busy putting new men in the hospital and visiting them afterward. Today the rivalries that early A.A. laughed off come back as rank: sober time, service titles, which program you came out of. Test it tonight: look at who sits where in your room, and ask whether any rivalry there is being taken seriously instead of laughed out.

6fd17fb6848a.t: The first groups laughed rivalries out of the room because the newcomer came first. Is any rank in my group being taken more seriously than the next drunk?

4be72fc3c27c.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 1 (Big Book, p. 563); Big Book pp. 159 and 161 (A Vision for You).

e817afaedf2f.t: January 13 — "The Powerful Cement." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. A shared disaster can fill a room, but the Big Book says it was never what held A.A. together.

2f0fa2a092c2.t: A shared disaster can fill a room, but the Big Book says it was never what held A.A. together. The Big Book (p. 17): "We are like the passengers of a great liner the moment after rescue from shipwreck when camaraderie, joyousness and democracy pervade the vessel from steerage to Captain's table." Steerage was the cheapest deck. Then the warning: "The feeling of having shared in a common peril is one element in the powerful cement which binds us. But that in itself would never have held us together as we are now joined." What held them was the next thing it names: "a common solution". Today many rooms are filled by something else again: a court order, a probation condition, a facility van that drops a dozen clients at seven and collects them at eight. The chairs are full, and the people in them share a requirement, not a peril or a solution. When the order runs out, they are gone, and a room built on them goes too. The Long Form asks for a whole that lives on its own (Big Book, p. 563): "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die." A requirement can't keep a group alive. Test it tonight: if every court slip and facility van stopped tomorrow, would your group still have enough members to open its doors?

368d751434d5.t: Shared trouble fills a room for a while, but only a common solution holds a group together. What is holding my group together?

a2377ca7c0a7.t: January 14 — "To Keep One Man." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. A group breaks Tradition One when it turns the Long Form's order around and puts one member's comf

62426518b82d.t: A group breaks Tradition One when it turns the Long Form's order around and puts one member's comfort ahead of the room. The order is plain (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward." Here is how it gets turned around. The group has outgrown its room, and newcomers stand along the back wall. A bigger hall is free on the same night. The group's best-known member, twenty years sober, says he won't follow. He likes the small room; he says so at the business meeting and hints he will go somewhere else. Nobody wants to lose him, and the vote goes his way. Within a year the people who stood at the back have stopped coming, because there was never anywhere to sit, and the group is twelve old friends. Nobody was cruel. The group arranged itself around one man, and the next drunk was the one given up. The essay that opens the Traditions in the Big Book says what a group is for (Big Book, p. 561): "We alcoholics see that we must work together and hang together, else most of us will finally die alone." Most of us, not the best known of us. Test it tonight: ask whose comfort your group arranges itself around, and look at who is standing at the back.

e4fde8b00807.t: The Long Form puts the room first and the member close behind, and a group can turn that around without noticing. Whose comfort is my group arranged around?

534458332abb.t: January 15 — "Not on Pioneers." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. In 1950 A.A. decided its unity would rest on principles, not people, and a meeting held together b

8312e5630063.t: In 1950 A.A. decided its unity would rest on principles, not people, and a meeting held together by a facility's staff has gone back to resting on people. That July, A.A.'s first international convention, in Cleveland, confirmed the Traditions. Bill W. said why it had to be then (A.A. Comes of Age): "In the future we could no longer depend upon the authority and influence of our pioneering people for A.A. unity. Henceforth we would have to rely upon spiritual principles, as set forth in the Twelve Traditions." If A.A. could not lean on its own founders, a group cannot lean on a counsellor. Yet that is how many rooms are held now: one staff member unlocks the door, picks the reader and keeps the list. The members never meet on their own business, so there is no group conscience to fall back on. When the contract ends or the staff member moves on, the meeting ends too. Bill wrote, on linking A.A. to other projects (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 25): "to maintain our unity is surely our greatest obligation". The Long Form says why (Big Book, p. 563): "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die." Test it tonight: if the person who unlocks your meeting's door left tomorrow, ask whether the members would know how to keep it open.

019f716a6de5.t: A.A. stopped leaning on its founders in 1950 so that unity would never rest on a person again. Does my meeting rest on a person, or on its members?

bd47144188ca.t: January 16 — "Worse Than the Worst." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. The quickest way for a group to wreck its own unity is to try to protect it with rules. Bill

a4861e9872a8.t: The quickest way for a group to wreck its own unity is to try to protect it with rules. Bill W. described it in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 12): "At this point the group enters the rule and regulation phase." Committees get the power to filter out undesirables. "Recalcitrants are cast into the outer darkness; respectable busybodies throw stones at the sinners." Recalcitrant means stubborn, refusing to fall in line. Then the result: "Most attempts at enforcement generate such waves of dissension and intolerance in the group that this condition is presently recognized to be worse for the group life than the very worst that the worst ever did." Dissension is open quarrelling. The rules meant to save the group split it. That is why the Long Form of Tradition One (Big Book, p. 563) puts "our common welfare" first and hands nobody a rulebook to enforce it with. A group stays whole by keeping its door open, not by guarding it. Today the rulebook often arrives ready-made: attendance sheets, behaviour contracts, a list of who may share and who may not, written by a program for its own clients. Test it tonight: ask whether your group has any rule that could put a drinker out, and who wrote it.

fab638cc4223.t: Bill W. saw groups that enforced rules split worse than any drunk had ever split them. Does my group have a rule somebody is waiting to enforce?

9ac992ad5cc2.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 1 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 12 (Bill W., 1946: Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?).

ff2ca9bf37a6.t: January 17 — "Its Own Rights." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. In the first groups the sacrifice for unity ran both ways: the members gave things up for the group

a841d28ee11f.t: In the first groups the sacrifice for unity ran both ways: the members gave things up for the group, and the group gave things up for each member. Bill W. looked back on it (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 49): "We found that each of us had to make willing sacrifices for the group itself, sacrifices for the common welfare. The group, in turn, found that it had to give up many of its own rights for the protection and welfare of each member, and for A.A. as a whole." In turn. A group does not get to take everything and give nothing back. That is the Long Form's last sentence for Tradition One (Big Book, p. 563), written for groups: "Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward." Close afterward means right behind. A member gives up his ambitions in the room. The group, in return, gives up its rights over him: no right to run his life, to charge him, to make him perform to belong. Those are the kinds of rights a group surrenders so that a drunk can walk in and stay. Today some rooms take them back quietly, a check-in sheet here, a required share there. Test it tonight: name one right over its members your group has given up, and ask whether anyone is taking it back.

598ee1dfef10.t: Tradition One makes every member the same size, and the threat today is a room that quietly sorts its people into two kinds. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole." Each member: not each member who chose to come, not each member in good standing. The Big Book's foreword says why the room can't be sorted (Big Book, p. xx): "Alcohol being no respecter of persons, we are an accurate cross section of America, and in distant lands, the same democratic evening-up process is now going on." No respecter of persons means it does not care who you are. Evening-up means levelling: whoever you were outside, in the room you are one more drunk. Now watch a meeting where a facility's van pulls up. The clients file in together, sit in a block, sign a sheet, and leave together before the coffee. The members sit on the other side. Nobody planned it, but there are now two rooms in one: people who are there because a program sent them, and people who belong. The client never learns that he belongs too. Test it tonight: look at where people sit, and ask whether a newcomer off a van would know this room is his.

f3f9555d998a.t: A group can split itself without a single argument, just by letting the same few friends keep the jobs. Picture it. The secretary hands the key to his friend, who hands it back a year later. The treasurer has been treasurer since anyone can remember. The real business happens at the friends' table after everyone else has gone home. Nobody is thrown out. The rest simply stop coming to anything but the meeting, and then some stop coming to that. Bill W. saw it at the first New York club, where the steering committees, he wrote (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 18), "tried to nominate their friends to succeed them" and found, to their dismay, that sober drunks would not be steered. A group run by a circle is really two groups: the circle, and everyone else. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) says each member "is but a small part of a great whole", and that includes the members holding the keys. Their part is no bigger for holding them. Today the circle often has an outside friend as well: the program that rents the room deals with the same two people every year, and the group's business gets done in its office. Test it tonight: ask when your group last put someone new in every service job.

91d46e51dc27.t: A group run by the same few friends has split in two, whether anyone noticed or not. When did my group last hand its jobs to someone new?

7c316eb6bb56.t: January 2 — "Counting Noses." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. Before there was a word of Tradition, two men counted their sober friends and got scared about wheth

ec79001505ec.t: Before there was a word of Tradition, two men counted their sober friends and got scared about whether they could stay together. A November day in 1937, Dr. Bob's living room in Akron. Bill W. told it at St. Louis (A.A. Comes of Age): "All told we figured that upwards of forty alcoholics were staying bone dry." They wept for joy. Then the fear came: "Would the forces that everywhere divide society finally invade and smash us up". The Steps were not yet written and the book was scarcely an idea. There were no rules to lean on, only the question: "How could we possibly hang together and cling to our new life line". A life line is the rope thrown to someone drowning. Nine years later that fear became the second sentence of the Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die." Not should. Must. Forty sober drunks were very nearly the whole of A.A. that afternoon, and if they split, there was nothing left for the forty-first. Today the forty-first is still out there, and a room is still all that stands between him and the bottle. Test it tonight: count the noses in your room, and ask what would be left for the next one through the door if this group came apart.

f8e157e83532.t: Forty sober drunks were nearly all of A.A. once, and their first fear was coming apart. What would be left for the next one if my group split?

cbb0c91847df.t: January 20 — "At His Destination." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. A.A. stays one fellowship from town to town only while no group in it belongs to anyone else, a

e9a3368b5758.t: A.A. stays one fellowship from town to town only while no group in it belongs to anyone else, and capture is what breaks that. In 1939 the book's writers set down a hope (Big Book, p. 162): "Some day we hope that every alcoholic who journeys will find a Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous at his destination." Not a fellowship. The same one. A drunk who got sober in one city could walk into a room in another and find the same thing: free, run by its members, belonging to the alcoholics in it. That sameness is what the Long Form calls "a great whole" (Big Book, p. 563). Every group is a small part of it, the way every member is. Now a man on a job far from home looks up a meeting and finds that the only one in town is held inside a treatment facility. The door is locked after eight. Staff run the format. A sign says the meeting is for residents and alumni. The schedule says A.A.; nothing else in the room does. Every room like it makes the name mean a little less, and the next traveller trusts it a little less. Test it tonight: if a stranger walked in from out of town, would he find the A.A. he left behind?

57e94d896025.t: A.A. is one fellowship everywhere only while no group belongs to anyone. Would a sober stranger from another city recognise my room?

a69e8b7e2d5c.t: Like People in a Sinking Ship

2130a168eee0.t: The common welfare comes first because of the people who are not in the room yet, and the Big Book says where they are. Chapter 11 (Big Book, p. 152): "Near you, alcoholics are dying helplessly like people in a sinking ship." Near you, tonight. That is the weight behind the Long Form's second sentence (Big Book, p. 563): "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die." Not a club that would be missed. A lifeboat. A group is one of the boats that goes out to the ship, and a group that sinks itself in a fight is one boat fewer. The fight is never about the drowning. It is about who chairs, whose format, whose literature, whose turn, and for the weeks it lasts the room is busy with itself. Nobody calls back the number on the list, because nobody is sure who has the phone. The man who walks in on the worst night of it hears shouting and decides he was right to stay away. Today's version is a room so taken up with its own business that the drunk becomes an interruption. Test it tonight: ask what your group's last big argument was about, and whether the drunk still out there came up in it once.

4b5cf5bfa909.t: The group comes first because alcoholics are drowning near it tonight. Has my group ever been too busy with itself to notice?

d1c3f7786a29.t: January 22 — "Those Damned Traditions." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. When the Traditions were first printed, most groups did not want them, and the only groups

55d7093de39b.t: When the Traditions were first printed, most groups did not want them, and the only groups that listened were the ones already in trouble. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "When first published the Traditions got a mixed reception. Only groups in dire trouble took them seriously." The angriest objections came from groups with long lists of protective rules. The rest were bored. Bill went around speaking on them, and the letters came back asking him to tell his drinking story instead: "But please don't talk any more about those damned Traditions." So the groups that learned the Traditions first learned them the hard way, in the middle of trouble. Then the rest caught up: "Several years later it was recognized that the Twelve Traditions were going to be just as necessary to the life of our society" as the Steps were to each member. A group that waits for trouble before it reads Tradition One reads it too late, with half the room already gone. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) is four sentences long and can be read in under a minute. Today the Traditions are still the part people skip: rushed through at the top of the meeting, or not read at all. Test it tonight: ask your group when it last spent a business meeting on one Tradition, from start to finish.

7ac1234840e2.t: The first groups to take the Traditions seriously were the ones already falling apart. Would my group read Tradition One before trouble, or after?

9a9461639c15.t: January 23 — "Nobody Can Compel." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. Nobody can enforce Tradition One on a group, and the rumour that somebody can is one of the ways

6adc353562ed.t: Nobody can enforce Tradition One on a group, and the rumour that somebody can is one of the ways rooms get taken over. Bill W. wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "Nowhere in A.A. is there to be seen any constituted human authority that can compel an A.A. group to do anything." Constituted means officially set up. No office, no committee, no old-timer, no staff member. So why do groups keep the Traditions at all? The same page: "The A.A. groups follow these other traditional principles for the very same reason that the individual A.A. follows the Twelve Steps to recovery. Groups see they would disintegrate if they didn't". Disintegrate means fall to pieces. A group keeps the Long Form's "our common welfare comes first" (Big Book, p. 563) because it has seen what happens when it doesn't, not because someone checks. Today the rumour runs the other way. A facility hands out its meeting guidelines and calls them A.A. rules. A staff member tells a room it will be shut down for breaking a Tradition. None of them has that power, and a group that believes they do has already given its conscience away. Test it tonight: when anyone says your group must do something, ask who in A.A. could make it.

f4ee1cb99cb2.t: No one in A.A. can force a group to do anything; groups keep the Traditions because they have seen groups fall apart without them. Who does my group believe could shut it down?

22938d925971.t: January 24 — "Not Yet Reached." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. A group breaks Tradition One when it decides the common welfare means the people already in the ro

84ec051a21cb.t: A group breaks Tradition One when it decides the common welfare means the people already in the room. Picture the business meeting. The hospital meeting on Thursdays is a long drive and only two members ever go. The group's number on the phone list rings at bad hours, and the member who answers it is tired. Someone moves that the group drop both. It passes, nine to three. The room is more comfortable by Friday, and no one in it is worse off. The ones worse off were not there to vote. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) says "our common welfare comes first", and the essay two pages earlier says whose welfare that is (Big Book, p. 561): "A.A. can, of course, mean just as much to uncounted alcoholics not yet reached." Uncounted means nobody knows how many. They are part of the common welfare before they ever find the door. A group that keeps itself comfortable by closing its windows is living for itself. Today the vote often comes with relief, because a program now runs the hospital meeting and the group feels free to stop. Test it tonight: ask what your group still does that reaches anyone who isn't already in the room.

da04d6e33a30.t: A group is most often captured through one of its own members: the one who loves A.A. and also works in the alcohol field. Bill W. described him in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "He strongly feels that A.A. ought to place its name and financial credit squarely behind any first-rate research, hospital or educational project. Seeing that A.A. now makes the headlines, he argues that we should freely loan out our huge goodwill." Goodwill is the trust people have in a name. Bill added: "The judgment of this enthusiast is sometimes beclouded by the fact he wants to make a career." Beclouded means fogged over. His answer, on the same page: "neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A." Today the enthusiast is a counsellor or program manager who also has a home group. He brings his clients, offers the program's room for free, and puts the meeting on the program's brochure. Each step looks like help, and within a year the group answers to his employer. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence our common welfare comes first." His career is not part of it. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your group earns a living from the people it serves, and what the group has agreed to through him.

dd114f107cce.t: January 26 — "Material Things." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. Money is one of the oldest ways a group comes apart, and the early members saw it coming before th

c6aaa6226c08.t: Money is one of the oldest ways a group comes apart, and the early members saw it coming before they had a treasury to fight over. Bill W. wrote in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 27): "We had no group funds, hence no group money troubles." Those were the first years: meetings in homes, coffee and sandwiches. Then groups rented rooms and opened clubs, and money came in with them. Bill named the danger: "Knowing that quarrels over material things have crushed the spirit of many a good undertaking, it is often thought that too much money may prove an evil for us too." Material things are money and property, as against the reason the group meets. A quarrel over the basket can empty a room faster than a quarrel over anything said in it: who spent what, who kept the receipts, whether the reserve should be bigger. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) puts "our common welfare" first, and the treasury exists for the common welfare, never the other way round. Today the money quarrel has a newer shape: a group with a large balance, or a facility offering to cover the rent, and the members split over who controls it. Test it tonight: ask how much money your group holds, and whether anyone can say what it is for.

0e627e9ff34c.t: January 27 — "Led, Not Pushed." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. The first A.A.s learned early that drunks cannot be held together by pressure, and the lesson cost

29c1f5bb26c4.t: The first A.A.s learned early that drunks cannot be held together by pressure, and the lesson cost them a friendship. Until 1937 the New York alcoholics met alongside the Oxford Groups, a religious movement Bill had joined when he got sober. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "But in the latter part of that year we most reluctantly parted company with these great friends." Why? The drunks would not stand for being run. "They always had to be led, not pushed." They would not accept the Oxford Groups' team guidance over their private lives: "It was too authoritarian for them." Authoritarian means demanding obedience. Bill did not hide what the parting cost: "Our debt to them, nevertheless, was and is immense, and so the final breakaway was very painful." So A.A.'s unity was never going to be the kind enforced from above. It had to be the kind the Long Form describes (Big Book, p. 563): "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole." Nobody is the boss of the whole. Today the pushing comes back as program rules dressed up as A.A.: check in, report your progress, be told what to share. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your room is pushing a member to do something A.A. never asked of anyone.

fae908a38457.t: A.A.'s first members parted from friends they owed a great deal rather than push drunks around. Is anyone in my room being pushed?

5c4d0e3852a8.t: January 28 — "So We Had to Evolve." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. The rumour is that Tradition One is a rule for your character; the Big Book says the Tradition

b45e6ea75432.t: The rumour is that Tradition One is a rule for your character; the Big Book says the Traditions were made for groups. The Foreword to the Second Edition (Big Book, p. xix): "As we discovered the principles by which the individual alcoholic could live, so we had to evolve principles by which the A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole could survive and function effectively." Two sets of principles: the Steps for the alcoholic's life, the Traditions for the life of the groups. Evolve means grow out of experience; nobody handed them down. Now listen to how Tradition One often gets taught: put others first, be a team player, don't make waves, your needs come last. Every one of those is advice to a person about himself. Read the Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) as it is written: "Hence our common welfare comes first." Our welfare, the group's and A.A.'s. It sets the order of business for a group, not the order of a member's heart. A group that turns its Traditions into talks on members' attitudes has nothing left to govern itself with. Test it tonight: the next time someone explains Tradition One at your meeting, listen for whether they are talking about the group or about you.

98d67acf0e9b.t: The Traditions are principles for groups and for A.A. as a whole, not twelve more lessons for the member. When my group talks about Tradition One, whose behaviour is it talking about?

463f92070987.t: January 29 — "One Alcoholic Talks With Another." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. A group can keep perfect order and still break Tradition One, if nobody in it eve

e2a976e7d3c6.t: A group can keep perfect order and still break Tradition One, if nobody in it ever talks to the new man. Picture a well-run meeting. It starts on time, the readings are read, the shares are good, the closing is said together. Then the regulars head for their cars in twos and threes, and the newcomer by the door, who came alone, goes home alone. Nobody was unkind. Nobody was anything. The Foreword to the Third Edition says where A.A. actually happens (Big Book, p. xxii): "In spite of the great increase in the size and the span of this Fellowship, at its core it remains simple and personal. Each day, somewhere in the world, recovery begins when one alcoholic talks with another alcoholic". The "great whole" of the Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) is made of those conversations, one drunk to another. A room of sober people who only talk to each other has become a closed circle, and a closed circle is a part of nothing. Today the gap often gets filled from outside: the newcomer leaves with a program's pamphlet and a counsellor's card instead of a member's phone number. Test it tonight: before you leave, find out whether the newest person in the room is going home with anyone's number.

7df4fd0b51d2.t: A.A. is held together by one alcoholic talking to another, not by a well-run hour. Who in my room went home tonight without being talked to?

ffe1b047f2ec.t: January 3 — "A Small Part." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. Tradition One makes every A.A. group a small part of one whole, and a meeting that belongs to somethin

00e01053baf4.t: Tradition One makes every A.A. group a small part of one whole, and a meeting that belongs to something else can't keep that promise. The Long Form opens (Big Book, p. 563): "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole." The whole is named: Alcoholics Anonymous. Not a clinic, not a recovery program, not a county service. The rumour runs the other way. In rooms run by facilities, unity gets taught as getting along with the house: keep to the schedule, don't question the staff, don't make trouble for the program that lets you meet. That is unity with a business. The short form says whose unity a drunk's life hangs on (Big Book, p. 562): "personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity." A.A. unity means groups that answer to their own members, joined to every other group by the same Traditions, with no owner, no contract and no fee. A meeting on a facility's schedule is also a small part of a great whole. The whole is the facility. Its staff can move the time, change the format or close the door, and none of them answers to the drunks in the chairs. Test it tonight: ask what your meeting is a small part of, and who could close it.

8865805df4f0.t: The Long Form names the whole every group belongs to, and it is A.A., not a program. What is my meeting really a part of?

ac52fe13ec6e.t: January 30 — "Benders." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. Capture doesn't only happen one group at a time; a whole town's groups can be taken together, and Bill war

a7875f1f33b9.t: Capture doesn't only happen one group at a time; a whole town's groups can be taken together, and Bill warned that movements go on binges too. Bill W. wrote in his foreword to the Traditions pamphlet (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 5): "For whole movements have, before now, gone on benders, too!" A bender is a drinking spree that runs for days. On the same page: "But A.A. unity cannot automatically preserve itself." A town's version goes like this. A big program offers to print one meeting list for the whole city, free. The list is handsome and everyone uses it. Next year the program asks listed meetings to post its intake number. Then to report attendance. Then to sign court cards its way. Group by group, each says yes, because everyone else did. Nobody voted to join anything, but the city's meetings now run on one outside body's terms. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die." In that town A.A. is still alive, on someone else's terms. Test it tonight: ask who prints your town's meeting list, and what a group has to do to stay on it.

4434019efde5.t: A whole city's groups can be captured together, one reasonable yes at a time. What does my group have to do to stay on the list it is on?

7ffd0d671cbe.t: January 31 — "Out of Great Weakness." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. The month ends where Bill ended his story of A.A.'s unity: it was forged under the threat of

8e75cefbb1d7.t: The month ends where Bill ended his story of A.A.'s unity: it was forged under the threat of collapse, and it lasts only while the groups keep choosing it. Bill W., at St. Louis in 1955 (A.A. Comes of Age): "Ours is not the usual success story; rather it is the story of how, under God's grace, an unsuspected strength has arisen out of great weakness; of how, under threats of disunity and collapse, world-wide unity and brotherhood have been forged." Forged means hammered into shape in the heat. And he said what holds it now. The Traditions, he said, "represent the distilled experience of our past, and we rely on them to carry us in unity through the challenges and dangers which the future may bring." The first of them is four sentences in the Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole. A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die. Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward." The whole first, the member close behind, and the drunk still out there the reason for both. Tomorrow, Tradition Two asks who decides for a group. Test it tonight: ask whether your group would still stand if every person in it were replaced, and why.

bfe164da40fe.t: A.A.'s unity was forged under threat, not handed down, and it lasts only as long as groups choose it. Would my group still stand if everyone in it were new?

bf9699b9907b.t: January 4 — "Rocking the Raft." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. A group can disagree as hard as it likes; it breaks Tradition One when a fight hardens into two ca

78920186c551.t: A group can disagree as hard as it likes; it breaks Tradition One when a fight hardens into two camps and the newcomer is caught between them. Bill W. compared the early days to a crew adrift in the Pacific after their plane went down (A.A. Comes of Age): "Nobody dared rock that raft, lest they all perish." Lest means for fear that. Then he admitted: "But some of our sick and careless members did rock the raft, and that scared us to death." Here is how a group rocks it now. The business meeting votes to move to a bigger room, nine to six. The six don't let it go. It comes back at the next business meeting, then at the coffee urn, then in shares. By spring the six have opened a meeting of their own, same night, same hour, two doors down. A new group is no harm; A.A. grows that way. The war is the harm. The man who came in that winter gets two phone numbers, and each one warns him about the other. The Long Form never asks a group to stop arguing. It asks what comes first (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence our common welfare comes first." Test it tonight: ask whether any old vote in your group is still being fought in front of the newcomers.

8d2e6cee68cf.t: Disagreement doesn't sink a group; camps do, with the newcomer in the middle. Is an old fight in my group still being carried into the meeting?

18a6874f607d.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 1 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy, Tradition One: the raft).

f13db7f9a078.t: January 5 — "Unity With Whom?." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. The short form's second half gets borrowed by programs that want the drunk to depend on them, and

43df89d50c8f.t: The short form's second half gets borrowed by programs that want the drunk to depend on them, and the Long Form takes it back. The short form (Big Book, p. 562): "personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity." Notice the letters: A.A. Not the program's, not the counsellor's, not the aftercare plan's. In a facility the line gets rewritten out loud: stay connected to us, stay in our groups, come back to our alumni meeting, because your recovery depends on it. The client hears Tradition One. What he is being sold is loyalty to a business. The Long Form says why unity matters, and the reason is the drunk, not a head count (Big Book, p. 563): "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die." Bill W. said it again in A.A.'s pamphlet on the Traditions (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 6): "Else, save few exceptions, we and our brother alcoholics throughout the world will surely resume the hopeless journey to oblivion." Oblivion means being blotted out, gone. A.A.'s unity keeps free rooms alive for that brother. A program's unity keeps its own seats filled. Test it tonight: when someone in your room says unity, ask unity with whom, and who gets paid when you keep it.

2527ecf24911.t: Tradition One says recovery depends on A.A. unity, and a program can borrow the words while selling loyalty to itself. When my room talks about unity, unity with whom?

2115df585ab4.t: January 6 — "Who Next?." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. The first thing early A.A. feared would kill it was the slip, and the groups learned it couldn't, so long

37c60ec01059.t: The first thing early A.A. feared would kill it was the slip, and the groups learned it couldn't, so long as the door stayed open. Bill W. (A.A. Comes of Age): "At first nearly every alcoholic we approached began to slip, if indeed he sobered up at all." A slip is a drink after getting sober. Each one hit the whole room. They would look at each other and wonder who was next: "We were afraid that alcohol might completely undo us." Years later Bill could say what the groups had learned. "Alcohol always threatens the individual," but, he went on, "we know that it cannot destroy the common welfare." That is the Long Form's last two sentences at work (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence our common welfare comes first. But individual welfare follows close afterward." The group outlives the slip, and the man who slipped is close behind, welcome back the night he walks in. Today the slip often gets treated the other way. In facility programs a drink can mean discharge, and a meeting run on the same house rules can leave a man feeling he has lost his seat. A.A.'s door was never the facility's door. Test it tonight: if a member came back tonight after drinking, would anything your group does make it harder for him to sit down?

d930ed581978.t: A slip can kill a man but it cannot kill the group, so the group keeps a seat for him. Would the one who slipped find his seat waiting in my room?

bc6dea569d5c.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 1 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy, Tradition One: the fear of slips).

91a896535f5b.t: January 7 — "Every Contestant." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. Tradition One was not handed down from above; it was dug out of the mail from groups that were fig

5e14f2517034.t: Tradition One was not handed down from above; it was dug out of the mail from groups that were fighting. By 1945 letters about group problems filled the files in New York. Bill W. (A.A. Comes of Age): "It seemed as if every contestant in every group argument wrote us during this confused and exciting period." A contestant is someone on one side of a fight. Then: "The basic ideas for the Twelve Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous came directly out of this vast correspondence." And: "A code of traditions could not, of course, ever become rule or law. But it might act as a guide for our Trustees, Headquarters people, and especially for A.A. groups with growing pains." The first version went into print in the Grapevine in May 1946, the Long Form you can still read (Big Book, p. 563): "Each member of Alcoholics Anonymous is but a small part of a great whole." It was written for groups, out of groups' own wreckage, so the next group would not have to learn it by losing members. Today it is rarely read where it was meant to be used, the business meeting, and rooms run by others hold no business meeting at all. Test it tonight: ask when your group last read the Long Form aloud at a business meeting, or whether it holds one.

817044bf814a.t: Tradition One was written from the letters of groups that were fighting, as a guide for groups. Does my group ever read it where it was meant to be used?

3039af6e4c43.t: January 8 — "Close Afterward." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. Tradition One puts the group first, and in the very next breath refuses to throw the member away. T

22af5239a86b.t: Tradition One puts the group first, and in the very next breath refuses to throw the member away. The Long Form's last sentence (Big Book, p. 563): "But individual welfare follows close afterward." Close afterward means right behind, not forgotten. The rumour leaves that sentence off. Then unity becomes a club: the member who asks who pays for the room, or why staff chair the meeting, is told he is hurting unity and should keep his head down. That is conformity, and the Long Form rules it out a few lines further down the same page, in Tradition Three: A.A. membership must never "depend upon money or conformity." Bill W. put the order in plain words (A.A. Comes of Age): "Probably no society sets a higher value on the personal welfare of the individual member than does A.A." And of all twelve Traditions: "The Traditions guarantee the equality of all members and the independence of all groups." Equal members, independent groups. A room where questions about who runs it are out of order is not protecting A.A. unity; it is protecting whoever runs the room. Test it tonight: ask out loud who decides how your meeting is run, and notice whether anyone tells you the question hurts unity.

ad225a2fee8a.t: The Long Form puts the member close behind the group, and never asks him to stop asking questions. Who in my room has been told a question hurts unity?

077bcff482c0.t: January 9 — "Violently Took Sides." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 1: Our common welfare should come first; personal recovery depends upon A.A. unity. A group breaks Tradition One when it turns its business meeting into a court over members' pri

44aa8ecf27f8.t: A group breaks Tradition One when it turns its business meeting into a court over members' private lives. Early A.A. learned this through what Bill W. called the triangle, an affair between members. He described what followed (A.A. Comes of Age): "People violently took sides." Whole groups, he wrote, "got into uproars, and a number of people got drunk." Then: "We trembled for A.A.'s reputation and for its survival." Here is how it happens now. Two members, both married to other people, leave together one night, and the whole room knows by morning. At the next business meeting someone moves that the group take a position. It is about the group's good name, they say. It turns into an hour on who did what to whom. Half the room votes one way and half the other, and the group now has an official side in a private fight. Within a month four people have stopped coming, and one of them is drinking. Nothing in the Long Form makes a group the judge of anyone's marriage. The group's business is the common welfare (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence our common welfare comes first." The room the next drunk needs is not served by a verdict. Test it tonight: ask whether your business meeting has ever voted on a member's private life, and who stopped coming afterward.

1fb2e600bfed.t: A group that takes sides in a private fight splits itself, and drunks pay for the verdict. Has my group ever made itself a judge of a member's private life?

382ec48763cb.t: Picture a group that says yes to a big outside gift — a bequest, no strings, everyone relieved. For a while the basket feels optional. Then the next gift arrives with a quiet expectation. Then a dispute over money nobody in the room earned. The Long Form doesn't soften it: accepting large gifts, or any contribution "carrying any obligation whatever, is unwise," and nothing "can so surely destroy our spiritual heritage as futile disputes over property, money, and authority." The danger was never the dollar. It's what the dollar asks for later.

79436aa78c4f.t: Flip the scramble for money and you find the discipline underneath: keep a prudent reserve — enough to cover the room if giving dips — and send the rest on. The Long Form warns against treasuries that "accumulate funds for no stated A.A. purpose." Enough is holy. More than enough starts asking to be fought over.

d6cce0d3f732.t: June 1 — "Build and Operate Our Own." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from

a632fbaa3f1f.t: Tradition Six begins by naming the three things that pull a group off its job: money, property and authority. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Problems of money, property, and authority may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim." To divert something is to turn it off its course, and the course is the drunk who is still drinking. Bill W. admitted how close A.A. came to going the other way (A.A. Comes of Age): "At that time hospitals did not want us, so we thought we would build and operate our own." The list kept growing: teach the public, change the laws, take on every other problem too. "Yes, we did dream those dreams. How natural that was, since most alcoholics are bankrupt idealists." Every dream on that list needed buildings, budgets and someone in charge of them. Each one would have put property and authority at the center of a fellowship that worked because one drunk talked to another for nothing. They tried the hospitals, and the hospitals bogged down. Tradition Six is what they wrote down afterward. Today the dream comes back already built: a facility with beds, staff and a budget, offering to be A.A.'s hospital. Test it tonight: ask what your group owns, what it pays for, and whether any of it gets more attention than the newcomer.

ea32936314b7.t: The Long Form names money, property and authority as the things that turn a group away from the drunk. What in my group is starting to take the attention the newcomer should get?

bf5970e093f3.t: June 10 — "Twelfth Step Houses." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our p

306504154cdc.t: The A.A. name is the one thing every group owns together, and Tradition Six keeps it off buildings. The Long Form, speaking of clubs and hospitals (Big Book, p. 564): "Hence such facilities ought not to use the A.A. name." The early members had to apply it to their own places first. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "We found it imperative even inside A.A. to remove the A.A. name from clubs and Twelfth Step Houses." Imperative means it couldn't wait. Even A.A.'s own places had to give the name back. "These strenuous adventures implanted the deep-rooted conviction that in no circumstances could we endorse any related enterprise, no matter how good." Strenuous means exhausting. If members' own clubhouses couldn't carry the name, nothing outside can carry it on a group's say-so. Capture today goes through the name. A facility advertises A.A. meetings on site as a feature of what the client pays for, and a group that meets there goes along. The Traditions don't govern the facility. They govern the group, and the group decides whether its meeting is offered as part of someone's product. A group can ask to be left off the brochure, and it can move. Test it tonight: find every place your group's meeting is advertised, and ask whether anyone is using it to sell something.

3a9a44c09aee.t: It Is Going to Take Millions

474118707f4f.t: Tradition Six answered a threat from inside: A.A. wanting to become what the treatment industry is now. Bill W. remembered the argument over money (A.A. Comes of Age). One side said: "One alcoholic carries the message to another. Let's keep it that simple and stay out of money trouble." The other side said: "We need hospitals, paid therapists, traveling lecturers, rehabilitation centers, and heaven knows what else. It is going to take millions." And where would the millions come from? "Well, we will get it from the public, just as most other good works do." Read that list again: hospitals, paid therapists, rehabilitation centers. If that side had won, A.A. would own buildings, carry a payroll and answer to donors, and the free drunk at the door would have become a cost. The short form keeps the reason in its last words (Big Book, p. 562): "lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our primary purpose." Prestige means standing in other people's eyes. The Traditions kept the groups on the simple side and put the hospitals well outside A.A. Today the second list exists, fully built, outside A.A., and it often wants A.A.'s rooms inside it. Test it tonight: ask whether anything your group does would need more money than the basket brings in, and who would be paying for the rest.

9e7603785a49.t: Some members once wanted hospitals, paid therapists and rehabilitation centers, paid for by the public. Does anything my group does need money the basket can't cover?

0e84f595bc2d.t: June 12 — "Co-operate but Never Compete." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us f

d411b547832c.t: A.A.'s first case was found in a hospital A.A. never owned, and that is the pattern Tradition Six wrote down. The Big Book's foreword tells it (p. xvii): "Hence the two men set to work almost frantically upon alcoholics arriving in the ward of the Akron City Hospital." The two men were Bill W. and Dr. Bob. They didn't run the ward; they walked in and talked to drunks. Bill W. named friends in medicine (A.A. Comes of Age): "Here great friends like Dr. Silkworth and Sister Ignatia came to our aid." Doctors and nurses treated the body, members carried the message, and nobody's name went on anybody else's door. Bill put the rule in one line: "Certain that we can do together what we cannot do separately, we shall always co-operate but never compete." To compete would have meant A.A. opening hospitals of its own. To affiliate would have meant A.A. becoming part of theirs. The Long Form allows the middle and nothing more (Big Book, p. 564): a group "may cooperate with anyone." Cooperation is visiting, carrying the message where the drunks are, and staying a guest. Today it often runs backward: the facility runs the room and calls it A.A. Test it tonight: ask whether your group goes into places as a guest carrying the message, or sits in them as part of the program.

724d8e51ab6b.t: The founders carried the message into hospitals they never owned or joined. Is my group a guest where it meets, or part of the program?

4a6ac3fe2908.t: June 13 — "Bind Itself to No One." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our

9a8e8b0e8076.t: The last sentence of Tradition Six's Long Form is the shortest, and it usually gets broken with a signature. The Big Book (p. 564): "An A.A. group can bind itself to no one." To bind is to tie, or to put yourself under an obligation someone can hold you to. No one means no one: not the facility, the court, the funder, or the kind people who mean well. Read it as a rule about promises. A group may carry the message into a hospital or a jail as a guest. It may not promise anyone a meeting as part of their program, a weekly slot their clients are counted at, an attendance record it will keep for them, or a chair it will fill on their schedule. The moment a group owes a meeting to someone, that someone can call in the debt. Today the binding comes as paperwork: an agreement to provide an A.A. meeting for a program's clients, a form signed to keep a room, a promise to report who came. None of them looks like giving up the group's freedom. Each one is. A group bound to no one can say no tomorrow without asking leave. Test it tonight: ask whether your group has signed, promised or agreed to anything with anyone outside it, and what they could demand because of it.

db26d6e38243.t: The Long Form ends with a group bound to no one, and paperwork is how most groups get bound. What has my group signed or promised to anyone outside it?

7e599cabe3e8.t: June 14 — "Thank You to the Group." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from ou

16ac8c3b3483.t: A group can break Tradition Six out of gratitude, in one vote, with nobody meaning harm. The group has eleven hundred dollars more than it needs for rent and literature. The detox across town, where half the members first dried out, is short of money. Someone moves to give it the surplus, and the motion passes to applause. Two months later the detox's fundraising letter goes out, with the group listed among its supporters under its A.A. name. Nobody asked for that; it was the detox saying thank you. The short form (Big Book, p. 562): "An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise". In one vote the group did all three. It financed the detox, and the thank-you lent the group's name and turned it into an endorsement. Every drinker who reads that letter learns that A.A. backs that detox, and may decide A.A. is the detox. A group that pays for a facility has tied itself to it, and the drunk can no longer tell the two apart. Members can give what they like out of their own pockets. The basket was given to carry the message. Test it tonight: ask where your group's extra money goes, and whether anyone outside A.A. has ever thanked your group by name.

f91ed574cf39.t: A grateful vote can finance a facility and lend it the A.A. name at the same time. Where does my group's extra money go?

d6f61aa20be3.t: Grounded in: Short form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 562); long form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 564).

1cc5d5f57306.t: June 15 — "Whoever Pays." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our primary

ae961f6a0b47.t: The Long Form says whoever pays for a facility runs the facility, and capture is when they start running the group too. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 564): "Their management should be the sole responsibility of those people who financially support them." Sole means only. Those who pay for a club or hospital manage it, and nothing else. Bill W. watched the line crossed both ways at the early clubs (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 20): "if an A.A. rotating committee tries to boss the club corporation or if the corporation tries to run the A.A. affairs of those groups who may meet at the club, there is difficulty at once." A rotating committee is the group's elected servants, changed often so nobody stays in charge. His cure: "If an A.A. group wishes to use a given club, let them pay rent or split the meeting take with the club management." The meeting take is the basket. Rent keeps the two apart. The group is a tenant, not a department. Today the facility often pays for everything, asks no rent, and in return picks the chair, sets the format and decides who may come in. That is the payer managing an A.A. group, which the Long Form never allowed. Test it tonight: ask who pays for the room your group meets in, and what that payer gets to decide.

9215df62af78.t: Put the A.A. name on a fund drive for a good cause, and you have handed it to every promoter in town. In the 1940s some groups, desperate for hospital beds, started public campaigns to raise money for "A.A. hospitals" of their own. Bill W. wrote what followed (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 16): "Instantly all sorts of doubts are generated; the projects bog down. Conservative A.A.s realize that business ventures or solicitations carrying the A.A. endorsement are truly dangerous to us all. Were this practice to become general the lid would be off. Promoters, A.A. and otherwise, would have a field day." A promoter is someone who sells a scheme to the public. The beds were badly needed. The danger was the name on the appeal. So the Long Form moved hospitals out of the groups' hands (Big Book, p. 564): "Secondary aids to A.A., such as clubs or hospitals which require much property or administration, ought to be incorporated". Incorporated means set up as a separate body with its own owners. The group carries the message; the bed belongs to someone else. Today the field day is open: galas, campaigns and appeals that use A.A.'s name, or "the recovery community," to raise money for buildings no A.A. group will ever own. Test it tonight: has your group's name, or A.A.'s, ever appeared on somebody's appeal for money?

b39deeeb5f81.t: June 17 — "His Work and Ours." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our pri

333e93829b6b.t: Before there was a Tradition Six, the Big Book already showed a hospital and A.A. working side by side without belonging to each other. Writing in 1939 about one eastern city, the book describes (Big Book, p. 162) "a well-known hospital for the treatment of alcoholic and drug addiction." Then: "We are greatly indebted to the doctor in attendance there, for he, although it might prejudice his own work, has told us of his belief in ours." His own work, and ours: two jobs with two owners. The doctor ran his ward: "Every few days this doctor suggests our approach to one of his patients." And A.A.'s part? "Many of us, former patients, go there to help." Members walked in as visitors and went home again. The hospital never became A.A.'s, and A.A. never became the hospital's. Seven years later the Long Form wrote that habit down: hospitals stay well outside A.A. and under doctors. Today the two jobs get folded into one. A facility runs the bed, the counselling and an "A.A. meeting" on its own timetable, so the visitor has become staff and the meeting has become part of the stay. Test it tonight: when your group carries the message into a hospital or detox, is it a guest there, or part of the program?

2423e26f6a9c.t: In 1939 the doctor had his work and A.A. had its own, and neither owned the other. When my group goes into a facility, whose work is it doing?

f6a6fbc17b1c.t: June 18 — "A Central A.A. Institution." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us fro

ca6404955cba.t: A secondary aid becomes a threat the day people start believing they can't recover without it. In the 1940s it was the A.A. club, a rented hall with coffee and company, and Bill W. watched members lean on it (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 17): "We might conceive them as a central A.A. institution". A central institution is the thing everything else hangs on. "At times club enthusiasts will act as though they really believed we could handle our alcoholic problems by club life alone. They are apt to depend upon clubs rather than upon the A.A. program." The Long Form gave clubs and hospitals their place in its own words: <0>secondary aids</0>. They come second, behind the one thing a group exists for, which is carrying the message to the drunk still drinking. Today the club has been replaced by the program: thirty days inside, then aftercare, then sober living, then alumni night, until a newcomer is told that A.A. is something you do after treatment, when treatment says so. The meeting has become one stage in somebody else's plan. A group that accepts that order has made itself secondary to a facility, which is the Tradition turned upside down. Test it tonight: ask a newcomer how they found your meeting, and whether anyone told them they had to go somewhere else first.

96124d268112.t: Clubs and hospitals are secondary aids, and the danger begins when people depend on them instead of on A.A. In my area, what has been put in front of the meeting as the thing you must do first?

706e922cf89f.t: June 19 — "Bigger Than the Walls." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our

00e31ca4c2e8.t: A group that buys its own building has gone into the property business, and the property starts running the meetings. Picture it: a hall comes up for sale, members lend the money for a down payment, and the vote passes with cheering. Three years on, the business meeting is about the roof, the insurance, the furnace and the tenant upstairs who is behind on rent. The newcomers get the last five minutes. The two members who signed for the mortgage carry more weight than everyone else put together, and nobody can suggest moving without insulting them. Bill W. saw it coming (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 21): "Acceptance of large sums from any source to buy, build, or finance clubs almost invariably leads to later headaches." And the walls don't stay big enough for long: "the growing A.A. will burst the walls of any clubhouse." The Long Form keeps the deed away from the group (Big Book, p. 563): "any considerable property of genuine use to A.A." is not the group's to hold. It "should be separately incorporated and managed" (p. 564), carried by the people who choose to carry it, so the group stays free to meet anywhere. Test it tonight: if your group had to move next month, who would have to agree to it, and what would it cost them?

0154445d27d1.t: June 2 — "On the Side Lines." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our prim

acc08369c7c3.t: Before there was a Tradition Six, New York members learned the hard way to keep a club's business apart from the group. In 1940 they rented the first clubhouse, an old stable on West Twenty-fourth Street. Bill W. remembered (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 18): "A couple of older members signed the lease. We painted and we scrubbed. We had a home." The lease company was named "Alcoholics Anonymous of New York, Inc." Bill wrote in 1947 (P-17, p. 19): "Only later did we realize we had incorporated the whole of New York State, a mistake recently rectified." To incorporate is to form a company in law. A company holding one lease had taken A.A.'s name for a whole state. They learned something bigger (A.A. Comes of Age): "the club had to be on the side lines and could not be managed by the A.A. groups as such." The Long Form wrote the lesson down (Big Book, p. 564): property of real use to A.A. "should be separately incorporated and managed, thus dividing the material from the spiritual." The material is rent, leases and money. The spiritual is the message, carried free. Today a group often meets under someone else's lease, and the landlord's rules come with the room. Test it tonight: ask whose name is on the lease for your group's room, and what that name can decide.

8595f210ab50.t: The first club's lease company took the name of A.A. in a whole state, and the members had to undo it. Whose name is on the lease for my group's room?

5eafe9842dd0.t: June 20 — "Left Definitely Outside." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from o

72ae9a31790a.t: A meeting place is a secondary aid, and the capture comes when the place starts owning the group. Bill W. said where the early clubs ended up once A.A. had learned its lesson (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 22): "The club is left definitely outside, where, in the opinion of many, it should be." Outside means the club belongs to the members who pay for it and enjoy it, and the groups use it or don't. Today the clubhouse is often an app. Picture a group that moves its meeting onto a recovery platform that costs nothing to use. The platform owns the link, the list of who attended and the rules for who may speak. It adds its own banner, its own counsellors' ads and its own check-in form for the newcomer to fill out. A year later the group wants to leave, and finds that its members' contacts and its meeting's address belong to someone else. The Long Form's order was the other way round: secondary aids are set apart so the groups can drop them, never so they can drop the groups. A room the group cannot leave is not set apart; it is in charge. Test it tonight: if your meeting is online, who owns the link, and could your group take it, and its members, somewhere else tomorrow?

945d64a0db62.t: The early clubs ended up outside, where the groups could take them or leave them alone. Could my group leave the place it meets without losing itself?

cfeedb276add.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 564); P-17, p. 22 (Bill W. on clubs, 1947).

753c24026889.t: June 21 — "The Name on the Drive." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our

bacfc0419f9e.t: The A.A. name gets lent to outside causes even when no group votes to lend it, and Bill W. recorded how. In 1955 he wrote about a member who ran an alcohol-education project and raised money for it in public drives, while telling everyone she was in A.A. The result (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 54): "many contributors were confused. They thought A.A. was in the educational field or else they thought A.A. itself was raising money when indeed it was not and didn't want to." Then the cost (p. 55): "So A.A.'s name was used to solicit funds at the very moment we were trying to tell people that A.A. wanted no outside money." To solicit funds is to ask for money. One drive became a pattern, he wrote: "public solicitations by A.A.s for money — money for drying-out farms, Twelfth Step enterprises, A.A. boardinghouses, clubs, and the like". Each is a place the Long Form keeps outside A.A., raised for in A.A.'s name. Today the drive is a crowdfunding page for a sober house, with A.A. in its story and a member's face on it. The cause may be good. The name was never theirs to spend. Test it tonight: look up the fundraisers in your town that mention A.A., and notice how many are spending a name no A.A. group can lend.

12650ee9401e.t: A member's public drives taught the public that A.A. was raising money when it was not. Is A.A.'s name being spent anywhere near my group without the groups' say?
