2677b1a5812d.t: June 22 — "Not Strictly A.A. Enterprises." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us

0c4812807417.t: The first rest farm A.A. members used was never A.A.'s, and that was the right shape before anyone wrote it down. Around 1940 a party of members visited a farm in the Connecticut hills, run as a charity by a woman they knew as Sister Francis. Bill W. recalled her offer (A.A. Comes of Age): "She offered us full use of the place if some of us would create a board of trustees to look after it." Some of us, not the groups. A few members took the property on as a separate job, and the groups went on carrying the message. The farm became a place to rest after hospital, and Bill never called it A.A.'s. Such places, he wrote, are "not strictly A.A. enterprises". Useful, loved, and outside. In 1946 the Long Form made that the rule (Big Book, p. 564): "hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A." A place of recuperation is somewhere to rest and get your strength back. Today such places multiply: retreats, sober houses and recovery centres, some of which call themselves A.A. places and hold house meetings their residents must attend. Test it tonight: ask whether any house or retreat near you calls itself A.A., and whether any A.A. group has a say in how it is run.

f9b477daa5cd.t: The first rest farm was looked after by a few members on a separate board, and the groups kept their one job. Which places near me call themselves A.A. without belonging to any group?

b2f80fef68ac.t: June 23 — "Regardless of Anyone." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our

7ef110310e8a.t: The rumour today is that a drunk needs a facility before A.A. can do anything for him, and the Big Book says the opposite. In "Working With Others," its chapter on carrying the message to the man still drinking, the book is plain about whom he depends on (Big Book, p. 98): "Burn the idea into the consciousness of every man that he can get well regardless of anyone. The only condition is that he trust in God and clean house." One condition, and no admission form in it. A doctor may be needed to get him through a dangerous withdrawal, and the Long Form keeps that well outside A.A. and under doctors. What no facility can be is the gate to A.A. A group tied to a facility ends up carrying a different message: get assessed first, get a bed first, then come to us. The Long Form closes that door from the group's side: an A.A. group can bind itself to no one, so it never has to send the drunk anywhere before it helps him. Today the line gets said inside the rooms themselves, as advice: you need treatment first, come back when you've done your thirty days. Test it tonight: listen for what your room tells the shaking newcomer he has to do before A.A. can help him.

7a9a0b37f6f1.t: The Big Book says a man can get well regardless of anyone, on one condition that no facility sets. What does my group tell a newcomer he needs first?

7ac19753f1d7.t: June 24 — "The Group's House." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our pri

cc372234e340.t: A group that houses newcomers has gone into business, and the business soon decides who gets helped. Picture a group moved by the men sleeping in cars outside its meeting. It votes to rent a house out of the treasury: four beds, a no-drinking rule, a meeting in the kitchen on Sundays. For a few months it feels like carrying the message with a roof on it. Then a resident drinks, and the business meeting has to vote on whether he is put out. Another can't pay his share, and the treasurer is chasing a sick man for money. The neighbours complain, the landlord phones the group's secretary, and the insurer wants to know who the owner is. Half the members stop coming to business meetings because they are sick of the house. The house was not a wicked idea. It was the wrong job for an A.A. group. The Long Form says so in ten words (Big Book, p. 564): "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business." As such means acting as a group. A group that runs a house becomes a landlord to the very drunks it exists to reach, including the one it just put out on the street. Test it tonight: is your group's treasury paying for anything that isn't the meeting itself or A.A.'s own services?

424a7d637165.t: June 25 — "Known as A.A.." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our primary

bcc4f002c56e.t: A facility that calls itself A.A.-based is borrowing a name that A.A. refused to lend, and refused in writing early. In 1946 Bill W. described how A.A. stood toward hospitals (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 33): "It is not a function of A.A. in the sense of management or ownership." A.A. visited and helped; it did not own a ward or run one. And the name stayed home: "But none of these institutions are known as" A.A. hospitals, he wrote. The Long Form fixed it as the rule for every club and hospital (Big Book, p. 564): "Hence such facilities ought not to use the A.A. name." Today the borrowing is quieter than a sign on the door. A program describes itself as 12-step based, puts the Big Book on its reading list, holds an "A.A. meeting" in its group room every Tuesday, and lists that meeting in its brochure as part of the treatment it bills for. None of that makes it A.A., and none of it makes A.A. answerable for it. But the family paying the bill believes it has bought A.A., and the newcomer believes A.A. is something that costs money. Test it tonight: if a meeting near you is held inside a facility, ask who decided it would happen, and whether the people in the chairs could vote it out of existence.

9fa08d42943d.t: June 26 — "Superintend It." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our primar

6369317ade0c.t: In 1937 even the founders planned an A.A. hospital. While A.A. was hoping for funds from John D. Rockefeller Jr., the man looking into the Fellowship as the basis for that request was steered first to Akron, and Bill W. gave the reason (A.A. Comes of Age): "If an A.A. hospital were to be put into operation, the Akron location would be better, and Dr. Bob would be available to superintend it." To superintend is to be in charge. The report came back glowing and asked for a large grant, to support two or three members and so that "a down payment on the hospital could be made". To the founders it looked perfect: "Here was medicine, here was religion, and here was a great good work, all in one package." Then: "Mr. Rockefeller flatly turned down this plea for a large sum". The hospital money never came. Nine years later the Long Form named what they had been walking toward (Big Book, p. 563): "Problems of money, property, and authority may easily divert us from our primary spiritual aim." Today the package is still on offer: a program that will fund the meeting, house the newcomers and employ the old-timers, all under one roof. Test it tonight: ask what your group would have to stop being in order to accept a package like that.

3a1ad9e8993a.t: The founders wanted an A.A. hospital, and the money to build it never came. What package would my group find hard to say no to?

c283b28c244c.t: June 27 — "Even Sober Drunks." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our pri

921f81450ede.t: Authority in A.A. grew wherever property did, and the first clubs found that out before any Tradition was written. Bill W. remembered those years with affection and honesty (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 18): "Growth brought headaches; growing pains, we call them now. How serious they seemed then!" A building needs someone to hold the keys, collect the rent and make the rules. Some ran the place like dictators. Drunks fell on the floor or broke up meetings. Steering committees, small groups set up to run things, tried to name their own friends to follow them, and found "to their dismay that even sober drunks couldn't be" steered. Nobody in A.A. has the power to govern anyone, and the property kept tempting people to try. What they worked out was to take the building's business away from the groups, so that whoever wanted the club could run it and the groups could stay what they were. The Long Form set that down in 1946 for every club and hospital: managed apart, by those who pay for it. Today the same pull works wherever one person holds the keys, the bank account or the meeting list, and the group starts asking his permission. Test it tonight: ask who holds the keys and the bank card for your meeting, and how the group would take them back.

e18eefd7a2db.t: Wherever the early members held property, somebody started trying to steer the rest. Who holds the keys to my group's room, and does the group still decide?

5ad55b0aa3fc.t: June 28 — "Decline to Marry." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our prim

6a1789e01355.t: A letter of support is how a program asks a group to vouch for it, and A.A. has already answered. Bill W. put it in one line in 1955 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 50): "We will cooperate with practically everybody, yet we decline to marry our Society to anyone." To cooperate is to work alongside: carry the message into a detox when asked, leave literature, answer the phone. To marry is to take on someone's name, terms and future as your own. The Long Form draws the same line from the group's side. Cooperation may go a long way, but never as far as affiliation or endorsement. Affiliation means belonging to someone; endorsement means vouching for them. Today the request comes as paperwork. A program applying for public money asks the local groups for a letter saying they support its work. Another wants a line for its website saying the groups recommend it. Each request is polite, each cause sounds good, and each one puts the group's name behind somebody else's business, where the drunk still drinking will read it and assume A.A. sent it. A group that signs has spoken for a program it does not run and cannot stop. Test it tonight: if a program asked your group for a letter of support tomorrow, who would answer, and what would they say?

fcd9f2627c10.t: A.A. cooperates with nearly everyone and marries no one. Has my group ever put its name behind someone else's work?

9f73dcfd202b.t: Grounded in: P-17, p. 50 (Bill W., "Why Alcoholics Anonymous Is Anonymous," 1955); long form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 564).

1ed8ebff4888.t: June 29 — "A Flyer on the Table." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our

bfb3affa5438.t: A group can endorse something without ever voting to, just by letting it sit on the literature table. Picture a member, years sober and well liked, who starts a business as a paid recovery coach. He asks to leave his cards next to the pamphlets. The secretary, a friend, mentions it during the announcements. Somebody adds his page to the group's website under local resources. Nobody voted on any of it. A newcomer picks up the card from a table full of A.A. literature, hears it read out at an A.A. meeting, finds it on the group's own page, and concludes that A.A. recommends paying this man to keep him sober. That is the opposite of what A.A. is: one drunk carrying the message to another, free, wanting nothing back. The Long Form saw this slide coming. A group may cooperate with anyone, but never as far as affiliation or endorsement, and it ends that sentence with three words (Big Book, p. 564): "actual or implied." Implied means said without being said out loud. A card on an A.A. table says it. Test it tonight: look at what's on your group's literature table and in its announcements, and ask whether a newcomer could mistake any of it for something A.A. recommends.

f0739e01d9a3.t: A business card on an A.A. literature table is an endorsement nobody voted for. What on my group's table or website speaks for us without our say?

5c2ae87dba29.t: June 3 — "Actual or Implied." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our prim

ac39e11a0e2c.t: Read the cooperation sentence of Tradition Six slowly, because the rumour about it leaves out its second half. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 564): "While an A.A. group may cooperate with anyone, such cooperation ought never go so far as affiliation or endorsement, actual or implied." Take it word by word. May cooperate: a group is allowed to work alongside others, not ordered to. Affiliation means being attached as a part or a member, the way a branch belongs to a company. Endorsement means putting your name behind someone and telling the public they are good. Actual or implied means it counts whether anyone signed anything or not. If a stranger walking in would fairly think the group belongs to the place, or vouches for it, the line has been crossed. The rumour says the Traditions encourage partnership with treatment, and it quotes only the first eight words. The sentence ends with a fence. Today the implied kind is the common one: a meeting printed on a facility's weekly program, the facility's logo on the group's flyer, staff calling it their A.A. meeting. Nobody signed a contract. The newcomer still learns that A.A. is part of the place that bills him. Test it tonight: look at your group's meeting listing and flyer, and ask what a stranger would think your group belongs to.

4e2092a5e62f.t: The Long Form allows cooperation and forbids affiliation and endorsement, even the implied kind. What would a stranger think my group belongs to?

f055de6f4c9c.t: June 30 — "Best Stay Whole." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our prima

5d8fe37b129c.t: Every capture this month has worked the same way: something outside the group gets a hold on it, through money, property or authority, until the group can no longer walk away. The Big Book introduces the Traditions as answers to two questions, and the second is this (Big Book, p. 561): "How can A.A. best stay whole and so survive?" Tradition Six answers it for a group's possessions and its friends. Hospitals and clubs are kept outside. The A.A. name stays off them. Cooperation stops short of a marriage. Under it all sits the last sentence: a group can "bind itself to no one." To bind is to tie, and the ties come dressed as help: a free room, a steady flow of clients, a grant, a partnership, a debt of gratitude. A group bound to no one can leave any room, refuse any money and turn down any partner, and still be an A.A. group the next morning. That keeps the door open to the drunk still out there, free. The same page says why: "We alcoholics see that we must work together and hang together, else most of us will finally die alone." Test it tonight: ask three questions. Who could close your meeting? Who pays for it? Who decides what happens in it? In an A.A. group the answers are the members, the members, and the members.

895630279c9f.t: The Traditions exist so A.A. can stay whole, and Tradition Six keeps a group free of every tie. Who besides its members could close my group?

96606137baab.t: Grounded in: Big Book p. 561 (The A.A. Tradition); long form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 564).

0bcb970cda38.t: June 4 — "Which Prospects Deserve Them." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us fr

6c54714e8d47.t: A group that starts paying for members' treatment has gone into business, and the business soon starts choosing among drunks. A newcomer can't afford a detox bed, so the group passes a second basket and covers it. It works once. By spring there is a fund, a treasurer for it, and business meetings that run an hour over arguing whose bill to pay. One man paid his back and two didn't. Somebody asks whether a man on his third slip should get it again. Bill W. saw it across the groups (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 15): "practically all group schemes to finance or guarantee hospital bills for fellow members have failed also. Not only do many such loans go unpaid, there is always the controversial question in the group as to which prospects deserve them in the first place." A prospect is a drunk who might join. A room open to any drunk is now sorting drunks by who is worth the money. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 564): "An A.A. group, as such, should never go into business." Lending money is a business, and so is buying beds. A member's own wallet is his affair; the group's treasury is for the message. Test it tonight: ask what your group's money paid for this year, and whether any of it was a judgment on a person.

13344ada2cfc.t: A group fund for hospital bills ends with the group deciding which drunks deserve help. Has my group's money ever been used to judge a person?

6f5ebcc3453a.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 564); P-17, p. 15 (Bill W., "Hospitals and A.A.," 1947).

bf71ae0daf90.t: June 5 — "Freely Discarded." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our prima

955f42e5d271.t: The Long Form makes the groups the ones who can walk away from a facility, and capture is when that gets turned around. Clubs and hospitals, it says (Big Book, p. 564), "ought to be incorporated and so set apart that, if necessary, they can be freely discarded by the groups." The Long Form calls them secondary aids: second in line, a help to A.A. and never part of it. Freely discarded means the groups can drop them without losing anything they need. Bill W. explained why that keeps them honest. Nobody is forced to pay for them, so (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 29) "they can never dictate, nor can they stray from the main body of A.A. tradition for very long." To dictate is to give orders. Now watch it run backward. A facility offers a group its room for free, coffee included. Two years on, the group has no treasury, no other room, and a facility rule about who may attend. The group can no longer discard the facility. The facility can discard the group, and the group knows it, so it doesn't argue. Nobody captured it by force. Comfort did it, one free month at a time. Test it tonight: if the place your group meets told it to leave tomorrow, ask whether the group would still meet next week, and who would decide where.

3814596c7ed2.t: The Long Form gives the groups the power to drop any facility, and a free room can quietly take that power away. Could my group walk away from the place it meets?

13e772642770.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 564); P-17, p. 29 (Bill W., "Money," 1946).

7434a4cc749f.t: June 6 — "Name and Financial Credit." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from

6b4768337d11.t: In 1947 the danger to Tradition Six walked in as an enthusiast with a good cause, asking for A.A.'s name. Bill W. described him (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "He strongly feels that A.A. ought to place its name and financial credit squarely behind any first-rate research, hospital or educational project." Financial credit is the trust that lets you borrow or raise money. "Seeing that A.A. now makes the headlines, he argues that we should freely loan out our huge goodwill." Goodwill is the public's trust in a name. Bill named a motive without pretending it was everyone's: "The judgment of this enthusiast is sometimes beclouded by the fact he wants to make a career." Beclouded means fogged. The A.A. name belongs to every group at once, built by drunks who never charged a cent, and he wanted to lend it out. That is why the short form says a group must never lend the A.A. name to any outside enterprise, and the Long Form keeps even A.A.'s own clubs and hospitals from using it. Today the enthusiast is often a member who works in the field and asks his home group to put its name on his program's open house or its brochure. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone has asked your group to put its name to their work, and what the group answered.

9794d7f7d014.t: The enthusiast wanted A.A.'s name and credit behind good projects, and sometimes he wanted a career. Who has asked my group for its name?

00e81ac40c99.t: June 7 — "Under the Direct Auspices." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from

6c82f89c086d.t: Before Tradition Six was settled, some groups ran drying-out places themselves, and Bill W. reported how it went. In those years cheap hospital beds for drunks were hard to find. He wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 15): "This urgency has tempted some A.A. groups to set up drying-out places of their own, hiring A.A. managers, nurses, and securing the services of a visiting physician. Where this has been done under the direct auspices of an A.A. group it has almost always backfired. It has put the group into business, a kind of business about which few A.A.s know anything at all." Under the direct auspices means run by the group itself, in its own name. Backfired means it blew up on them. Drunks who knew how to carry a message were suddenly hiring nurses, chasing bills and fighting over who was in charge, and the message got whatever time was left. The Long Form, first printed in 1946, had already drawn the line (Big Book, p. 564): "But hospitals, as well as other places of recuperation, ought to be well outside A.A.—and medically supervised." Places of recuperation are where people dry out and get their strength back. Today the pull runs the other way: facilities want groups inside them. Test it tonight: ask whether your group runs, staffs or answers for any place where drunks are treated.

e54d8cbea1fb.t: Groups that ran their own drying-out places found themselves in a business they knew nothing about. Does my group answer for anything that belongs to doctors?

6580fbfd7ada.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 564); Big Book p. 561 (the Long Form first printed in 1946); P-17, p. 15 (Bill W., "Hospitals and A.A.," 1947).

defd5a84b404.t: June 8 — "Medicine Is for Doctors." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from ou

cc9e4ce0ceaa.t: A.A. is not a treatment, and the Long Form says so by putting treatment outside it. The rumour today is that meetings are a kind of therapy, one more service a program counts in its hours. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 564) puts hospitals and places of recuperation "well outside A.A." and adds "medically supervised." Medically supervised means a doctor is responsible, not a drunk with a few years sober. Bill W. was plain about the division (A.A. Comes of Age): "We know that theology is for clergymen and that the practice of medicine and psychiatry is for doctors." Theology is the study of God, the clergy's work. Doctoring the very sick, Bill wrote, was "not and could not be A.A.'s business." A.A.'s business is one drunk carrying a message to another, free. The Big Book lists what the member's job takes (p. 97): "innumerable trips to police courts, sanitariums, hospitals, jails and asylums." The doctor treats the drunk; the member makes the trip to see him. Neither becomes the other. Today the line blurs from the treatment side: a client's meeting attendance logged as treatment, staff chairing the meeting as part of a shift. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your room has been told the meeting is part of their treatment, and who told them.

d0188c95e60e.t: Bill W. left medicine to doctors and kept A.A. to the message, free. Is anyone in my room being told the meeting is their treatment?

9e2c1e9048d8.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 6 (Big Book, p. 564); A.A. Comes of Age (Tradition Six: medicine is for doctors; hospitals as friends); Big Book p. 97 (Working With Others).

01a5961a360a.t: June 9 — "Spiritual Entities." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 6: An A.A. group ought never endorse, finance or lend the A.A. name to any related facility or outside enterprise, lest problems of money, property and prestige divert us from our pri

83fba41dd9b8.t: A group goes into business one good idea at a time, and nobody ever votes for the moment it stops being a group. It starts with a literature table. Then medallions, mugs and shirts with the group's name, because they sell. The anniversary dance needs tickets, a hall deposit and a DJ, and it makes money, so next year there are two. Somebody has to keep the stock, chase the deposits and do the books. The business meeting that used to ask who would go out on the next call now spends forty minutes on inventory and ten on the drunk. Every item passed by a fair vote. Bill W. wrote in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 29): "More and more, the A.A. groups are realizing that they are spiritual entities, not business organizations." An entity is a thing that exists in its own right. A group is one with a single job, and the job isn't retail. Literature carries the message, so the table isn't the problem. The problem is a group that needs its sales to pay its rent, because then the sales come first. The Long Form says flatly that a group should never go into business. Test it tonight: at your group's next business meeting, count the minutes spent on money and stock, and on the drinker still out there.

46b547894652.t: A group drifts into business through fair votes on good ideas. How much of my group's business meeting is about the drunk?

733012266b93.t: March 1 — "One Alcoholic Judging Another." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. Tradition 3 grew out of a 1946 essay by Bill W. about A.A. groups deciding which drunks deserved

2a7d875adc49.t: Tradition 3 grew out of a 1946 essay by Bill W. about A.A. groups deciding which drunks deserved a seat. He looked back at the membership rules the groups had made and at who they would have caught (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 11): "Most of the early members of A.A. would have been thrown out because they slipped too much, because their morals were too bad, because they had mental as well as alcoholic difficulties. Or, believe it or not, because they did not come from the so-called better classes of society." Then his verdict (p. 12): "Imagine, if you can, one alcoholic judging another!" That is the danger this month's Tradition answers. Not the drunk who walks in, but the sober ones deciding who counts. The Long Form shuts the question down (Big Book, p. 563): "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism. Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover." Refuse none: not the one who slipped last week, not the one with a record, not the one with no money and nowhere to sleep. Today the judging comes dressed as policy: a room that only seats people who are enrolled, insured or referred. Test it tonight: count every rule, written or not, a newcomer has to get past to sit down in your room.

74979801ceaa.t: The early rules would have thrown out the very people who built A.A., so the Long Form says refuse none. Who would my group's unwritten rules keep out?

83dc87e61932.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, pp. 11–12 (Bill W., "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

0004c1642e91.t: March 10 — "Money or Conformity." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The two things the Long Form says membership may never hang on are the two things a program runs on. The L

0ebfd895974b.t: The two things the Long Form says membership may never hang on are the two things a program runs on. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Nor ought A.A. membership ever depend upon money or conformity." Money means a fee, a bill, an insurance code. Conformity means following someone else's rules to keep your place. Bill W. listed what A.A. has instead (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 37): "no fees, no dues, no rules and regulations, no demand that alcoholics conform to A.A. principles, no one set in personal authority over anyone else." Even the basket can be passed by. Money given in A.A., he wrote, is "in no wise a condition of our A.A. membership" (p. 28). Now watch the capture. A program bills for a stay, and the stay includes A.A. meetings. Attendance goes on the chart as compliance. Miss enough of them and you lose your bed. The meeting itself has not charged anyone a cent, but the seat was paid for by someone, and kept by obeying. That is membership depending on money and conformity, run through a building instead of a basket. Test it tonight: is anyone in your meeting there because they will lose something if they leave?

caec28927aa4.t: A.A. has no fees, no dues and no demand to conform, and a program can supply all three around a free meeting. Is anyone in my room there because a program will punish them for leaving?

c374034db7c3.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 37 (Bill W., 1947, on personal government) and p. 28 (Bill W., 1946, on money).

1a6362fcbc0c.t: March 11 — "You Can't Keep Us Out." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The danger Tradition 3 answers was real: A.A. groups did try to throw alcoholics out, and failed. Bill W

0b79a75368e5.t: The danger Tradition 3 answers was real: A.A. groups did try to throw alcoholics out, and failed. Bill W. admitted it (A.A. Comes of Age): "Groups have tried to expel members, but the banished have come back to sit in the meeting place". Expel means to put out for good; banished means sent away. What they said, sitting back down: "This is life for us: you can't keep us out." They were right, and Bill said why. Nothing in A.A., not its board, its conference, "nor the humblest group committee can issue a single directive to an A.A. member and make it stick". A directive is an order. The Long Form turned their stubbornness into the rule for every group (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover." The drunk is the reason the room exists, and a group that tries to bar him has forgotten what it is for. Today the expelling is done by others, and they can make it stick: a facility bars a former client from the meeting in its building, or a program discharges a man and he loses the meeting along with the bed. Test it tonight: if someone were told they could not come back to your meeting, who would have the power to say it, and would your group stand for it?

2d1c80072eb9.t: Groups tried to expel members, and the banished came back saying it was life for them. Who could keep someone out of my meeting today?

1105ed00e1cf.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy — Tradition Nine and expulsion); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

ca6b368593af.t: March 12 — "Many Backgrounds." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. In 1939, years before any written Tradition, the Big Book already described a fellowship of people who would

c046ce2b0f63.t: In 1939, years before any written Tradition, the Big Book already described a fellowship of people who would never have chosen each other. Chapter 2 (Big Book, p. 17): "All sections of this country and many of its occupations are represented, as well as many political, economic, social, and religious backgrounds. We are people who normally would not mix." The Foreword to the Fourth Edition is honest about how far that was from true at the time. The line, it says (p. xxiii), referred to a Fellowship "composed largely of men (and a few women) with quite similar social, ethnic, and economic backgrounds." The first members wrote a door wider than the room they were sitting in, and the Foreword says those words "have proved to be far more visionary than the founding members could ever have imagined." Visionary means seeing further than the present. What held them together, p. 17 says, was a common solution, not a common background, and the Long Form later made the wide door every group's duty. Today some rooms sort themselves anyway: a meeting for one program's graduates, where a stranger feels the chill before anyone speaks. Test it tonight: who in your town would feel out of place at your meeting, and what in the room tells them so?

9f7d9bbcd04c.t: The Big Book promised a fellowship of people who would not normally mix before it had one. Who would not normally mix with the people in my room?

59d6f96ca37f.t: Grounded in: Big Book, p. 17 ("There Is a Solution"); Big Book, p. xxiii (Foreword to Fourth Edition); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

ae22f4e36a0d.t: March 13 — "Diagnose Yourself." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A.A. leaves the question of who is an alcoholic to the alcoholic, and rooms that hand it to a professional h

87a8039c8229.t: A.A. leaves the question of who is an alcoholic to the alcoholic, and rooms that hand it to a professional have changed who gets in. The Big Book (p. 31): "We do not like to pronounce any individual as alcoholic, but you can quickly diagnose yourself." To pronounce is to declare it officially, and A.A. declines to. The book gives the reader the test and leaves him alone with it (p. 44): "If, when you honestly want to, you find you cannot quit entirely, or if when drinking, you have little control over the amount you take, you are probably alcoholic." The Long Form builds membership on the same ground (Big Book, p. 563): "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism." All who suffer, by their own account. Not all who score high enough on someone's intake form. Today the pronouncing is done for him. An assessment decides he has a disorder and assigns him meetings; another decides he does not qualify, and the meetings stop. Either way someone with a clipboard has answered the one question A.A. leaves to the drinker, and the room has let them. Test it tonight: when a newcomer walks into your meeting, does anyone ask him for anything but his first name?

e4afb7d5deb4.t: The Big Book will not pronounce anyone an alcoholic; it leaves that to the drinker. Who decides whether a person belongs in my room?

8c5f45e68482.t: Grounded in: Big Book, p. 31 ("More About Alcoholism"); Big Book, p. 44 ("We Agnostics"); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

485c2e33515d.t: March 14 — "As a Group." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The Long Form never asks a member to give up his church, his party or his job; it asks the group, as a group, to be

c8e22d7da5ae.t: The Long Form never asks a member to give up his church, his party or his job; it asks the group, as a group, to belong to nothing. The words are exact (Big Book, p. 563): "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." The Big Book shows both halves on one page. The members (p. xx): "By personal religious affiliation, we include Catholics, Protestants, Jews, Hindus, and a sprinkling of Moslems and Buddhists." The fellowship, a few lines earlier: "Alcoholics Anonymous is not a religious organization. Neither does A.A. take any particular medical point of view". Every member brings his own ties through the door. The group takes on none of them. Now picture a group breaking it on its own. The church that hosts the meeting asks whether it would like to be listed as one of the church's ministries. A coalition invites the group to sign on as a member organization. A program offers to print the meeting on its alumni page. Each time the members vote yes, because the people asking are kind and the cause sounds good. And each time the group, as a group, becomes part of something else. Test it tonight: is your group listed anywhere as belonging to, partnering with or serving under anyone, and did your group ever vote on it?

4e6d28a08145.t: Members carry every affiliation there is; the group carries none. Has my group signed itself on to anything?

7d09ddb8d114.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); Big Book, p. xx (Foreword to Second Edition).

a7c6cb5b8a57.t: Tradition 3 — March 15: Court of Last Appeal | Daily Traditions | Recovery Starts

a3fb4aaa8b9e.t: March 15 — "Court of Last Appeal." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A meeting that only a facility's residents may attend has closed A.A.'s door on the drunk it was built fo

25681226ece2.t: A meeting that only a facility's residents may attend has closed A.A.'s door on the drunk it was built for. Bill W. described the moment the early groups stopped being afraid of newcomers (A.A. Comes of Age): "Who are we to keep anybody out? To many a desperate drunk A.A. is the court of his last appeal. How can we slam the door on anybody who stands outside?" A court of last appeal is the last place you can go when every other court has said no. For the man still drinking, the hospitals, the jails and his family have often said no already. The Long Form makes the open door the duty of every group (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover." Now watch it get hollowed out. A treatment centre holds a meeting on its locked unit, or in its residence after hours, and calls it A.A. The residents attend. The drunk off the street, with no insurance and no bed there, cannot get past the front desk. Nobody voted to refuse him. The building did it. A room he cannot enter is not keeping Tradition 3, whatever it reads at the start. Test it tonight: if a stranger smelling of drink walked up to your meeting's door, would anyone but the members decide whether he came in?

7b7e25970608.t: To a desperate drunk, A.A. is the last court that has not said no. Is there a door, desk or lock between my meeting and the man still drinking?

29aee415e481.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy — Tradition Three); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

c0bbf758049b.t: Tradition 3 — March 16: Republican A.A. Groups | Daily Traditions | Recovery Starts

c3a33ab65bac.t: March 16 — "Republican A.A. Groups." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. Tradition 3 ends on a clause that keeps A.A. in one piece, so that a drunk never has to pick a side to

c783065dbd92.t: Tradition 3 ends on a clause that keeps A.A. in one piece, so that a drunk never has to pick a side to get in the door. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." Affiliation means being officially joined to something else. Bill W. spelled out the danger (A.A. Comes of Age): "Obviously we could not very well have Catholic A.A. groups, Protestant A.A. groups," nor, he went on, Republican, Democratic or Communist ones. Picture that meeting list. A drinker from the wrong church or the wrong party reads it and finds no room that is simply his. Every second label on a group marks the door for somebody and against somebody else. Notice, too, how Bill says the line is kept: any group is "urged—though never commanded—not to make any other affiliation." Nobody polices it from above. The groups hold it themselves, or it isn't held. Today the second label is rarely a party. It is a treatment program, a clinic or a recovery residence, printed beside the words "A.A. meeting." Test it tonight: read your meeting's name and listing out loud, and ask whether a drinker from anywhere would hear his own room.

82ede59e7a6f.t: Any second name on a group marks its door for some drinkers and against others. Whose name besides the group's own is attached to my meeting?

495efb95f353.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy).

7e094ec12ba9.t: March 17 — "The Home Which Had Sheltered Them." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The hardest affiliation to give up is one with people who have been good to you, and Akron's

87fc8d595b45.t: The Home Which Had Sheltered Them

b6ab06dc3ac5.t: The hardest affiliation to give up is one with people who have been good to you, and Akron's first alcoholics gave one up anyway. Their early meetings were held in the home of T. Henry and Clarace Williams, members of the Oxford Groups, the movement where Bill and Dr. Bob had first found help. Bill W. remembered (A.A. Comes of Age) that T. Henry "was bighearted enough, nevertheless, to let us alcoholics come to his house for meetings" alongside his own friends. The drunks repaid him with "cigarette burns on their carpets." Then the break. It was "not until later, and well after the A.A. book was published," Bill says, that Akron's members withdrew from the Oxford Groups "and finally from the home which had sheltered them so well." There is no bitterness in the telling. Bill counts the Williamses "in the front rank of A.A.'s pioneers." The Long Form later wrote down what Akron had done (Big Book, p. 563): two or three alcoholics may call themselves an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." A group can owe thanks to anyone. It can belong to nobody. Test it tonight: list who has been kind to your group, a landlord, a church, a hospital, and ask whether any of them has quietly become part of it.

846cd3fc8feb.t: Akron's alcoholics left the movement and the house that had sheltered them, and stayed grateful to both. Has anyone who helped my group become part of it?

9313cb1cceab.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Recovery: the First Legacy — Akron and the Williams home); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

4c51b9daf7d5.t: March 18 — "Thrown Out of a Club." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. No program, house or club can end anyone's A.A. membership, because none of them ever started it. Bill W.

0ea40396ec53.t: No program, house or club can end anyone's A.A. membership, because none of them ever started it. Bill W. wrote in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 14): "Though he may be thrown out of a club, nobody thinks of throwing him out of A.A. He is a member as long as he says he is." A club is a building with rules, run by the people who pay for it. A.A. is not a building. The Long Form says why the difference matters (Big Book, p. 563): "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism. Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover." Today the confusion runs the other way. A woman finishes a program, or breaks a rule at a sober house, and is discharged. The "A.A. meeting" she went to every night was the program's, held in its building for its residents. She leaves believing her place in A.A. went out the door with her bag. Her bed may be gone. Her A.A. is not, because it was never theirs to hand out or take back, and every A.A. group in town has to take her in tonight exactly as she is. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your room has been told by an outside body that they no longer belong, and whether your group would tell them they do.

444ec4746698.t: A program can discharge someone and a house can evict them, but neither ever held their A.A. membership. Would my group make sure the person who was put out knows that?

c011301d1a01.t: Grounded in: P-17, p. 14 (Bill W., "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

5e9acb546392.t: March 19 — "Thirty Days to Speak." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A group can make its newest members second-class with one well-meant vote, and the Long Form leaves it no

c1935a019d19.t: A group can make its newest members second-class with one well-meant vote, and the Long Form leaves it no room to. The business meeting is nearly over. Shares have been rambling, someone says, and the new people talk about drinking instead of recovery. A motion: anyone under thirty days listens and doesn't share. It passes with a few hands against. Now look at who it lands on. The man with two days, shaking, who came because he needs to say it out loud to people who understand, is told his voice comes later, once he has behaved. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Nor ought A.A. membership ever depend upon money or conformity." Conformity means doing what is expected of you in order to be accepted. A rule that says get sober first, then speak, makes a member's voice depend on exactly that. Bill W. put how it really works in four words (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "We conform because we want to." People take up A.A.'s way because they have watched it work in the room, not because a vote ordered them onto it. The ones who most need to talk are the ones the rule silences. Test it tonight: read your group's format and ask whether anything in it makes the newest drunk earn his place.

985b4ed8aca2.t: A rule that the newest members must wait to speak makes their place in the room depend on behaving first. Does anything in my group's format make a newcomer earn a voice?

c057f4f422c2.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 38 (Bill W.).

c4c18ca43fa1.t: March 2 — "Limited to Alcoholics." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. Before there was a written Tradition 3, the first alcoholics in New York walked away from the movement th

ccf4e9b49613.t: Before there was a written Tradition 3, the first alcoholics in New York walked away from the movement that had helped them get sober, because staying tied to it would cost the drunk. Bill W. had joined the Oxford Groups when he left the hospital. Then (A.A. Comes of Age): "Until the middle of 1937 we in New York had been working alongside the Oxford Groups. But in the latter part of that year we most reluctantly parted company with these great friends." Why? "Naturally enough, they did not think too highly of our objective, limited as it was to alcoholics." Bill never called them anything but friends: "Our debt to them, nevertheless, was and is immense, and so the final breakaway was very painful." Gratitude did not buy an affiliation. Nine years later the Long Form wrote down what New York had already done (Big Book, p. 563): two or three alcoholics may call themselves an A.A. group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." Today the friend is a program that really did help, and now wants its name beside the meeting's. Test it tonight: if your group owes someone a debt, is it paying with thanks or with its name?

defc1691274b.t: The first A.A.'s owed the Oxford Groups an immense debt and still would not carry their name. Whose name rides along with my group's?

006aa1cb7d8d.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Recovery: the First Legacy — the 1937 parting); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

3d3e4365d3b8.t: March 20 — "Leave Them Alone." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. Clubs and offices stay servants of A.A. only while the members are free to walk away from them, and a meeting

7a84a1148a5c.t: Clubs and offices stay servants of A.A. only while the members are free to walk away from them, and a meeting that lives inside a treatment centre has nowhere to walk. Bill W. wrote of the clubs and offices A.A. members paid for (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 28): "These are places of service; they cannot really control or govern A.A. If any of them were to become inefficient or overbearing the remedy is simple enough. The average A.A. would stop his financial support until conditions were changed." Overbearing means bossy, pushing people around. The members could always take a facility or leave it alone, because their membership never hung on it. The Long Form keeps it that way (Big Book, p. 563): "Nor ought A.A. membership ever depend upon money or conformity." Now turn it around. The meeting is held in a treatment centre, on the centre's schedule, opened by its staff. A drinker who dislikes how the centre runs things has no basket to withhold, because the centre doesn't need his dollar. If he leaves the centre alone, he leaves the meeting with it. The simple remedy Bill counted on is gone. Test it tonight: if your landlord turned overbearing, could your group pack up and meet somewhere else next week, under the same name, with the same members?

b119d4514d6f.t: Members can only keep a facility in its place if they can walk away from it without losing their meeting. Could my group leave its building next week and still be itself?

95aa6a88beee.t: Grounded in: P-17, p. 28 (Bill W.); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

8a1348d153e2.t: March 21 — "Any Way They Liked." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The Long Form gives two or three alcoholics a freedom so wide it alarms people, because the alternative is

229ece1d5a39.t: The Long Form gives two or three alcoholics a freedom so wide it alarms people, because the alternative is someone with the power to decide what A.A. is. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." Bill W. did not soften it (A.A. Comes of Age): "This means that these two or three alcoholics could try for sobriety in any way they liked. They could disagree with any or all of A.A.'s principles and still call themselves an A.A. group." He saw the threat on the other side. Without that liberty, A.A. could harden into "a frozen set of dogmatic principles that could not be changed even when obviously wrong." Dogmatic means laid down as law, not to be questioned. And he trusted the bottle to do the correcting no office could: "In the end the innovators would have to adopt A.A. principles—at least some of them— in order to remain sober at all." Notice the one line the clause does draw. Not style, not format, not belief. Affiliation. Today the danger arrives as somebody's list of approved meetings. Test it tonight: when someone says a group "isn't real A.A.," ask whether they mean it has another affiliation, or only that it does things differently.

ed4060444528.t: The Long Form lets two or three alcoholics do it their own way, and draws its one line at affiliation. When my group calls another group "not real A.A.," which line is it using?

8cb393ec366b.t: March 22 — "Homes Were Thrown Open." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. Years before the Long Form was written, Cleveland showed what alcoholics could do with nothing but a do

26343e6486b7.t: Years before the Long Form was written, Cleveland showed what alcoholics could do with nothing but a door of their own. In 1939 the Cleveland Plain Dealer ran a series on Alcoholics Anonymous and the calls poured in. The first Cleveland meeting had started that June in a member's home. When it ran out of space it split three ways: one part to another home, one to a hall, one under a new name. Bill W. wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "These multiplying and bulging meetings continued to run short of home space," so they moved on "into small halls and church basements." The old-timers in New York and Akron could only watch, Bill admits, "with deep misgivings." About twenty members, "not very experienced themselves," were facing hundreds of newcomers. "But a year later we did know; for by then Cleveland had about thirty groups and several hundred members." Every one of those groups was alcoholics in a room they had found, answering to themselves. That is the shape the Long Form put in writing (Big Book, p. 563): "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group". Nobody handed Cleveland its groups. The alcoholics opened them. Test it tonight: if your meeting place closed tomorrow, could your members open a door somewhere else by next week?

f8f77133763e.t: Cleveland's groups were alcoholics in rooms they had found, answering to nobody but themselves. If my group lost its room, would it still exist?

a39b4812a0b6.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (When A.A. Came of Age — Cleveland, 1939); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

6929914edb6f.t: March 23 — "Refuse None." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The short form's "only requirement" is often heard as a test that somebody gets to give, and the Long Form takes t

b7fb6a3e9b33.t: The short form's "only requirement" is often heard as a test that somebody gets to give, and the Long Form takes that power away from everyone. The short form (Big Book, p. 562): "The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking." Read alone, "requirement" can sound like a gate with a guard on it. Read the Long Form beside it (p. 563): "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism. Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover." Hence means therefore. Because membership belongs to every alcoholic, nobody in the room is given the job of refusing one. The desire is the drinker's own business, and he is the only one who can say whether he has it. Today the gate gets a guard anyway. A newcomer admits his wife made him come, or his boss did, and someone tells him he doesn't have the desire yet and should come back when he does, as if anyone else could measure it. The Long Form leaves no seat for that judge. It puts the refusing power at exactly zero, and it does that on purpose, so the drinker who isn't sure is still in. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your room has ever told a newcomer he wasn't really a member yet, and on whose authority.

3eecd8ea6e8f.t: The Long Form says the groups may refuse none who wish to recover, so nobody gets to test the wish. Has anyone in my room ever made themselves the judge of a newcomer's desire?

4bdeee758c9f.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); short form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 562).

6feed18c58e3.t: March 24 — "Five Dollars at the Door." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A group that charges at the door has made membership depend on money, however good its reason, and th

1f0b642969c4.t: A group that charges at the door has made membership depend on money, however good its reason, and the Long Form rules that out in plain words. The rent goes up. The basket has been thin for months. At the business meeting someone proposes a simple fix: five dollars at the door, waived for anyone who really can't pay. It sounds fair, and it passes. Now picture the man on his first night with nothing in his pockets, who has to say so to a stranger with a cash box before he gets a chair. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Nor ought A.A. membership ever depend upon money or conformity." The rent is real, and A.A. never pretended otherwise. When the money question got a hard look at the 1955 convention, Bill W. reported (A.A. Comes of Age): "There was complete unanimity that through voluntary contributions the legitimate bills of groups, areas, and A.A. as a whole must be paid or we could not properly carry our message." Voluntary contributions pay the bills. The principle Bill names in the same passage is "no compulsory fees or dues." The answer to a thin basket is to tell the members, not to charge the drunk. Test it tonight: ask whether someone could sit in your meeting for a year without paying a cent, and be just as much a member.

988642492819.t: A door charge, even one that can be waived, makes the newest drunk explain his empty pockets before he sits down. Could someone come to my group for a year without paying and still be a full member?

906b50362df6.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (When A.A. Came of Age — the St. Louis convention, 1955).

968f73e3f531.t: March 25 — "Gathered for Sobriety." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. An A.A. group is alcoholics who gathered themselves, and a room of clients gathered by a counsellor is s

f76e6cb12015.t: An A.A. group is alcoholics who gathered themselves, and a room of clients gathered by a counsellor is something else, whatever the sign says. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group". Look at who does the gathering, and why: alcoholics, for sobriety, calling themselves a group. Now the captured version. A counsellor books the room, takes attendance, opens with the program's announcements and closes by reminding everyone the hour counts toward their plan. The people in the chairs are alcoholics, but they did not gather themselves, and attendance is the point. Bill W. wrote about that kind of pressure long before anyone built a business on it (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 37): "Time out of mind, families, friends, employers, doctors, clergymen, and judges have tried their hand at disciplining alcoholics. Almost without exception the failure to accomplish anything by coercion has been complete." Coercion means forcing someone. A.A. worked where all of that failed because nobody in it held the power to force anyone. Put a counsellor with that power at the front of the room and you have rebuilt what failed, under A.A.'s name. Test it tonight: ask who called your meeting into being, who keeps the attendance, and who could cancel it.

f2a590faa858.t: A group is alcoholics who gather themselves for sobriety, not clients gathered for a requirement. Who called my meeting into being, and who could cancel it?

6ad37570d032.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 37 (Bill W.).

19a76b28d65c.t: March 26 — "None Can Be Forced." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. Had A.A. insisted that every newcomer accept the Twelve Steps exactly as written, thousands would never hav

3f7466e07fdf.t: Had A.A. insisted that every newcomer accept the Twelve Steps exactly as written, thousands would never have come in, and Bill W. said so plainly. A Presbyterian minister trying to start A.A. in Thailand took the Steps to the head of the largest Buddhist monastery in his province. The monk liked them, wondered about "good" in place of "God," then saw the words "as you understand Him" and was satisfied. Bill's comment (A.A. Comes of Age): "But here we must remember that A.A.'s Steps are suggestions only. A belief in them as they stand is not at all a requirement for membership among us. This liberty has made A.A. available to thousands who never would have tried at all had we insisted on the Twelve Steps just as written." Then the line that settles it: "Alcoholics may be led to believe in God, but none can be forced." That is the Long Form's word conformity at work (Big Book, p. 563): "Nor ought A.A. membership ever depend upon money or conformity." The threat was never a monk with an edit. It was a fellowship demanding agreement at the door. Today it comes dressed as being serious: a room that treats a newcomer's doubts as proof he isn't really in. Test it tonight: ask whether a drinker who believes nothing yet could sit in your room and be counted a member.

a8c1473b0abb.t: A.A. made its Steps suggestions so that no belief would ever be the price of getting in. Could someone who believes nothing yet be counted a member in my group?

6191967287bd.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy — the Buddhist monastery in Thailand); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

d5f04a6bca96.t: March 27 — "Twos and Threes and Fives." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. In 1939, before there was any Tradition, A.A. was already spreading the way the Long Form would late

9aa466d72a1e.t: In 1939, before there was any Tradition, A.A. was already spreading the way the Long Form would later describe: in little knots of alcoholics who needed nobody's permission. The Big Book's last chapter reports it (Big Book, p. 162): "Some of us are salesmen and go about. Little clusters of twos and threes and fives of us have sprung up in other communities, through contact with our two larger centers. Those of us who travel drop in as often as we can." The two larger centers were Akron and New York. Then the book turns to the reader. "Thus we grow. And so can you," it says, even if you are (p. 163) "one man with this book in your hand." Seven years later the Long Form gave those clusters their standing (p. 563): "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group". Size was never the test. Two was enough, if they were alcoholics, gathered for sobriety, belonging to no one else. Today a cluster like that is sometimes told it isn't a real meeting until somebody bigger takes it on. Test it tonight: ask whether your members could start another meeting across town if one were needed, and who they think they would have to ask.

6a9c9ce981fe.t: In 1939 two or three alcoholics in a strange town were already enough to begin. Does my group believe it would need anyone's permission to start another meeting?

3ef9d87e905d.t: Grounded in: Big Book pp. 162–163 (A Vision for You); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

bf5d96ca7b42.t: March 28 — "May Call Themselves." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The Long Form needs nobody's permission to make an A.A. group, and the rumour that it does hands the group

22277e53a0c3.t: The Long Form needs nobody's permission to make an A.A. group, and the rumour that it does hands the groups to whoever claims to give that permission. The Big Book (p. 563): "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." Count what the sentence asks for. Two or three. Alcoholics. Gathered for sobriety. No other affiliation. It does not ask for a building, a charter, a registration, a facility to host it or an office to approve it. "May call themselves" means the group names itself; nobody names it for them. Today people who want to start a meeting are sometimes told they first need a church or a centre to take them on, or someone's approval before it counts. The ones who believe it go looking for a host, and the host is exactly how the other affiliation gets in. A meeting list is a service that tells drinkers where to find groups. It is not a licence, and being left off one makes a group no less A.A. The words that make a group were written for the two or three, not for anyone above them. Test it tonight: ask your group whether it believes it exists because of its members, or because of someone's permission.

a3eb19eb2216.t: The Long Form lets two or three alcoholics call themselves a group, and nobody else gets a say in it. Does my group think it exists because of its members, or because someone allowed it?

57c806313eeb.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

d68e7ebfe10d.t: March 29 — "Who Holds the Password." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A meeting that only lets in people its members already know has started refusing the very drinker the L

d0c5de52ad9d.t: A meeting that only lets in people its members already know has started refusing the very drinker the Long Form says it may not refuse. It begins with a real problem. An online meeting gets disrupted twice, strangers shouting into the screen. The group votes for a waiting room and a password, sent by a member to anyone who asks. Months later, the password only travels between friends, and the host lets in the names they recognise. Nobody voted to close the door. It closed by habit. Meanwhile the drinker who found the link at two in the morning sits in a waiting room nobody checks. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism. Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover." Bill W. put the groups' side of it in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 14): "We do not wish to deny anyone his chance to recover from alcoholism." The password was meant to stop the people who wreck meetings. It ended up stopping the people meetings are for. A door that only friends can open is a private party, however good the reason it was locked. Test it tonight: find out how a drinker who knows nobody in your group would get into your next meeting, and try it the way he would.

d88f0745be7e.t: A door that only opens for people somebody knows has already refused the stranger who needs it most. How would a drinker who knows nobody get into my group's next meeting?

e5d49b78f743.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 14 (Bill W., 1946).

95b8765c3664.t: March 3 — "Only in the Long Form." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The clause that stops a treatment centre from owning an A.A. group is not in the short form most rooms re

11215de56c10.t: The clause that stops a treatment centre from owning an A.A. group is not in the short form most rooms read aloud. The short form (Big Book, p. 562): "The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking." True, and it says nothing about who a group may belong to. The Long Form, one page on, finishes the thought (p. 563): "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." Affiliation means being attached to some other body: belonging to it, answering to it, carrying its name. The Big Book says why it prints the longer version at all (p. 561): the Long Form "is more explicit and of possible historic value". A room set up by a program, staffed by a program and listed on the program's schedule can read the short form every night and never hear the sentence that says it is not an A.A. group. That is how the rumour works: quote the half that sounds open, leave off the half that sets a limit. Test it tonight: ask whether your group's name is attached to anyone else's, on a door, a schedule or a website.

6e62c77f8765.t: The short form tells you who may join; only the Long Form tells you a group may belong to no one else. Which version does my room read aloud?

1864594db775.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); short form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 562); Big Book, p. 561.

092a40ffa88b.t: March 30 — "The Alumni Group." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A group that takes a program's name has taken an affiliation with it, however proud its members are of where

1ab1daa345ea.t: A group that takes a program's name has taken an affiliation with it, however proud its members are of where they got sober. Graduates of a treatment program want to keep meeting, so they start a group. The program offers its room for free. The group names itself after the program, opens with the program's news and welcomes each new graduating class. Every member is an alcoholic. But the group as a group now belongs to the program: its room, its name and its newcomers all come from one place, and a drinker who never went there can tell the room was not meant for him. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." As a group. Each member can be grateful to anyone; the group cannot carry the debt. Bill W. saw the same line from the other side (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 33): "Years ago we used to think A.A. should have its own hospitals, rest homes and farms. Nowadays we are equally convinced we should have nothing of the sort." If A.A. should not own the facility, the facility should not own the group. Test it tonight: ask whether your group's name, room and newcomers would all survive the program closing tomorrow.

5fc1bae1f32e.t: Members may be grateful to the program that helped them, but a group that carries its name belongs to it. Would my group's name, room and newcomers survive that program closing?

90a7093dd26e.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 33 (Bill W.).

34185e195419.t: March 31 — "Never Exclusive." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. March ends where Tradition 3 begins: the threat to A.A. was never who might walk in, but a fellowship that wou

b37013e5581d.t: March ends where Tradition 3 begins: the threat to A.A. was never who might walk in, but a fellowship that would start choosing. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) says it in four sentences: "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism. Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover. Nor ought A.A. membership ever depend upon money or conformity. Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." All who suffer. None refused. No price and no test. No owner. Bill W. said where the groups had come to by 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 14): "We wish to be just as inclusive as we can, never exclusive." Exclusive means keeping people out. The Big Book had already set the goal for any town where a few A.A.s land (p. 164): "there will be no stopping until everyone in that town has had his opportunity to recover". Everyone in that town, including the one nobody in your room would have picked. A month of readings comes down to that drinker and a door no outside body controls. Test it tonight: picture the person you would least expect at your meeting, and ask whether your group's door, its rules and its landlord would all let them in.

add1dd5c84fa.t: The Long Form asks for every alcoholic, refuses none, charges nothing and answers to no one. Who is the drinker my group would least expect, and would our door open for them?

87842857da2a.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 14 (Bill W., 1946); Big Book p. 164 (A Vision for You).

57978bc071fd.t: March 4 — "For the Good of the Movement." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A group can break Tradition 3 with one vote, cast by sober people who mean well. Picture the busin

0ce307ad8a0d.t: For the Good of the Movement

97010047de21.t: A group can break Tradition 3 with one vote, cast by sober people who mean well. Picture the business meeting. A man has come back drunk three times this year, and once he shouted. Someone moves that he not be welcome until he has thirty days. It sounds like protecting the room. It is a membership rule, and the Long Form has already answered it (Big Book, p. 563): "Hence we may refuse none who wish to recover." Bill W. wrote down how such votes look years later (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 13): "Every older A.A. shudders when he remembers the names of persons he once condemned; people he confidently predicted would never sober up; persons he was sure ought to be thrown out of A.A. for the good of the movement." Some of those very persons, he went on, have since been sober for years and are now among the old-timer's best friends. So the old-timer asks himself: "What if A.A. had slammed its door in their faces? Where would they be now?" Thirty days is a fine thing to want for that man. It is not a thing a group can demand of him before he may sit down. Test it tonight: has your group ever voted on who may come, and could the person it was aimed at still walk in tomorrow?

bc717118d5c5.t: Old-timers shudder at the names of people they once wanted thrown out, because some of them got sober. Has my group ever voted to keep someone out for the good of the room?

62e88fecd0f3.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); P-17, p. 13 (Bill W., "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946).

a29ea59d131f.t: March 5 — "A Brand of Treatment." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A group tied to one kind of treatment has stopped being an A.A. group, and Bill W. said so in plain words.

397ce4b98ea4.t: A group tied to one kind of treatment has stopped being an A.A. group, and Bill W. said so in plain words. Explaining the Long Form's "no other affiliation", he wrote (A.A. Comes of Age) that an A.A. group should not ally "itself with any particular brand of medical or psychiatric treatment." A brand of treatment is a method somebody sells or runs: a clinic's program, a hospital's model, a facility's phases. And the name, he added, "must be reserved for us only." Us means the alcoholics in the chairs. Here is how the capture runs. A facility starts a meeting for its clients, in its building, on its schedule. Staff open the room, choose the readings and take attendance for the chart. Counsellors tell clients the meeting is part of their treatment plan. No sign in the room says affiliated, yet everything in it is. The Long Form draws the line where the facility cannot argue (Big Book, p. 563): two or three alcoholics may call themselves an A.A. group, "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation." Who opens the door, who picks the readings, who takes the attendance: those answers show who the group belongs to. Test it tonight: if the program that runs your meeting's building changed its method tomorrow, would your meeting have to change too?

a4187c42066f.t: Bill W. ruled out an A.A. group allied to any brand of treatment, and kept the name for the alcoholics alone. Does my meeting run on anyone's treatment plan?

d54e647824bb.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy — "no other affiliation"); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

8681f91839ec.t: March 6 — "Won't There Be Criminals?." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. The first threat to Tradition 3 came from inside A.A.: sober alcoholics afraid of who else might come

610a15aa5782.t: The first threat to Tradition 3 came from inside A.A.: sober alcoholics afraid of who else might come through the door. When the publicity came and strangers began arriving, Bill W. remembered what the members asked each other (A.A. Comes of Age): "Won't there be mighty queer people? Won't there be criminals? Won't there be social undesirables?" And his own judgment of it: "Mixed with a certain amount of snobbishness and smugness, this was downright fear." Years later Bill told of sitting in his office with a member who held the title of countess, then going to a meeting that same night where a mild little man was taking everyone's coats, for nothing. Somebody told him who the man was: "He used to be one of Al Capone's mob." Same fellowship, same door. The Long Form made it the rule for every group (Big Book, p. 563): "Our membership ought to include all who suffer from alcoholism." All. Not all who are respectable, or safe, or easy to have around. Today the same fear works through a front desk that asks for referral papers, and rooms that quietly steer the man from the shelter somewhere else. Test it tonight: who is the person your room would least like to see taking the coats, and would he be welcome?

e68ebb9f7520.t: A.A.'s first fear was criminals and undesirables, and the answer was a countess and a man from Capone's mob in the same fellowship. Who does my room quietly hope stays away?
