c7e0fb59effb.t: March 7 — "No Alcoholic Excluded." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. Before Tradition 3 was written down, the groups had already fought over membership, and the Big Book reco

8845d8359df6.t: Before Tradition 3 was written down, the groups had already fought over membership, and the Big Book records what they settled. Its Foreword to the Second Edition tells how A.A. grew to thousands of members by the end of 1941, and the test that came with them (Big Book, p. xviii): "Would there be quarrels over membership, leadership, and money?" There were (p. xix): "Soon A.A. was beset by these very problems on every side and in every group." Out of those quarrels came principles for the groups, and the first one the Foreword names is about the door: "It was thought that no alcoholic man or woman could be excluded from our Society". Excluded means shut out. Not voted out, not screened out, not priced out. The groups did not learn this from a book of rules. They learned it from trying the other way in their own rooms, and the Long Form later wrote it into the Tradition that binds every group. It came out of quarrels, not out of theory, which is why it holds. Today exclusion seldom announces itself: a meeting held where only enrolled clients may enter, a door that needs a key card after hours. Test it tonight: could any alcoholic in your town walk into your meeting without asking anyone's permission?

2f005b5180c7.t: The groups fought over membership everywhere, and what came out was that no alcoholic could be excluded. Is there anyone who needs permission to enter my meeting?

edcb61409fae.t: Grounded in: Big Book, pp. xviii–xix (Foreword to Second Edition); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

4fe284f94a7e.t: March 8 — "He Signs Nothing." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. An A.A. meeting is not a checkpoint, and the paper passed around many rooms today turns it into one. Bill W. d

96d929c4097c.t: An A.A. meeting is not a checkpoint, and the paper passed around many rooms today turns it into one. Bill W. described the door in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 13): "Our A.A. door stands wide open, and if he passes through it and commences to do anything at all about his problem, he is considered a member of Alcoholics Anonymous. He signs nothing, agrees to nothing, promises nothing. We demand nothing. He joins us on his own say-so." Say-so means his own word, nobody else's. That is the Long Form's promise that membership never depends on money or conformity, put into the plainest terms there are. Now look at the paper. A sign-in sheet at the door that staff collect for a facility's records. A court slip, signed at the end by whoever is chairing, so that a seat in the room becomes proof for a probation file. The drunk sent by a judge is as welcome as anyone; that door stands open to him too. What changes is the room. Once a signature is the reason people sit down, the meeting is keeping records for someone else, and the person who walks in with no paper at all starts to look like he is in the wrong place. Test it tonight: does anything get signed, collected or reported in your meeting, and who is it for?

10bf62091589.t: A member signs nothing, agrees to nothing and promises nothing; he joins on his own say-so. What paper passes through my meeting, and whose file does it end up in?

31fb5190f303.t: Grounded in: P-17, p. 13 (Bill W., "Who Is a Member of Alcoholics Anonymous?", 1946); long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563).

a595569970fa.t: March 9 — "No Monopoly." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 3: The only requirement for A.A. membership is a desire to stop drinking. A group breaks Tradition 3 the day it starts telling newcomers to do it the group's way or find another room. The L

4df416b6b6cb.t: A group breaks Tradition 3 the day it starts telling newcomers to do it the group's way or find another room. The Long Form has one word for what a group may never demand (Big Book, p. 563): conformity, which means fitting a pattern someone else set. Picture how it creeps in. A group grows proud of how it works. Its old-timers decide a newcomer should share a certain way, use certain words, read certain pages and agree with certain opinions, or stop coming. Nobody votes. The pressure builds until the man who does it differently quietly drops away. The Big Book itself refused to work that way. In "Working With Others", the chapter on carrying the message to the alcoholic who is still drinking, it says of the man who wants a different road (Big Book, p. 95): "If he thinks he can do the job in some other way, or prefers some other spiritual approach, encourage him to follow his own conscience. We have no monopoly on God; we merely have an approach that worked with us." A monopoly is sole ownership. If the book that carries the message will not demand conformity from a drunk, no group has the right to. Test it tonight: is there anything your group expects of newcomers that the Long Form never asked of anyone?

6943188eb0c0.t: The Big Book tells us to let a man follow his own conscience, and the Long Form bars conformity as a condition. What does my group expect newcomers to fall in line with?

924d2d799def.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 3 (Big Book, p. 563); Big Book, p. 95 ("Working With Others").

611f09ca75ee.t: May 1 — "Our Real Reason for Existence." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Tradition Five gives every A.A. group one job, and the threat it answers i

d4cdbe0caeb9.t: Tradition Five gives every A.A. group one job, and the threat it answers is a fellowship trying to do everything. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." An entity is a body that acts as one. One purpose, not five. And the alcoholic who still suffers is the one still drinking tonight, not the member already in a chair. In the early years, members wanted A.A. to build hospitals, educate the public and change the laws. Bill W. wrote what experience taught them instead (A.A. Comes of Age): "Most emphatically, then, A.A. has but one single purpose: to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. That is our basic objective, our real reason for existence." Doctors, teachers and lawmakers have their own work. A group that takes on a second purpose doesn't double its good. It splits its attention, and the drunk who hasn't found the door yet is the one who gets dropped. Today the second purpose usually arrives looking helpful: a project, a partner, a program that would like the group's name. Test it tonight: ask what your group did this month that reached someone still drinking.

5ef217e52af6.t: An A.A. group has one purpose, and it points at the drinker who hasn't arrived yet. What did my group do this month for someone still drinking?

934e6370ab37.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 5 (Big Book, p. 563); A.A. Comes of Age (Tradition Five).

aef2f09bf0df.t: May 10 — "As No One Else Can." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The message works because it comes from a drunk, and a program that replaces the dru

19e5567417fd.t: The message works because it comes from a drunk, and a program that replaces the drunk with staff keeps the words and loses the message. Bill W. wrote of A.A.'s one purpose (A.A. Comes of Age): "It is our experience as alcoholics that makes us of unique value on our sector of the total alcoholic front. We can approach sufferers as no one else can." Unique value means worth that nobody else has. Today that approach gets handed off. A counsellor, a case worker or a paid recovery coach does the talking, makes the plan and runs the meeting as one part of the program. Some of those workers have their own sobriety. They are still paid to be there, and the drinker can tell. One alcoholic who wants nothing back can say something no paid worker can: I was where you are, and nobody is paying me to sit here. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) gives the job to the group, not to a facility: "carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." When a group lets a program carry the message for it, the group may still meet every week, but its one purpose has moved out of the room and onto somebody's payroll. Test it tonight: ask who in your town reaches the drinker first, a program or your group's members.

b0b97c937fb8.t: A drinker can be reached by another alcoholic as by no one else. Who reaches the drinkers in my town first, my group or a program?

2e17ae4c41b9.t: May 11 — "Bankrupt Idealists." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Early A.A. was nearly pulled off its purpose by its own big dreams. Bill W. admitted

8c3e016c4918.t: Early A.A. was nearly pulled off its purpose by its own big dreams. Bill W. admitted it (A.A. Comes of Age): "We thought our society of Alcoholics Anonymous might prove to be the spearhead of a new spiritual advance. Our principles might transform the world!" A spearhead is the point that leads a charge. Sober for the first time in years, the early members imagined fixing politics, factories and everything else. Bill said why: "How natural that was, since most alcoholics are bankrupt idealists." A bankrupt idealist is someone who wanted to do great good and ran out of everything trying. The danger was that A.A. would chase the whole world and lose the one person it could actually reach. What the founders found instead was a paradox, something that sounds backwards but is true: "The more A.A. sticks to its primary purpose, the greater will be its helpful influence everywhere." The Long Form makes that each group's rule: "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (Big Book, p. 563). Today the dream comes back when a group wants to be a voice for every recovery cause in town. Test it tonight: ask whether your group's plans for this year are about changing the world or reaching one more drinker.

4ca7ea0ff7a0.t: The more a group sticks to its one purpose, the further it reaches. Are my group's plans about the world or about the next drinker?

cb7d65345103.t: May 12 — "The Prime Object." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The first A.A. meetings were built for the newcomer, and the Big Book says so in plain

311f97a11231.t: The first A.A. meetings were built for the newcomer, and the Big Book says so in plain words. After Akron's first few men got sober, they gathered in each other's homes almost every evening. The Big Book describes them (p. 159): "happy in their release, and constantly thinking how they might present their discovery to some newcomer." Then a weekly meeting began, and it had a stated reason (p. 160): "Aside from fellowship and sociability, the prime object was to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems." Prime object means main aim. Fellowship came along with it. Sociability, the pleasure of each other's company, came along too. Neither one was the point. The meeting existed so that a drinker, or a worried family, had somewhere to come. That was a group with one purpose before anyone had written a Tradition to say it. When the Long Form came, it said the same thing for every group: "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (Big Book, p. 563). Today many meetings run as if the fellowship were the prime object, and a newcomer is welcome if he happens to wander in. Test it tonight: ask what your meeting would change if its only job were to give a new person somewhere to bring their problem.

efe7f32dd977.t: The first weekly meeting was held for the new person. Who is my meeting held for?

112bcfd73879.t: Grounded in: Big Book, pp. 159–160 (A Vision for You); long form, Tradition 5 (Big Book, p. 563).

50af5aed9b78.t: May 13 — "Carry This Message." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. "Carrying its message" in Tradition Five means going to the drinker, and the Big Boo

8c0c7b3c33da.t: "Carrying its message" in Tradition Five means going to the drinker, and the Big Book's own instructions say so. The rumour says you carry the message by sharing at meetings, by being a good example, by showing up. Those are fine things, but they all happen inside the room. The Big Book's chapter on this work, "Working With Others," opens (p. 89): "Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics." Immunity means protection. Then comes the instruction: "Carry this message to other alcoholics!" To other alcoholics: people outside, still drinking. The chapter goes on to say how to find them, when to go, and what to say at the bedside. It is a rescue, carried out in the drinker's world, not a talk given in ours. The Long Form gives that same work to every group as one body: "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (Big Book, p. 563). Today the word carry has shrunk to mean attend. A group full of members who never leave the meeting to find a drinker has kept the words and dropped the work. Test it tonight: ask how many in your group have carried the message to someone still drinking this year, outside any meeting.

f1a2a07d7dbc.t: Carrying the message means taking it out to the drinker. When did my group last carry it outside the room?

4f30a356baf3.t: May 14 — "The Most Sordid Spot." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A group breaks Tradition Five when it waits for the drunk to be delivered. Think o

c8e40334ab24.t: A group breaks Tradition Five when it waits for the drunk to be delivered. Think of a group that once had members visiting the detox ward and the jail every week. Those members moved away or got tired, and nobody took their place. Now new people arrive only when a court or a program sends them, and the group has come to think that is simply how newcomers happen. No vote ended the outreach. It just stopped. The Big Book (p. 102) describes the opposite: "Your job now is to be at the place where you may be of maximum helpfulness to others, so never hesitate to go anywhere if you can be helpful. You should not hesitate to visit the most sordid spot on earth on such an errand." Sordid means filthy and miserable. That is where the drinker usually is, and a group sitting at its own door will never meet most of them. The Long Form puts the duty on the group itself, as one body (Big Book, p. 563): "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Carrying is something you do on your feet. Test it tonight: ask your group who is going to the detox, the shelter or the jail this month, by name.

384d81ffa997.t: A group that only waits for newcomers has stopped carrying the message. Who from my group is going out this month?

79af1f805696.t: May 15 — "Stop Preaching." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Turn an A.A. meeting into a class and it has been captured, because A.A. learned at the

5cf60a404f21.t: Turn an A.A. meeting into a class and it has been captured, because A.A. learned at the very start that lecturing drunks does not sober them. In his first months sober, Bill W. preached at alcoholics in a New York hospital and a mission. He wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "At the end of six months nobody had sobered up." Dr. Silkworth, the doctor at that hospital, told him why: "you're having nothing but failure because you are preaching at these alcoholics." When Bill finally sat down with Dr. Bob, he did not lecture. It was one drunk telling another what had happened to him. Today the class comes from outside. A facility runs a meeting where a counsellor picks the topic, hands out worksheets, and keeps the talk on the program's lessons. The words A.A. and Big Book may be on the board, but it is a lecture, and the drinker gets what Bill's first prospects got. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) gives the group its own message to carry: "having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." That message is one alcoholic's own story told to another, not a lesson handed down to a class. Test it tonight: ask whether the person at the front of your meeting is telling their own story or teaching somebody else's lesson.

55ddfc0be250.t: The message is one drunk's story to another, not a lecture. Is my meeting a story or a class?

262eac7f768a.t: May 16 — "Heaven Knows What Else." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Tradition Five exists because A.A. was once tempted to become everything for eve

1d1a8aaa1cb7.t: Tradition Five exists because A.A. was once tempted to become everything for every drunk, and that would have cost it the one thing only it could do. Bill W. recalled the debate (A.A. Comes of Age). The conservatives said: "One alcoholic carries the message to another. Let's keep it that simple and stay out of money trouble." The radicals answered: "We need hospitals, paid therapists, traveling lecturers, rehabilitation centers, and heaven knows what else." A rehabilitation center is a place where people live for weeks under a program. The fellowship let that dream go: "When we got rid of our grandiose ideas about hospitals, research, rehabilitation, and education, not much of a bill was left to pay." Grandiose means far too big. What was left is the Long Form's one sentence (Big Book, p. 563): each group "ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Now read the radicals' list again. It is today's treatment industry, almost item for item, and some of it calls its rooms A.A. The early members looked at that whole list and said no, so the groups would stay free to do the one job. Test it tonight: ask whether anything your group runs, hosts or lends its name to is on that list.

b40fef2a11db.t: The early members turned down hospitals, paid therapists and rehabilitation centers so their groups could do one thing. Is anything on that list part of my group now?

7c686219be18.t: May 17 — "Our First Failure." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Before there was a Tradition Five, the first sober drunks in Akron spent their days o

3d773f2aaed1.t: Before there was a Tradition Five, the first sober drunks in Akron spent their days on the hardest drinkers they could find, and failure did not stop them. Bill W. wrote of the summer of 1935 (A.A. Comes of Age): "Dr. Bob and Bill D. and I went frantically to work with more of those alcoholic characters at the City Hospital. We had a long string of failures." Frantically means with everything they had. One of the failures was Eddie. "Every time Eddie got drunk he wanted to jump off the Cleveland docks." Years later Bill could report: "He finally did make the grade and recently wrote me that he has been sober for seven wonderful years." Nobody screened Eddie for promise. Nobody waited until he was ready, polite or referred by someone. Three men, all newly sober, kept walking back into a hospital ward for the man still drinking. That habit, kept by a handful before anyone wrote a rule, is what the Long Form later asked of every group (Big Book, p. 563): "carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Today a group can quietly decide some drunks aren't worth the trouble: too many slips, too much chaos, too many tries already. Test it tonight: ask whether there is a drinker your group has stopped going after because he failed before.

788bcfd57c78.t: The men who started A.A. kept going back to drunks who had already failed, and one of them got sober years later. Is there a drinker my group has given up on?

8eb5a1568679.t: May 18 — "But One." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The Long Form gives an A.A. group one purpose, and the little word but in it means one, not the

3a4e4e4ebd9e.t: The Long Form gives an A.A. group one purpose, and the little word but in it means one, not the first of several. The Big Book (p. 563): each group "ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." The short form says it the same way (p. 562): "Each group has but one primary purpose." But means only here, as when we say but a few. The rumour reads the word primary as permission: first the drunk, then whatever else the group likes, a housing list, a social club, a place to talk through the week. The Tradition names no second purpose. A room still needs rent and coffee, but those serve the one purpose; they are not purposes of their own. Why so strict? The Big Book answers (p. 152): "Near you, alcoholics are dying helplessly like people in a sinking ship. If you live in a large place, there are hundreds." Every purpose a group adds takes its hours, its money and its volunteers away from that ship. Today the extras usually arrive as good causes, and each one sounds too kind to refuse. Test it tonight: list everything your group spends its time on, and cross off whatever never reaches a drinker.

e3667cadd14c.t: The Long Form says but one purpose, and the extras a group picks up are not on it. What does my group do that never reaches a drinker?

7c54697627b9.t: May 19 — "Tumors and Tapeworms." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A group breaks Tradition Five on its own when its meeting slowly becomes about eve

4328a9499ed4.t: A group breaks Tradition Five on its own when its meeting slowly becomes about every trouble in life except the one the drinker walked in with. Bill W. put it in a doctor's picture (A.A. Comes of Age): "If we had discovered a widely applicable cancer cure, we would be begged to attend to that and that only. We would not try to look after all tumors and branch out into tuberculosis and tapeworms besides." A remedy that works for one illness is not improved by spreading it over all of them. Picture a home group a few years on. The topics drift: work stress, a divorce, the news, somebody's diet. Every share is honest. Nobody votes to change anything. But a man three days off a bender sits through the whole hour and hears no one say how they drank, how they stopped, or what happened next, and he does not recognize himself in the room. The Long Form gives the group one job (Big Book, p. 563): "carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Members have the rest of the week, and each other, for everything else. The meeting belongs to the drunk. Test it tonight: listen to your meeting as if you were three days sober, and ask whether you heard the way out.

5e84f06c1630.t: A cure for one illness isn't made better by spreading it over every trouble. Would a man three days sober hear the way out in my meeting?

51ea7f4688d3.t: May 2 — "Another Alcoholic to Talk To." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Before there was a Tradition Five, there was one drunk in a hotel lobby who

317a419a1a32.t: Before there was a Tradition Five, there was one drunk in a hotel lobby who understood that his sobriety depended on finding another drunk. In May of 1935, in Akron, Ohio, Bill W.'s business deal had just fallen apart and he was alone in a strange city with about ten dollars. The bar at one end of the lobby was filling up. He told it later (A.A. Comes of Age): "I remembered that in trying to help other people, I had stayed sober myself." He did not go into the bar. He went to a church directory and a telephone, and called stranger after stranger, asking to be put in touch with an alcoholic. The list ran down to its very last name. That call led him to Dr. Bob, and before long to A.A.'s first group. Notice the direction. Bill did not go looking for someone to get him through the night. He went looking for a drinker to carry the message to, and that is what kept him sober. Years before the Long Form gave each group "but one primary purpose" (Big Book, p. 563), A.A. began with one alcoholic going out to find another. Test it tonight: ask who in your group last went looking for a drinker, rather than waiting for one to show up.

b34542230caf.t: A.A. started with one alcoholic going out to find another. When did my group last go looking?

d436b06b1540.t: May 20 — "No Sole Vocation." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The message an A.A. group carries is one drunk's experience given to another for nothi

2a660684ba11.t: The message an A.A. group carries is one drunk's experience given to another for nothing, and a paid helper cannot carry it, however kind. The Big Book's writers said so about themselves (p. 19): "None of us makes a sole vocation of this work, nor do we think its effectiveness would be increased if we did." A vocation is a full-time job. They meant the work would not get better if somebody did it for a living. What reaches a drinker is a man who drank like him and wants nothing back, not even a paycheque from someone else. Today that role is for sale. Programs hire recovery coaches and peer workers, put a recovery story on the résumé as a credential, and send them into rooms called A.A. to be the newcomer's first friend, on the clock. The drinker is no longer met by one alcoholic wanting nothing. He is met by staff with a caseload and an employer. The Long Form gives that job to the group (Big Book, p. 563): "carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." A group whose first welcome is a paid one has handed its one purpose to a payroll. Test it tonight: ask who in your room is there because someone pays them to be, and who decides what they say.

71af0693dd6a.t: The Big Book's writers said the work would not improve if anyone made it a job. Is the first welcome in my room a paid one?

bd8f61349447.t: May 21 — "Schemes to Do Good." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Money in a treasury goes looking for good works, and that is how it threatens Tradit

e3650bbf6cd5.t: Money in a treasury goes looking for good works, and that is how it threatens Tradition Five. A woman died and left A.A. $10,000 in her will, and the trustees of the Foundation, the board that held A.A.'s funds, had to decide whether to take it. The office was badly short of money that year. Bill W. recorded the warning (A.A. Comes of Age): "The pressure of that fat treasury would surely tempt the Board to invent all kinds of schemes to do good with such funds, and so divert A.A. from its primary purpose." Divert means turn aside. Nobody feared the money would be stolen. They feared it would be spent well, on something other than the drunk. The trustees declined it, and declined all such gifts after it. The same pull reaches a home group. The treasury grows past rent and literature, and the business meeting starts hunting for a worthy cause: a donation here, a community event there. Each idea is generous. Each one moves the group's attention a step away from the alcoholic still drinking. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) gives each group "but one primary purpose." Test it tonight: ask what your group's money did last year, and how much of it helped reach a drinker.

fa9fdf61f688.t: The trustees turned down $10,000 because a full treasury invents good causes and forgets the drunk. What has my group's money been doing?

7a439ec4d4d4.t: May 22 — "So Freely Given." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Before there was any group, A.A. began as one sober drunk looking past himself to the t

b3656a085600.t: Before there was any group, A.A. began as one sober drunk looking past himself to the thousands still drinking. Bill W. wrote of his last days in the hospital (Big Book, p. 14): "While I lay in the hospital the thought came that there were thousands of hopeless alcoholics who might be glad to have what had been so freely given me. Perhaps I could help some of them. They in turn might work with others." That is the whole chain in three sentences: freely given, freely passed on, passed on again. He soon found it kept him sober too (p. 15): "I soon found that when all other measures failed, work with another alcoholic would save the day." Mark the order, though. The thought in the hospital bed came first, and it was about them, the hopeless ones still out there. Tradition Five takes that one man's thought and gives it to every group (p. 563): "carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Today the order can get turned around: the drunk still out there becomes an exercise for the members' sobriety, and when the members feel fine, the visits stop. Test it tonight: ask whether your group's work starts with the drinkers still out there, or with what it does for the people already inside.

0125a2a089f6.t: A.A. started with a man in a hospital bed thinking about thousands of drunks he hadn't met. Who does my group think about first?

0893dce2f733.t: May 23 — "Anything Whatever." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. In A.A., service means whatever helps a group reach the alcoholic still drinking, and

38c354e2b2f9.t: In A.A., service means whatever helps a group reach the alcoholic still drinking, and nothing in the Long Form gives the word a smaller job. Bill W. said it at St. Louis (A.A. Comes of Age): "An A.A. service is anything whatever that legitimately helps us to reach fellow sufferers." Then he named the first and greatest: "the Twelfth Step call is the greatest of A.A.'s services." A Twelfth Step call is going to a drinker who has asked for help. Everything else counts by how it serves that call: "the car we rode in, the gasoline we paid for, and the cups of coffee we bought him." Him is the drunk. The rumour says service is a ladder of chores: make the coffee, set up the chairs, chair the meeting, and those keep you sober. Coffee is service when it is poured for the stranger who just walked in. A position held only so the room can look after its regulars is a job, not service in Bill's sense. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) gives each group "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Test it tonight: take each service job in your group and ask which drinker it reaches.

d2375b70bf68.t: May 24 — "Would Disintegrate." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A group breaks Tradition Five on its own the night it votes to stop going out to the

a2d5a36afa38.t: A group breaks Tradition Five on its own the night it votes to stop going out to the drinker. Picture the business meeting. For years the group has sent two members to the detox ward on Thursdays. Lately the slot is hard to fill. Someone says the facility runs its own meeting now. Someone else says the local A.A. office handles hospitals. The motion passes: drop it. Nothing else changes. The meeting still opens on time, and the coffee is still good. Bill W. wrote in 1947 about what lasting groups do instead (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "they stick to their single purpose of helping alcoholics to recover." And why: "Groups see they would disintegrate if they didn't." Disintegrate means come apart, slowly, piece by piece. A group that has stopped reaching drinkers has nobody new coming through the door, and in a few years it is the same twelve people, then eight. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) gives the job to each group, not to a committee somewhere else: "carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Test it tonight: ask what your group did last month that reached a drinker who wasn't already in the room.

d326782121b6.t: May 25 — "Never Force Yourself." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A.A.'s message is offered to a drinker who wants it, and a room run as a court's a

4ad52ae24a9c.t: A.A.'s message is offered to a drinker who wants it, and a room run as a court's attendance office has traded that offer for an order. The Big Book's instructions for carrying the message (p. 90): "If he does not want to stop drinking, don't waste time trying to persuade him." And: "If he does not want to see you, never force yourself upon him." The whole approach rests on the drinker's own wanting. Today the forcing comes from outside. A court, a probation officer or a program orders someone to attend so many meetings and get a paper signed at each one. The group never chose this, and the Long Form says we "may refuse none who wish to recover" (p. 563), sent or not. The capture is quieter. The meeting rearranges its hour around the paper: a line for signatures, a chair whose real job is the stamp, a room half full of people counting meetings instead of drinks. The Long Form points the group at "the alcoholic who still suffers," the drinker, not the docket. A docket is a court's list of cases. Test it tonight: ask whether your meeting's routine is built for the drunk who wants out, or for the paper someone else wants signed.

fa918bc10cb6.t: The Big Book says never force the message on anyone, and a court's paper is force from outside. Is my meeting's hour built around the drinker or the signature?

6d756c4a3ded.t: May 26 — "The Distant Alcoholic." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Tradition Five gives the message to every group because in 1937 it was in the han

abed7d4b6ec4.t: Tradition Five gives the message to every group because in 1937 it was in the hands of a few men in two cities, and that was a danger. That November, Bill W. and Dr. Bob sat counting recoveries: upwards of forty alcoholics were staying sober. Bill wrote (A.A. Comes of Age): "Then came a mighty sobering thought. This knowledge, this precious know-how, was still in the hands of too few of us. Must every alcoholic come to New York or Akron in order to get well? No, that would never do; that would be impossible." And then the question: "Could we carry the message to the distant alcoholic?" Distant meant every drunk who didn't live near those two men. The answer that grew was the group: wherever a few sober alcoholics met, the message lived, and could go out again from there. So the Long Form hands the purpose to each group, not to a headquarters or a few gifted members (Big Book, p. 563): "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Today a group can act as though someone else carries it: the central office, the old-timer who takes the calls. Test it tonight: ask whether the drinker nearest your meeting would ever hear the message from your group.

5042b6429f02.t: In 1937 the message was in too few hands, and the answer was every group carrying it. Would the nearest drinker hear it from mine?

17b0dce2ae4c.t: May 27 — "Twos and Threes." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The Big Book was written to start groups that would carry the message themselves, years

b4a3e0947d13.t: The Big Book was written to start groups that would carry the message themselves, years before Tradition Five said so. Its writers expected readers to rise and go to others (p. 153): "They will approach still other sick ones and fellowships of Alcoholics Anonymous may spring up in each city and hamlet, havens for those who must find a way out." A hamlet is a very small village; a haven is a safe harbour. Read who the havens are for: not the members, but "those who must find a way out," the drinkers still looking. By 1939 it had begun (p. 162): "Little clusters of twos and threes and fives of us have sprung up in other communities, through contact with our two larger centers." No rule told those clusters what to do. The book simply took for granted that each would go to the next sick one, as the first members had. Tradition Five later wrote down what they already did (p. 563): "carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Today a group can treat itself as the harbour where its members dock, and forget that harbours exist for ships still at sea. Test it tonight: ask whether your group is a haven for those who must find a way out, or only for those who already have.

cf7d8c66b1cb.t: The Big Book pictured little groups in every hamlet as havens for drinkers still looking. Who is my group a haven for?

c85c29f46080.t: May 28 — "He Talked My Language." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The message a group carries is its own, one alcoholic's experience told to anothe

ae29f093d60a.t: The message a group carries is its own, one alcoholic's experience told to another, and no program's curriculum can stand in for it. Dr. Bob said what reached him (Big Book, p. 180): "he was the first living human with whom I had ever talked, who knew what he was talking about in regard to alcoholism from actual experience. In other words, he talked my language." Dr. Bob was a doctor. He had read widely and heard the experts. What he had never heard was a drunk who had found a way out. The Long Form says each group carries "its message" (p. 563): the group's own, the experience of the alcoholics in its chairs. The rumour treats the message as any recovery content at all, so a meeting can be filled with whatever a program teaches: worksheets, coping skills, its vocabulary, a counsellor's talk. A curriculum is a set course of lessons. It is not A.A.'s message, and a drinker who came for that message gets a class instead. Today this happens most in rooms a facility runs and calls A.A. Test it tonight: ask whether the last newcomer in your room heard an alcoholic say how he drank and how he got out, in his own words.

ff489bae86cb.t: May 29 — "The Telephone." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A group breaks Tradition Five quietly when the drinker calls and nobody answers. The Big

dedf9e474159.t: A group breaks Tradition Five quietly when the drinker calls and nobody answers. The Big Book warned the first members what carrying the message would cost (p. 97): "Your telephone may jangle at any time of the day or night." Jangle means ring harshly. They expected to pay that price, because a call is often the drinker's one moment of willingness. Picture a group's listing. It once gave a member's number, someone who agreed to take the late calls. That member moved away. Nobody volunteered, so the group put a general line on the schedule, and the line goes to a voicemail box no one has checked since spring. The meeting still runs every week. But the drinker who works up the nerve at two in the morning hears a recording, hangs up, and pours another. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) gives each group "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Carrying starts with being reachable. Today a group's whole public face may be one listing online, and if it leads nowhere, the group has closed its door without ever voting to. Test it tonight: call the number your group gives out, and see who answers.

7cef38fa6c0c.t: The first members expected the phone to ring at any hour, because the call is the drinker's moment. Who answers when someone calls my group?

e0d23591daac.t: May 3 — "The Alcoholic Who Still Suffers." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. Read the last words of Tradition Five slowly, because the rumour about t

9e6cb05a3838.t: Read the last words of Tradition Five slowly, because the rumour about them points the wrong way. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Whose purpose? The group's, as one body. How many? One. Toward whom? The alcoholic who still suffers, and "still" is the word that matters. That person is still drinking. A member three weeks sober and shaky is struggling, and the group is glad to have them, but they are already inside the door. The rumour says an A.A. group exists to support its members, a circle where the people in the chairs look after each other. That turns the Tradition around to face inward. Nothing in the sentence makes the group's purpose the people already there. The members matter to it because they are the ones who carry the message out. Today the inward version is everywhere: meetings that describe themselves as support for whoever attends, with no word for the drinker who hasn't come. Test it tonight: listen to how your meeting describes itself when it opens, and ask whether the drinker outside is in that description at all.

f3e35268b617.t: "Still suffers" means still drinking, and that is the person a group exists for. Does my meeting's opening speak to the drinker outside, or only to the people inside?

e05d89fc58fe.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 5 (Big Book, p. 563).

927dee4b1d68.t: May 30 — "Without Charge or Obligation." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A.A.'s message reaches a drinker free and owing nothing, and once it is so

2912cabdcb7f.t: A.A.'s message reaches a drinker free and owing nothing, and once it is sold inside a package it is no longer A.A.'s message. Bill W. wrote that A.A. could complete its mission only if, as a movement (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 4): "we remain a spiritual entity concerned only with carrying our message to fellow sufferers without charge or obligation." Without charge means no fee. Without obligation means he owes nothing afterward, not even thanks. "Spiritual entity" is the Long Form's own phrase for a group (Big Book, p. 563). Today the capture comes on an invoice. A treatment program sells aftercare, and the package lists "A.A. meetings" among its services, held in its building, led by its staff, logged in its file. The drinker, or his insurer, has paid. He has a counsellor's expectations to meet and a report going somewhere. Every word of Bill's line is broken at once: charged for, with obligation, carried by someone paid to carry it. A group that lets its name sit in that package has let its one purpose be sold. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your room was billed, by anybody, for the hour they are sitting in.

1b591ef4e43e.t: Bill wrote that A.A.'s message goes to the sufferer without charge or obligation. Was anyone billed for the hour in my room?

48704e0187b3.t: May 31 — "Everyone in That Town." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The month ends where Tradition Five begins: every A.A. group exists for the drink

2a3394bdd941.t: The month ends where Tradition Five begins: every A.A. group exists for the drinker it hasn't reached yet, and the threat is forgetting he is out there. The Big Book ends its story of the first groups with one member just starting out in a big city, and says what follows once a few men there find their feet (p. 164): "there will be no stopping until everyone in that town has had his opportunity to recover— if he can and will." Everyone in that town. Not everyone who comes to the meeting. The book isn't counting members; it is counting drinkers, all of them, and it doesn't stop until each has had his chance. That is the Long Form's sentence in a picture (Big Book, p. 563): "carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers." Everything this month has warned against, the good causes, the paid helpers, the court's paperwork, the dead phone line, the class instead of the message, does the same thing: it lets a group forget the town. A group can be warm, solvent, well run and full, and still be doing nothing for the man drinking alone three streets away. Test it tonight: think of your group's town, and ask how many drinkers in it have had their opportunity from you.

d31f68bf0cd4.t: The Big Book counts success by everyone in town having a chance to recover, not by a full room. How many drinkers in my group's town have had theirs?

15f5a7689303.t: May 4 — "The Card Players." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A group can break Tradition Five without voting on anything, just by turning its chairs

d3c43df4ecf6.t: A group can break Tradition Five without voting on anything, just by turning its chairs inward. Imagine the same twelve people meeting on Tuesdays for years. They know each other's children and each other's jokes. The coffee is good and the talk afterward runs late. A stranger comes in shaking, sits at the back, and leaves before anyone has crossed the room to him. Nobody did anything wrong, and nobody did the one thing the group is for. Bill W. watched the same thing happen in the first A.A. clubs. Among the growing pains he listed (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 19): "card players were impervious to any suggestion that they talk to new people". Impervious means nothing got through to them. The cards were never the problem. The problem was a room that had become about the people already in it. The Long Form gives a group "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (Big Book, p. 563), and a stranger at the back of the room is the closest that alcoholic may ever come to us on his own. If he leaves without a word from anyone, the group has missed its one job. Test it tonight: count how many members spoke to the newest person in the room before the meeting began.

887bed88ae5a.t: A group can drift off its purpose just by enjoying itself. Who in my group talked to the newest person last week?

ef0283c1a6ae.t: May 5 — "No Axes to Grind." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A meeting run by a facility can use A.A.'s words and still lose what made the message w

f8210fb4dcfe.t: A meeting run by a facility can use A.A.'s words and still lose what made the message work. The Big Book (p. 18) lists the conditions that make a sober alcoholic believable to a drinking one: "that there are no fees to pay, no axes to grind, no people to please, no lectures to be endured". An axe to grind is a private reason for helping. Now walk into a room that a treatment program runs and calls an A.A. meeting. Someone on staff opens it. The hour is on the client's schedule, and often on the bill. The person at the front has an employer to please and notes to write afterward. Most of those conditions are broken before anyone has said a word. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563) asks each group to be "a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose", and a facility has other purposes it must serve first: beds, outcomes, payment. That is not a judgment on anyone's heart. It is how a business has to work, and it is why a business can't be an A.A. group. The drinker can feel the difference, even if no one in the room says it out loud. Test it tonight: ask of your meeting whether anyone in it is paid, and whether anyone running it answers to someone outside the room.

8cee644966bd.t: The message works when nobody carrying it wants anything back. Does anyone running my meeting answer to an employer?

c1af0c5ee448.t: Grounded in: Big Book, p. 18 (There Is a Solution); long form, Tradition 5 (Big Book, p. 563).

5cb3ca0696b9.t: May 6 — "Straight A.A.." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. In 1947 the threat to A.A.'s one purpose came from members who loved A.A. too much. Bill W

f2d6fc8cb05d.t: In 1947 the threat to A.A.'s one purpose came from members who loved A.A. too much. Bill W. described the "do everything" member (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "he also thinks we have the answer for everybody and everything touching alcohol." That member wanted A.A.'s name and credit behind research, hospitals and education, and he argued that millions could be raised for good works. It sounded generous. Bill's answer, from experience, was flat: "neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A." Straight A.A. means the plain work and nothing added: alcoholics carrying the message to the alcoholic. The Long Form says it in one line. Each group has "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (Big Book, p. 563). Every side activity a group adopts takes time, money and attention away from the drinker it exists for, and it gives the public reason to wonder what A.A. is really for. A drinker who thinks A.A. is a campaign has one more reason to stay away. Today the pull is a cause that sounds close to home: a rally, an awareness walk, a joint event with a program. Test it tonight: list everything your group puts its name or money into, and ask which of them carries the message.

35dd00a23acd.t: A group that does many good things can lose the one thing only it can do. What does my group put its name to besides the meeting?

c2cbf03f8c4e.t: Grounded in: P-17, p. 24 (Dangers in Linking A.A. to Other Projects, 1947); long form, Tradition 5 (Big Book, p. 563).

b43a1667e423.t: May 7 — "A First Class Prospect." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. The first A.A. group began with two sober drunks asking a hospital for the worst

6bef6b90bb78.t: The first A.A. group began with two sober drunks asking a hospital for the worst case it had. The Big Book tells it (p. 156): "One day they called up the head nurse of a local hospital. They explained their need and inquired if she had a first class alcoholic prospect." A prospect is someone you hope to win over. She had one: a lawyer who had been in eight times in six months and was strapped down in his bed. There was no meeting for him to find. They went to him and told him their own drinking stories until he recognised himself in every one. Within days he walked out of that hospital, and he never drank again. Then the three of them went looking for the next one. The Big Book (p. 158): "there were three alcoholics in that town, who now felt they had to give to others what they had found, or be sunk." Be sunk means be finished. That was a group before any Tradition named it: alcoholics going out to the one still drinking, because their own lives depended on it. The Long Form later gave every group "but one primary purpose" (Big Book, p. 563). Test it tonight: ask whether anyone in your group has ever asked a hospital, a detox or a shelter where the drinkers are.

34e1e0f63d9d.t: The first group went to the drinker; it did not wait for him. Does my group know where the drinkers in my town are tonight?

215d58d2b1b4.t: May 8 — "A Spiritual Entity." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. "Spiritual entity" in Tradition Five says what a group must not become, and the rumou

92bd7ab727f4.t: "Spiritual entity" in Tradition Five says what a group must not become, and the rumour has turned it into a mood. The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "Each Alcoholics Anonymous group ought to be a spiritual entity having but one primary purpose". An entity is a body that acts as one. The rumour hears the word spiritual and thinks of soft voices, candles and a certain way of talking. That reading is about the feelings of the people in the room, and it lets a group feel spiritual while it is run like anything at all. Bill W. wrote down what the word was guarding against in 1946 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 32): "an A.A. group is a spiritual entity, not a business concern." A business concern is a company. So a group is a spiritual entity in the Long Form's sense when it has nothing to sell, no client to bill and no payroll to protect. Then its one purpose, the drinker still out there, has nothing competing with it. Today the rumour lets a room with a price tag behind it call itself spiritual because the talk sounds that way. Nobody's private beliefs decide the question. The books do. Test it tonight: set aside how your meeting sounds, and ask whether anyone makes money because it exists.

4fdc864838f4.t: In the Long Form, a spiritual entity means a group that is not a business. Does anyone earn a living from my meeting?

beb81e4cccf1.t: May 9 — "The Less Business, the Better." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 5: Each group has but one primary purpose—to carry its message to the alcoholic who still suffers. A group can drift off its one purpose one motion at a time, and every moti

e439cd591352.t: A group can drift off its one purpose one motion at a time, and every motion can sound reasonable. The business meeting is where a group decides how it will carry the message, and that is exactly where the drift starts. A motion for an anniversary dinner. A motion for group shirts. A motion for a speaker night, then a committee to plan it, then a fund for the hall. An hour goes by. Nobody mentions the detox ward across town that hasn't seen an A.A. member in a year, or the outreach list that hasn't been updated. Bill W. learned this lesson when groups tried to run their own drying-out places, and wrote (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 15): "We have been obliged to see that an A.A. group is primarily a spiritual entity; that, as a group the less business it has to transact, the better." To transact business is to carry it out. None of those motions is wicked. Each one takes a piece of the group's time, money and attention, and the Long Form gives a group "but one primary purpose—that of carrying its message to the alcoholic who still suffers" (Big Book, p. 563). Business crowds the purpose out quietly, because it always feels urgent. Test it tonight: at your next business meeting, time how long the group spends on anything that reaches a drinker.

87645001c32b.t: Every piece of business a group takes on competes with its one purpose. How much of my group's last business meeting was about the drinker?

12dcf226cf53.t: November 1 — "The Credit." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. May 1940. The catcher for

7236d4f35e9c.t: May 1940. The catcher for the Cleveland Indians had just caught a no-hit game pitched by Bob Feller, and Rollie H. told the papers he had been sober in A.A. for a year. Before you decide what you think of him, take the reason. His drinking had been public knowledge, and when the story of his recovery broke, the credit went to the Oxford Group — he had stayed on with them after the Akron members left. Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers records what happened: "At that time, however, Rollie broke his silence and said no, the credit for his sobriety belonged to Alcoholics Anonymous." He did not do it for attention. He did it to correct a record that had A.A.'s work under somebody else's name. And it worked, exactly as he hoped. Bill W. wrote later (Pass It On) that "it did us plenty of good, temporarily, because alcoholics flocked in." Hundreds of them. It was also the first anonymity break the Fellowship had ever had at the national level, and A.A. has been arguing with itself about that week ever since.

93d3eabee01c.t: A man broke his anonymity to give A.A. credit it was being denied, hundreds of alcoholics came in because of it, and it was still the break that started everything. When has the generous thing I did spent something that wasn't mine to spend?

7752d97347e5.t: November 10 — "Filmed Beside It." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Nobody has to claim

38c09ec7a142.t: Nobody has to claim an endorsement to collect one. The mechanism is proximity, and it is almost impossible to object to. A film crew shoots outside the building where the meeting is held. A promotional video is recorded in the hall an hour before the chairs go out. A photograph is taken at the door, with the sign in shot. No word is spoken about A.A. and none needs to be — the viewer supplies the connection, which is the entire reason the location was chosen. What has happened is that an outside body has borrowed the visual credibility of a Fellowship that has no mechanism for lending it and no committee that could have refused. The long form's phrase (Big Book, p. 565) is "Our relations with the general public should be characterized by personal anonymity," and the difficulty here is that nothing personal was broken. A building was filmed. But the building is where the anonymity lives, and after that footage runs, everyone who walks in has been seen walking in.

7f7a83bcb06e.t: No one claimed anything and no name was given — a building was filmed, and afterwards everyone who walks in has been seen walking in. What have I been associated with purely by standing near it?

8c1f43fe093d.t: November 11 — "Carried Away With the Desire to Serve." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films

4965a00843f8.t: Carried Away With the Desire to Serve

b8f50bb058af.t: October 1939. There was no Tradition Eleven — there were no Traditions at all — and a man in Detroit who had never made a speech in his life got himself onto the radio. A.A.'s history of its co-founder sets down the date (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "In October 1939, Archie managed to get a six-minute radio interview about his recovery in A.A. It was heard in a number of Midwest cities and certainly represented a first for the area." His own account sits in the Big Book (p. 254), and the phrase he chose for himself years afterward is the one to keep. "I, carried away with the desire to serve A.A., gave what was probably one of the first radio broadcasts about A.A., living through a case of mike fright and feeling like a million dollars when it was all over." Carried away with the desire to serve. He is not confessing to vanity and there is no sign of any — he was frightened, he did it anyway, and it helped. But notice what he could not possibly have had: any way of knowing where that ends. Nobody had it yet. This Tradition exists because a great many people just like Archie were each, individually, right.

9ca26506a776.t: A frightened man got himself on the radio out of nothing but a desire to help, and there was no way yet for anyone to know where it led. What am I doing for good reasons whose cost nobody has worked out yet?

8af1660836eb.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (October 1939); Big Book p. 254 ("The Man Who Mastered Fear").

8402b59e14d3.t: November 12 — "There Was No Dr. Armstrong." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. On 1 Marc

d4065820677a.t: On 1 March 1941 the <0>Saturday Evening Post</0> ran Jack Alexander's article, and A.A. was never small again (Big Book, p. xviii) — "By March 1941 the membership had shot up to 2,000," and within the year it was four times that. Read the article and you meet a physician (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) who is "still struggling to patch up his practice. The going is hard. He is in debt because of his contributions to the movement and the time he devotes gratis to alcoholics." The book calls him Dr. Armstrong. There was no Dr. Armstrong. It was Dr. Bob, printed under a false name to protect his own — the co-founder of A.A. appearing in the most important article ever written about it as somebody else entirely. Later, when a second Alexander piece was being prepared, Sister Ignatia asked Bill to keep her name out of that one. She was not a member; she was the nun who had admitted alcoholics to St. Thomas Hospital when nobody else would. Bill's answer drew the line exactly where the Tradition draws it. "To be anonymous, Sister, you'll have to take a little drink."

56b0bea57996.t: A.A.'s co-founder let himself be printed as a stranger so that the rule he asked others to keep would hold for him first. What would I give up to keep a rule I have asked other people to follow?

5bc7e457d8a5.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (the Post article; Sister Ignatia); Big Book p. xviii.

f2543cc693d8.t: Not in the Meaning of This Tradition

9b6a30e316a6.t: This is the line the internet gets wrong more often than any other, and getting it wrong costs people at the margin. A.A.'s own literature, plainly (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "When people are asked what led them to seek A.A. help, the answer given most often is: "An A.A. member." Their chances would have been slim if all of us had remained completely in hiding. But many of us have chosen to tell our friends, neighbors, employers, co-workers, doctors, or spiritual advisers that we are in A.A. — and when we do so, we are not breaking our anonymity in the meaning of this Tradition." We are not breaking our anonymity. Telling your doctor is not a break. Telling your employer is not a break. Telling the man at work whose hands shake at nine in the morning is the single most effective thing anyone has ever done for this Fellowship, and it is precisely what the Tradition was built to keep possible. The level named is press, radio and films. Not the kitchen. Not the ward. Not the front seat of a car in a parking lot at four in the afternoon.

fd63d84d8e80.t: Telling one person face to face is not a break — it is what most members say brought them in. Who is the one person I could say it to quietly, with no camera anywhere near it?

32bdd80442ee.t: Grounded in: P-43 (Tradition Eleven); long form, Tradition 11.

6b4f62508c19.t: November 14 — "A Stranger on a Deadline." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A reporter

efa09c368c89.t: A reporter rings the number on the intergroup site, because the paper is running something about the new detox unit and wants a line from A.A. The GSR takes it, since she is the one who answers that phone. She is careful. She says she can't speak for A.A. as a whole. She gives the meeting times, explains what the Fellowship does and does not do, and gives her name the way she gives it in the rooms — first name, last initial. The reporter is decent and barely interested in her. But a copy editor at ten at night has a house style, the paper does not print initials, and her surname is in the phone book. It runs on page five beneath the words Alcoholics Anonymous. She did everything right except the one thing nobody had told her: the decision about how her name appeared was never hers to make. A.A. put it as sharply as it can be put (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) — an A.A. "who permits his name to appear in the press in connection with matters pertaining to A.A." has broken this Tradition. Permits. Nobody asked her.

0ec7b5385a42.t: She did everything right, and how her name appeared was decided by a stranger on a deadline. What am I trusting somebody else to get right on my behalf, without ever having agreed it?

1d6e0de615c5.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 11; Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (the A.A. Grapevine, February 1969).

92a8409b7ba8.t: November 15 — "Statistics Do Not Move Money." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A chari

30e84542f2da.t: A charity that helps the same people A.A. helps has to raise money before the quarter closes, and the appeal needs one story. Statistics do not move money. A person does. So somebody who got well is asked for four paragraphs, and he writes them gladly, because the charity did help him and he wants it to survive. The appeal goes out with his photograph, his first name, and the sentence that makes the whole thing work: he found sobriety in Alcoholics Anonymous. Every word of it is true. Nobody has claimed A.A. supports the charity. But that letter now carries A.A.'s name as the guarantor of an outcome it is selling, inside a document whose only purpose is to produce a donation — and A.A.'s name is doing the part of the job the charity's own record could not do by itself. The Tradition warns against "sensational advertising," which sounds antique until you notice what advertising is: somebody else's message, with our credibility loaned to it, working.

193278908e06.t: Nobody lied and nobody claimed anything — one true sentence about where he got well did the work a charity's own record could not. What true thing about me has been used to carry an argument I never made?

010ba9c10580.t: November 16 — "On Celluloid." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. By the mid-1940s A.A. h

0f5eff1a3a6a.t: By the mid-1940s A.A. had become something it never planned to be — fashionable. A.A.'s own biography records it (Pass It On): "A.A. was by now a household word; it had gotten almost unanimously good reviews in the national press; and if it had not quite become "smart" to be a member, at least to confess your membership publicly was to evoke admiration." Admiration is the pressure this Tradition was built against, and it is far harder to stand than hostility ever was. Then came the case that tested the Tradition's own vocabulary. "A film star had gone so far as to break her anonymity on celluloid with the ﬁlming of her life story." Celluloid. Films — the third word in the Tradition, and the one nobody had expected to need. She broke it first in 1946 or 1947; the autobiography came in 1954; the picture in 1955. And then A.A.'s account of her adds a single short sentence and stops. "She subsequently drank again." No comment. No moral. No blame. The fact, set down where it can be read, and nothing built on top of it.

9eeba49bd89a.t: A.A.'s record of the most public break in its history adds one short sentence about what happened to her afterward, and then says nothing at all. What would I have added — and would it have helped anyone?

13b9b4e4fe5b.t: November 17 — "At All Hazards." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. In 1938 Frank Amos tr

228e4088abdb.t: In 1938 Frank Amos travelled to Akron for John D. Rockefeller, Jr. to find out whether this thing was worth money. His reports are the earliest written record of what A.A.'s founders were afraid of, and the fear is not the one you would guess. They were not afraid of being ignored. They told him (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) "early publicity would be ruinous—because it would result in the few present workers' being swamped with requests from relatives and friends and from alcoholics themselves. As a consequence, the whole movement probably would bog down." Ruinous. Around forty people were sober across two cities, and the thing that frightened them was too many people wanting in. Amos recorded the other conviction the same year, and it is the sentence that has held for nearly ninety: "commercialization of this movement must at all hazards be avoided." At all hazards. Not where convenient, not where affordable. Both of those were written down eight years before there were any Traditions, and both survived into the wording of this one.

487a3b0f38f2.t: With forty people sober in two cities, what the founders feared most was too many people wanting in. What am I guarding so carefully that I have stopped asking whether anyone can reach it?

77fa52228418.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (Frank Amos's 1938 reports to Rockefeller).

c1c3c1390061.t: November 18 — "It Was Tottering and It Had to Fall." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films.

e2cc30e1f96d.t: It Was Tottering and It Had to Fall

995e6f5f8d52.t: There is a page in the Big Book (p. 385) where a man describes the summit of his career, and he does it with a list that ought to stop any A.A. member cold. "My professional life looked fine on the surface. I was now head of a publishing venture in which nearly a million dollars had been invested. My opinions were quoted in Time and Newsweek along with pictures. I addressed the public by radio and TV. It was a fantastic structure, built on a crumbling foundation. It was tottering and it had to fall." Read that list against the Tradition. Quoted, with pictures. Radio. TV. He is not describing an anonymity break — he was nowhere near sober and A.A. was nothing to him yet. He is describing what those things were doing for him, which was propping up a man who was already coming apart. That is why this Tradition names those media and not others. They are not dangerous because they are public. They are dangerous because of what being in them does to an alcoholic who is unwell, and his story is in the book so a member can recognise the feeling before he recognises the situation.

95b1108c6f02.t: He listed the press, the pictures, the radio and the television as the structure holding up a man who was already coming apart. What am I appearing in that is holding something up?

4c6357a52105.t: Grounded in: Big Book p. 385 ("Me an Alcoholic?").

514e614d7a8c.t: November 2 — "I Don't Want to Capitalize on Humility." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films

2f4b4e04c518.t: I Don't Want to Capitalize on Humility

ccb999c0555b.t: On 2 February 1954 Bill W. wrote to the Secretary of Yale University and turned down an honorary Doctor of Laws. He did not pretend it was cheap (Pass It On): "Were I to accept, the near term benefit to Alcoholics Anonymous and to legions who still suffer our malady would, no doubt, be worldwide and considerable." Yale had already solved the obvious problem for him — the citation would name him only as W. W. "True, the splendid citation you propose, which describes me as 'W. W.,' does protect my anonymity for the time being." He refused anyway, because a courtesy is not a record. "So, while I might accept the degree within the letter of A.A.'s Tradition as of today, I would surely be setting the stage for a violation of its spirit tomorrow. This would be, I am certain, a perilous precedent to set." He offered them an alternative: give the citation to A.A. itself, and "In such an event, I will gladly appear at any time to receive it on behalf of our Society." Then he asked the few who knew to say nothing about any of it — "I don't want to capitalize on humility."

51bdd8c1aafc.t: He refused an honour that would have helped A.A., and then made sure nobody heard he had refused it. What good thing have I done that I quietly arranged for the right people to find out about?

b1a0f6abe6b3.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (the Yale letter, February 2, 1954).

00214021c0af.t: November 20 — "The Machine Only Carries the Ones Who Do." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and fi

9c421ea9ee61.t: The Machine Only Carries the Ones Who Do

f0b62b1c5e13.t: This one has no villain in it, which is exactly what makes it hard to argue with. A platform has to decide what to show people. It measures what holds attention, and what holds attention is a face, a name, a day count, and a story told by someone who plainly means it. So it shows more of that. Recovery content made by people who identify themselves reaches thousands; the same content made anonymously reaches almost nobody. No outside body decided this. No meeting was captured. But the result is a mechanism that continuously selects for the exact conduct this Tradition asks members to avoid, and quietly buries the members who keep it. Given enough time that stops being a question about distribution and becomes one about doctrine, because the version of recovery the public can see is the version the machine promoted. And A.A.'s literature names a cost here that has nothing to do with the Fellowship's reputation (A.A. pamphlet P-43): personal anonymity breaks in the public media "not only may discourage timid prospects; they may threaten the anonymity-breaker's own sobriety." The machine cannot see that cost. It is paid, quietly, by the person the machine rewarded.

81acefffce13.t: The version of recovery most people can see is the one a machine chose to carry, and it carries the members who put their names on it. What have I come to think is normal purely because it was the part I could see?

890235fc9ac2.t: November 21 — "Well, Why Not." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. An earlier break than

4ae7c92391fc.t: An earlier break than the film star's, and a harder one, because Bill had said yes to it. Pass It On is direct about why: "Her case was a particularly sensitive one, because she was a close personal friend of Bill's. In addition, Bill strongly supported her work in alcoholism education." Marty M. was going out to tell the public that alcoholics are sick people and that something can be done for them — work Bill believed in and had encouraged — and she was formidable at it. "Marty made excellent newspaper copy as she toured the country." Bill's own account of how it started (A.A. pamphlet P-17) does not spare him. "A close A.A. friend of mine wanted to go in for alcohol education. A department of a great university interested in alcoholism wanted her to go out and tell the general public that alcoholics were sick people, and that plenty could be done about it. My friend was a crack public speaker and writer. Could she tell the general public that she was an A.A. member? Well, why not?" Well, why not. "I thought it an excellent idea and therefore gave my blessing." The uproar that followed was the Fellowship's. The permission had been his.

e7a85b402222.t: Bill encouraged the work, gave the permission, and then the Fellowship's anger landed on her rather than on him. When did I approve something and let somebody else carry what came of it?

e706ba2595ab.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (Marty M.); P-17, p. 52.

178b14f1cc86.t: November 22 — "The Best Protective Gadget." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A noted r

dd548579fcdd.t: A noted radio commentator broke his anonymity on the air and in the press, to an audience estimated at twelve million. Bill wrote about it to Jack Alexander — the <0>Saturday Evening Post</0> journalist, a friend of A.A. and not a member — and the letter is the clearest thing he ever put down about why this Tradition is not squeamishness (Pass It On). "Of course, this looks like wonderful publicity to folks outside A.A." Then the turn: "it is a danger signal." Not because the man was cynical. "He really thinks he is doing us a favor; he hasn't the slightest idea that he is busting the best protective gadget our Fellowship will ever have." A gadget. Bill did not reach for a spiritual word there, he reached for a mechanical one, because he was describing a device that does a job. Then he named the force it has to hold against, and noted that the force only grows: "As the value of the A.A. name for money raising and publicity purposes increases, so will the temptation." And finally why one man on the radio was worth a letter at all. "Most of us deeply realize that enough repetition of such blasts could alter the whole character of our Society."

ade9a543d5e7.t: Bill called anonymity a gadget — a device built to hold against a pressure that only ever increases. What in my life is doing a quiet mechanical job that I have mistaken for a nicety?

c123b00e77d8.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (Bill's letter to Jack Alexander).
