ad27f3a14491.t: November 23 — "He Is Almost Never Only Carrying Himself." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and fi

4a7bf9163f27.t: He Is Almost Never Only Carrying Himself

5488577cc238.t: The part that gets forgotten is that a break is rarely one person's. A member who goes public goes public with a room behind him — the sponsor who gets named, the friend whose story is told because it makes the point better, the man whose relapse is useful as an illustration. The Big Book set the domestic version down in 1939 (p. 125), long before anybody imagined a camera in a pocket: "Another principle we observe carefully is that we do not relate intimate experiences of another person unless we are sure he would approve. We find it better, when possible, to stick to our own stories." Unless we are sure he would approve. That is already a high bar across a kitchen table. At the level of press, radio and films it is effectively unreachable, because the people whose stories travel along are not in the room when the decision is made, and they will find out the same way strangers do. A member can only ever consent for himself. The difficulty is that he is almost never only carrying himself.

36dba89fbf0a.t: November 24 — "Six Hundred and Forty Dollars." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. The gr

b22bf2c3815d.t: The group has money — not much, eleven hundred dollars past the prudent reserve, gathered over four years of good Thursdays. Somebody points out, correctly, that there are people in this town who do not know A.A. exists. So they take a month on the bus shelter outside the hospital: the group's name, the meeting time, the address, one plain line about drinking. It costs six hundred and forty dollars. Two people come because of it and one of them stays, and that is not nothing — that is a life, and everyone involved was right about the need. Here is the difficulty, and it is not that advertising is wicked. The long form (Big Book, p. 565) says A.A. "ought to avoid sensational advertising," and a bus shelter is not sensational. But a group has just spent members' contributions to promote itself, publicly, under the A.A. name — a decision with no obvious stopping point that nobody in that room was authorised to take. Next year it will be two shelters. Because it worked.

8cd511772b18.t: A man came in off that bus shelter and stayed, and the group had spent members' money to promote itself under a name it was never authorised to spend. When has a thing working stopped me asking whether it was mine to do?

03cba6606471.t: November 25 — "Trained Doubters." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Start with the debt

0c34be301c00.t: Start with the debt, because it is real and A.A. states it plainly (A.A. Comes of Age). "Without its legions of well-wishers, A.A. could never have grown as it has. Throughout the world favorable publicity has been the principal means of bringing alcoholics into our fellowship." Not one means among several — the principal one. And it is said without grudging: "Veteran newsmen, trained doubters that they are, have gone all out to carry A.A.'s message." So this mechanism has no villain in it either. A journalist wants to write something that will genuinely help. Her editor wants a named human being, because an unnamed one reads as unverifiable, and he is not wrong about that. The pressure lands on a member — not as a demand but as a favour, asked by somebody doing A.A. a kindness. Say no and the piece runs thinner, later, or not at all, and people who would have walked in won't. Say yes and the Tradition is gone in a single paragraph. There is no clever answer to this. There is only the fact that A.A. decided in advance, and in writing, which of those two costs it was going to pay.

2eed099b1b84.t: There is no clever answer to it; A.A. simply decided in advance which of the two costs it would pay. What have I left to be decided in the moment that would be far better settled now?

4c012c71568f.t: November 26 — "May Have Signed." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. August 1939. "At thi

fbd93a9e6ab4.t: August 1939. "At this time, Dr. Bob wrote and may have signed an article on A.A. and the Big Book that appeared in the August 1939 issue of a magazine called Faith." May have signed. A.A.'s own history of its co-founder (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) cannot establish whether his name was on it — and then it does something very few organisations would do. It writes down what that would mean. "The possibility that Dr. Bob signed this article means that he may have been among the first to break his anonymity at the public level—before there were any A.A. Traditions." Sit with the shape of that sentence. An official history, published by the Fellowship, raising in print the possibility that one of its two founders was among the first to do the thing the Fellowship now asks everyone not to do. It is not defended. It is not explained away. It is set down with the qualifier intact, because the qualifier is the honest state of the evidence. There was no rule in August 1939. The rule came out of what happened next.

440f9d121835.t: A.A.'s own history raises the possibility that a co-founder was among the first to break this, records it with the uncertainty intact, and defends nothing. What do I know about myself that I have never simply written down without attaching an explanation?

8d60933fa3b6.t: November 27 — "A Society Composed Largely of Promoters." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and fil

1c5aabe8300c.t: A Society Composed Largely of Promoters

4626a06000de.t: A.A. arrived at its public relations policy by first admitting, in print, what kind of people were writing it (A.A. Comes of Age). "By temperament many of us had been irresponsible promoters, and the prospect of a society composed largely of promoters was frightening." Frightening — about themselves. And Bill did not pretend the alternative was self-evidently wrong; he set the two side by side without any contempt for the other one. "A worthy charity wants to raise money, and so its letterhead shows the names of every distinguished person whose support can be obtained. Much of the political, economic, and religious life of the world is dependent upon publicized leadership. People who symbolize causes and ideas fill a deep human need. We of A.A. do not question that." Do not question it. It works, for other people, and he says so. "But we do have to face the fact that being in the public eye is hazardous, especially for us." So they took the other road — not because it was nobler, but because of who they were. "So we resorted to the idea that it would be far better to let our friends do this for us. And they have done it to an amazing extent."

3f92be8d4ec3.t: They wrote the policy by first admitting in print that they were, by temperament, promoters — and that a society of promoters frightened them. What do I know about my own temperament that I have never said out loud?

5afadf4aa27e.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (the attraction-and-promotion passage).

f7f435974da7.t: Somebody Has to Sit With Them

48b74bd34c98.t: Anonymity is not a reason to leave the room empty, and A.A. settles that by simply assigning the work (A.A. pamphlet P-43). "Giving the general public an accurate picture of A.A. is the chief job of our public information committees. In addition, they often carry the message to certain groups — from police ofﬁcers to personnel directors — whose work includes contact with active alcoholics." Police officers. Personnel directors. Somebody has to sit with those people and explain what this actually is, and A.A. structures the job so that it can be done without a personality attached to it. That is the answer to the objection this Tradition always attracts — that anonymity leaves A.A. unaccountable and unreachable. It would, if the Tradition were the whole of the policy. It isn't. The Tradition governs how a member appears. The committee governs how A.A. is explained. A group with no answer for the local hospital is not being careful about anonymity; it has left a job undone and given the omission a virtuous name.

2dea32ca3e05.t: A group with no answer for the local hospital has not been careful — it has left a job undone and called the omission a principle. What am I not doing that I have given a virtuous name to?

52be9471f1ed.t: November 29 — "Two Hundred Strangers." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. He is ten year

ffb09d177acb.t: He is ten years sober on the fourteenth, and the group's oldest member hands him the medallion at the Tuesday meeting. Afterwards, in the parking lot, he photographs it in his palm and posts it that night with four words about being grateful. It is a good post and he meant every word — and telling people he is sober, even that A.A. saved his life, one face at a time, is the most effective thing a member can do. But this is not one face at a time. It is two hundred, most of them strangers to that room. The photo is taken on the table by the door, the group's laminated meeting card lying beside it — name and night perfectly legible — and his own face in the reflection off the coin. In one post he has become what A.A. looks like for two hundred people, and he has taken the group along with him: its name, its night, its hall, and nobody in that room was asked. He carried it well, as it happens. That is luck. The Tradition asks that the Fellowship's face never be one man's face — however good the man.

7283c1129850.t: One good post made him A.A.'s face for two hundred strangers and carried the group's name along, and nobody was asked. What have I attached to the things I share without noticing?

3094862b66cd.t: November 3 — "Whether or Not the Name Is Given." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A.A.

6125bae44a32.t: Whether or Not the Name Is Given

0206bd9206d3.t: A.A. answered the television question decades ago, and the answer is more exact than most members realise. From A.A.'s own literature (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "According to a Conference opinion, members are breaking their anonymity when they are identiﬁed on TV as A.A.'s and their faces are shown — whether or not their names are given." Whether or not their names are given. The face is the identification; the name was never the point. That sentence was written when television meant a studio, a crew, a broadcaster's permission and somebody else's decision. It now describes a phone held at arm's length by the person it protects. And notice that A.A. did not respond by refusing the medium. It went to real trouble to use it without supplying a face: "masks; screens; back-lighting that shows A.A.'s only as silhouettes; camera angles showing them only from the back." Elaborate, slightly ridiculous, and entirely deliberate. The reason is seven words long and it is the whole Tradition in miniature. "For we are not selling personalities — we are explaining A.A."

fe5ad93b513d.t: A.A. worked out that a face identifies a member as surely as a name, and then went to absurd lengths to appear on television without giving one. What do I show that says more than anything I actually said?

81f79bfc3764.t: Grounded in: P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated (Tradition Eleven).

cdc68747fc04.t: November 30 — "People We Do Not Control." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. The Traditi

168451f492b4.t: The Tradition ends on a sentence that sounds like modesty and is in fact a supply chain (Big Book, p. 565). "There is never need to praise ourselves. We feel it better to let our friends recommend us." A.A.'s whole growth was built on that arrangement — doctors, clergy, judges, newspapermen and the man at the next desk, all recommending A.A. because they had watched it work and had nothing whatever to gain. Now hold the arrangement up and change one thing. The friend still recommends A.A. He is also being paid a referral fee, or he has beds to fill, or his platform earns on the click. Every word he says may be true. But the recommendation is no longer free, and a recommendation that is not free is an advertisement wearing a friend's face. A.A. cannot audit this, and has no standing to try. Which is why that closing sentence has to be read as the whole thing it is — not merely that we should stay quiet about ourselves, but that we depend, completely and permanently, on the honesty of people we do not control.

139a3b23f700.t: The entire arrangement rests on people who had nothing to gain saying so anyway. Who has spoken well of me when there was nothing in it for them — and have I ever told them it mattered?

37ce6a82a036.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 11; Big Book p. 565.

9a6f588d5cef.t: November 4 — "Thirty-One People and a Cake." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. The grou

663cc29062cd.t: The group turns forty this month and somebody brings a camera. Thirty-one people, a sheet cake with the group's name piped across it in blue, the banner on the wall behind them. It is a good photograph. It goes up that evening with the group's name and the date, because that was the point of taking it. Twenty-nine of those people are perfectly happy. Two are not, and their reasons are nobody's business — that is the point. Whether a member appears in public as a member is a decision A.A. leaves to that member alone, every single time. The camera just made it for two people while they smiled, because saying no in a room full of friends costs more in the moment than it seems worth. The long form is specific about the medium (Big Book, p. 565): our names and pictures as A.A. members "ought not be broadcast, filmed, or publicly printed." Nobody in that hall broadcast anything. They took a nice picture at a party. The photograph is the broadcast — and it published a decision that was never the group's to make. Not because membership is a secret; because it is each member's own to tell.

afaff2a7a1f4.t: The photograph made a choice that belonged to each member alone, and two people smiled while it was made for them. Whose choice have I made by assuming they would be fine with it?

ab6b1895b8c1.t: November 5 — "The Face That Costs Nothing." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. A treatme

a76e660bbcd5.t: A treatment centre needs one thing it cannot manufacture: somebody credible saying it worked. Outcome figures are contested, the staff are paid, and everybody knows both. What settles a frightened family's doubt is a person who has been there, looking into a camera, telling the truth. So the facility asks a grateful former patient, and gratitude is real, and the answer is usually yes. Now look at what changed hands. That man's recovery very likely happened in church basements, for free, among people who never sent him a bill — and his credibility was built there. It is being spent here, in a market, on a business. A.A.'s own literature explains exactly why he is the one worth asking (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "Alcoholics who have recovered through our program are themselves the strongest attraction that A.A. has." He is the attraction. That is the asset. And when he mentions where he goes to meetings, an endorsement nobody voted on arrives attached to a name that has never endorsed anything, and there is nobody sitting on A.A.'s side of that table to say so.

b0a81ccfc0d5.t: His credibility was built for free among people who never billed him, and it got spent on a business that did. What did I earn in one place and spend somewhere else entirely?

318f6beb72b5.t: November 6 — "Bill the Broker." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Bill W. told this sto

05621299b4ea.t: Bill W. told this story on himself for years. The ballplayer's break had worked spectacularly, and Bill's reaction was not caution (Pass It On). "Soon I was on the road, happily handing out personal interviews and pictures. To my delight, I found I could hit the front pages, just as he could. Besides, he couldn't hold his publicity pace, but I could hold mine." Read that again. He was competing. With a member, for column inches. "At the time, this looked like the thing to do. Feeling justified, I ate it up. What a bang it gave me when I read those two-column spreads about 'Bill the Broker,' full name and picture, the guy who was saving drunks by the thousands!" He called himself A.A.'s number one anonymity breaker. And here is the part that makes him worth trusting: it was not quite true. Lois's diary shows he barely left New York that year, and his real breaks came two years later. A.A.'s own biography says so — "But the truth is that he did not act on those feelings" — and explains why he told it worse than it was. He was "never afraid to use himself as a negative example (something he would not do to anyone else)."

abcbbbaeeea6.t: Bill accused himself in public of a break he had not quite committed, because he would use himself as the bad example and never anybody else. Whose example do I reach for when I want to make a point land?

b1b8b279898d.t: Grounded in: Pass It On (Bill's own account, and the book's correction of it).

e5bd2024cc9c.t: November 7 — "Two Ways to Break It." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Most of what peo

ac21c9e6e9ec.t: Most of what people believe about this Tradition is one half of what Dr. Bob actually said. Warren C. recalled him laying it out complete (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "He [Dr. Bob] said there were two ways to break the anonymity Tradition: (1) by giving your name at the public level of press or radio; (2) by being so anonymous that you can't be reached by other drunks." Two ways. The second one is never quoted, and it is the one most groups are guilty of. Dr. Bob's own conduct followed the same line in both directions. He would not have his name in a newspaper — but when Akron members wanted to speak to Rotary and Kiwanis clubs in the 1940s, he approved it, and Joe P. remembered why: "he didn't think we would get anyplace if people didn't know we belonged to A.A. He had the firm conviction that you should let yourself be known as an A.A. member in the community, and he was always sure to tell you about it every time you met him." Every time you met him. He worried people would take the hiding half and stop there.

3e043d3fc42c.t: Dr. Bob said you break this Tradition by being unreachable just as surely as by being in the papers, and he repeated the second half every time he saw you. Which half have I been quietly comfortable with?

f56234dd94a1.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (Warren C. and Joe P. recalling Dr. Bob).

e33525b975c9.t: November 8 — "Too Quiet to Be Found." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. Here is the fai

a99582d4af1d.t: Here is the failure nobody feels guilty about. A group meets in a hall with no sign. Its listing has an old phone number that rings out. Nobody answers the email because nobody agreed to hold the account. The address circulates by word of mouth among people who already know it, and everyone involved believes they are protecting something. A.A.'s literature puts the cost plainly (A.A. pamphlet P-43): "Suppose a sick alcoholic never has the good fortune to meet an A.A. How is such a person going to ﬁnd us? The search will be difﬁcult if the local group thinks it should be anonymous, too." The group thinks it should be anonymous, too. That is the error stated exactly — personal anonymity read as institutional invisibility. The Tradition protects a member's name at the level of press, radio and films. It says nothing whatever about a meeting being hard to find, and a meeting nobody can find is not keeping a Tradition. It is just a room with the lights off.

2f134ce06b77.t: A meeting nobody can find is not protecting anyone's anonymity — it is only difficult to reach. Where have I called something discretion when it was mostly just easier?

999fb1c19821.t: November 9 — "The Recording Stayed Up." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 11: Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion; we need always maintain personal anonymity at the level of press, radio and films. It was a hard

e87398422fe8.t: It was a hard winter and the group did a decent thing. Half the regulars couldn't get out, so somebody set up a camera at the back and streamed the meeting, and it worked — twelve people who would have sat at home alone were in the room instead. Nobody thought about the archive, because nobody was thinking about September in February. In March a man shared for eleven minutes about his brother, who had died in November, and about what he had said to him the last time they spoke. He was facing the camera. He did not know he was. What he consented to was a room: those faces, that night. The archive handed his story to an audience he never agreed to and cannot call it back from — in September his brother's widow finds it, because his brother's name is in it and she was searching for it. Everything about that group's decision was kind. But who hears a member's story is the member's own decision, made fresh each time he tells it — and a recording goes on making it for him long after the winter ends.

02307ad37a5d.t: A group did a kind thing for people who couldn't get out, and nobody was thinking about September in February. What am I doing right now that will still be findable long after the reason for it has passed?

ce244f6fee4a.t: October 10 — "A Silence That Large." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A.A.'s size gets used as testimony for positions nob

ab39b81c944a.t: A.A.'s size gets used as testimony for positions nobody in A.A. was ever asked about, and that is one more reason A.A. holds none. Someone arguing for a law, a funding model or a treatment contract reaches for the biggest number of sober alcoholics there is, and it appears in the submission as if those people agreed with the conclusion. Nobody asked them, and nobody has the standing to answer for them. The long form closes the door from A.A.'s side (Big Book, p. 565): "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one. Concerning such matters they can express no views whatever." Bill W. gave the reason in 1955 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 4): "if we steadfastly decline all political, sectarian, or other alliances, we shall avoid internal division and public notoriety". An alliance means taking a side together with somebody else. Division is the danger to the drunk: a fellowship split over a law is a fellowship arguing instead of answering the phone. Today the borrowed number shows up whenever a program or a campaign says it speaks for millions in twelve-step recovery. Test it tonight: when someone tells you what people in recovery want, ask who asked them.

dd712def770e.t: No one can say what A.A.'s members want in an outside fight, because A.A. holds no view to report. When have I said what "people in recovery" think?

e273661abc01.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565); P-17, p. 4 (Bill W.'s foreword, 1955).

ca63524b74ff.t: October 11 — "The Other Side of the Same Fight." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Both sides of the liquor fight wanted th

3b182ddd6824.t: The Other Side of the Same Fight

d75994d373f7.t: Both sides of the liquor fight wanted the same thing from A.A., its name on their side, and A.A. gave it to neither for the drunk's sake. Bill W. told how close it came (A.A. Comes of Age): a liquor trade association wanted to hire an A.A. member as an educator, to teach that alcoholics cannot drink at all, and to say in all its publicity that he was a member of Alcoholics Anonymous. Then the arithmetic: if the liquor trade got its educator, "the “drys” would instantly hire another A.A. member" to educate for their side. The drys were the people fighting to ban liquor. A.A. would have been on both sides of a fight it had no business in. Then the sentence this whole month stands on: "We simply could not take sides in this fight and do business with sick alcoholics too." Business, meaning the one job A.A. has: the man still drinking, who may work for the brewery or vote to close it. The member who was offered the job saw it himself: "Alcoholics Anonymous saved my life. It comes first." Today both sides of every alcohol-policy fight still claim the people in the rooms. Test it tonight: if someone at your meeting argues a drinking law, ask whether he is speaking as himself or for the room.

25f59d9e6b03.t: The wets and the drys wanted the same thing from A.A., and A.A. gave it to neither, because the drunk might be on either side. Which side of a fight about drinking does my room look like it's on?

a2d2d5aebc5a.t: October 12 — "A War Machine That Would Never Fight." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A weapon kept only for protection ge

060f41ad2de6.t: A War Machine That Would Never Fight

eb3616427487.t: A weapon kept only for protection gets used, so A.A. refused one that would have put it in public lawsuits. After a film studio nearly misused the A.A. name, the board's chairman proposed an act of Congress to protect it. The General Service Conference, the delegates the groups had sent, said no, and Bill W. recorded why (A.A. Comes of Age): "Under enough provocation, we would be bound to start public lawsuits and thus enter the field of public controversy. It would be like building a war machine on the theory that it would always stay home and never fight." A fellowship in court is a fellowship on one side of a public fight, and the papers print the side. The committee's resolution named the cost: A.A. could become tangled in lawsuits without end, and the expense and the publicity could threaten its very existence. So the Conference chose to "rely upon group and public opinion for our ultimate protection." Picture the drinker who reads that A.A. is suing somebody. He does not learn that A.A. is free; he learns that it fights. Today the war machine is a lawyer's letter sent in A.A.'s name. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone near you has threatened legal action for A.A., and who gave them the right.

98ce35cebcbf.t: A.A. turned down the power to sue because a fellowship in court has taken a side in public. Has anyone threatened a fight in my group's name?

39f34efcee25.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Tradition Ten: the Congressional Charter; the Conference resolution).

d9330dca2528.t: October 13 — "Known." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A member known to be in A.A. who takes a public side can implicate

5ab68f6767a5.t: A member known to be in A.A. who takes a public side can implicate A.A. without once saying its name. The long form is exact about when a member's opinion becomes A.A.'s problem (Big Book, p. 565): only when it is expressed "in such a way as to implicate A.A." That is the whole of it; his own vote, faith and views are his. But implicating A.A. does not need the word. A man everyone in town knows got sober in those rooms, standing at a microphone for one side of a drinking law, is heard as the rooms speaking, whatever he says about himself. The Big Book's first Foreword told the public what A.A. is (p. xiv): "We are not allied with any particular faith, sect or denomination, nor do we oppose anyone. We simply wish to be helpful to those who are afflicted." Nor do we oppose anyone. A known member at a podium can make that sentence look false to the one person it was written for: the drinker on the other side, who concludes the rooms are against him. Today it is the professional recovery voice, introduced at hearings and on panels by how long he has been sober. Test it tonight: when someone is introduced by his sobriety before he argues a cause, ask what the audience will hear.

9cf8b55d52e4.t: A member can implicate A.A. without naming it, just by being known and taking a side. When I take a side in public, what do people who know I'm sober hear?

da21b142c194.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565); Big Book p. xiv (Foreword to the First Edition).

30158ce07435.t: October 14 — "However Good." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A group cannot sign its name to any other cause, however goo

b5f71037f3e7.t: A group cannot sign its name to any other cause, however good, and Bill W. wrote the good case into the refusal on purpose. The letter is true: a detox is closing, a program for drunk drivers is losing its money, and other organizations have signed. A member asks for the group's name too. Nobody wants the group's opinion; they want its standing. Bill W. answered in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "we can say quite emphatically that neither A.A. as a whole nor any A.A. group ought to enter any activity other than straight A.A. As groups, we cannot endorse, finance or form an alliance with any other cause, however good". However good. He knew every real request would be a good one; a line that bent for good causes would bend for all of them. Straight A.A. means the message carried to the drinker, and nothing else. The long form gives the reason (Big Book, p. 565): "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one." A group that signs for one side of a funding fight has opposed the other, and some drinker is on the other side. Today it arrives as a sign-on letter or a coalition list. Test it tonight: ask whether your group's name is on any letter, list or coalition, and who put it there.

440b0dde4269.t: Bill wrote "however good" into the refusal because every request that reaches a group is a good one. Has my group's name gone on anything that isn't straight A.A.?

639c5f366a4c.t: Grounded in: P-17, p. 24 (Bill W., 1947); long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565).

90c56cf53a0c.t: October 15 — "A New Instrument for Social Action." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A.A. was praised as a new instrument f

675d83a06bc8.t: A New Instrument for Social Action

4cf27882bdaf.t: A.A. was praised as a new instrument for social action and never took the job, and that refusal is why its good spread. The Lasker Award citation of 1951 sits in the back of the Big Book (p. 571): historians might one day see A.A. as "a great venture in social pioneering which forged a new instrument for social action". An instrument for social action is a tool for changing society, which is the job description of a reform movement. It was meant as praise. A.A. printed it and kept doing one thing. Bill W. told what that restraint bought (A.A. Comes of Age): "We saw that the more A.A. minded its own business the greater its general influence would become." Medicine, religion and psychiatry began to borrow its ideas, while A.A. lent its name to no cause but its own. Minding its own business is what keeps the door open to the drunk: a man who needs A.A. tonight does not have to agree with anyone's plans for society to walk in. Today the capture comes as praise: programs and campaigns that describe A.A. as a platform for their cause, a partner in their mission. Test it tonight: when someone describes A.A. as part of something bigger, ask what the bigger thing wants from it.

d95cb7f8b78e.t: A.A. was praised as an instrument for social action and chose to mind its own business, and its influence grew. Is anyone describing my room as part of a bigger cause?

73726db5d875.t: Grounded in: Big Book p. 571 (Appendix IV, the Lasker Award citation); A.A. Comes of Age (Tradition Six).

f07401db3297.t: October 16 — "Which Drunks Go to Jail." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A.A. once had members deciding which drunks went

098f049d8f9d.t: A.A. once had members deciding which drunks went to jail, and A.A. had never given them any view to carry. Bill W. (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 54): "A.A. members began to take us into politics. They began to tell state legislative committees — publicly, of course — just what A.A. wanted in the way of rehabilitation, money and enlightened legislation." Just what A.A. wanted. Nobody had asked A.A., and A.A. holds no view to ask for. Then: "Thus, by full name and often by pictures, some of us became lobbyists. Other members sat on benches with police court judges, advising which drunks in the lineup should go to A.A. and which to jail." A lobbyist is someone who works on lawmakers for one side. Now stand in that lineup. The drunk looking up at the bench sees an A.A. member helping decide his sentence. The one place that was supposed to want nothing from him has become part of the court. The long form says the groups "oppose no one" (Big Book, p. 565). Today the bench is a signature: a meeting that signs court slips and reports who attended has a hand in who goes back to jail. Test it tonight: ask who your meeting reports to, if anyone, and what happens to the man whose slip goes unsigned.

5384e8035fa6.t: Members once sat beside judges choosing which drunks went to jail, and every drunk in that lineup learned A.A. could be against him. Does my room report on anyone?

299f8ec04ffc.t: Grounded in: P-17, p. 54 (Bill W.); long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565).

6961ba402081.t: October 17 — "The Disappointed Friend." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. The man who carried A.A. into Canada hoped it wou

065d168f11ef.t: The man who carried A.A. into Canada hoped it would become a dry crusade, and the drunks he brought together would not do it; they only wanted the next drinker. Bill W. (A.A. Comes of Age): "Sometime in 1940 a temperance worker at Toronto showed the A.A. book to an alcoholic who had resisted all other attempts at rescue." A temperance worker is someone campaigning against drink. His name was George Little, a minister as well, and he had every reason to expect an ally. Instead, Bill wrote, he "was not a little disappointed that his strange new flock showed no interest whatever in getting everybody bone dry. They insisted they were concerned only with local imbibers who wanted A.A." An imbiber is a drinker. The first Canadian A.A.s owed this man a great deal and still gave him no say in what they stood for. "Here it was definitely proved for the first time that A.A. could never become a dry crusade". The drinker who wasn't ready yet could still find them later, because they had not made themselves his enemy. Today the friend is a funder or an agency that sends people to meetings and expects the meetings to share its cause. Test it tonight: ask whether anyone who helps your group expects a say in what it stands for.

1def60700639.t: The man who handed Toronto its first A.A. got no say in what A.A. stood for, and the drunks kept their door open to every drinker. Does anyone who helps my group expect a say in what it stands for?

591d88d1d3cb.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Canada, 1940).

0a4fbf132ad4.t: October 18 — "Even a Worthy One." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A.A. stays out of every public fight, even the good one

8a021e43db70.t: A.A. stays out of every public fight, even the good ones, because recovery is life itself to the drunk and a fellowship in a fight can die. Bill W. said (A.A. Comes of Age) that A.A. had known from the beginning that "no matter what the provocation," it "must never publicly take sides" — "in any fight, even a worthy one." Provocation means something that tempts you to hit back. Even a worthy one: he wrote the hard case into the principle, not beside it. Then the reason: "we do not enter into public controversy, because we know that our fellowship will perish if we do." Perish means die. And the sentence that says whose life is at stake: "Recovery from alcoholism is life itself to us, and we wish to preserve in full strength our means of survival." The means of survival is the rooms, open to any drunk. A worthy fight still has two sides, and the man still drinking may be on the other one. Today the worthy fight arrives with a death toll and a deadline, and someone says this one is different. Test it tonight: when someone says the rooms should speak up on something, ask whether the drinker on the other side would still walk in.

c1efa83f0533.t: Bill wrote "even a worthy one" into the principle because the worthy fights are the ones that pull. Is there a cause I want my room to speak up for?

29fcbeb4ff20.t: Grounded in: A.A. Comes of Age (Unity: the Second Legacy — Tradition Ten).

1d62f3a1bd11.t: Tradition 10 — October 19: The Flyer | Daily Traditions | Recovery Starts

5eae8d2f413e.t: October 19 — "The Flyer." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A candidate at the podium in campaign season tells every voter

b5ff71ae3e34.t: A candidate at the podium in campaign season tells every voter on the other side that this room is not his. The invitation was innocent: he is a good speaker with long sobriety, and this year he is also running for office, and the flyer carries his name. The Big Book describes who fills A.A.'s rooms (p. 17): "many political, economic, social, and religious backgrounds. We are people who normally would not mix." People who normally would not mix. That only works in a room that has no side. The A.A. Preamble, printed at the front of pamphlet P-17, says what A.A. is: "not allied with any sect, denomination, politics, organization or institution; does not wish to engage in any controversy; neither endorses nor opposes any causes." A newcomer comes that night who knows the speaker's name from the lawn signs on his street. He watches a room full of alcoholics applaud the man he voted against. Nobody endorsed anyone; the flyer and the applause did it. Today it is the speaker night or anniversary that doubles as a campaign stop, or the local official invited to say a few words. Test it tonight: look at who has been invited to speak at your meeting this year, and ask what else their name stands for right now.

724e3cfa744c.t: A.A.'s rooms hold people who would not normally mix, and one campaign flyer can tell half of them to leave. Who has my meeting put at the podium lately?

aa3ae7c7b6e3.t: Grounded in: Big Book p. 17 (There Is a Solution); the A.A. Preamble (printed in P-17).

185964076d70.t: October 2 — "As We Elect." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Dr. Bob's last major talk said A.A. would grow or die by what

79a157e03ec1.t: Dr. Bob's last major talk said A.A. would grow or die by what it refused to get mixed up in. Detroit, 1948 (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers): "It is possible for us to grow or not to grow, as we elect." Then his conditions: "If we fight shy of entangling alliances, if we avoid getting messed up with controversial issues (religious or political or wet-dry), if we maintain unity through our central offices, if we preserve the simplicity of our program, if we remember that our job is to get sober and to stay sober and to help our less fortunate brother do the same thing, then we shall continue to grow and thrive and prosper." Wet-dry was the fight over whether liquor should be legal. Religious, political, wet-dry: the same three fights the long form of Tradition 10 names (Big Book, p. 565). And the list ends on the drunk, the less fortunate brother still drinking. The refusals come first because they protect that job. Today it is quieter: an "A.A. meeting" printed on a program's schedule beside the program's public positions on drug policy or funding. Nobody at the meeting says a word, and the meeting is allied anyway. Test it tonight: whose name besides the group's is on your meeting's door or schedule, and what is that name on record for?

04eea5bd823f.t: Dr. Bob put the fights A.A. refuses ahead of everything else, and ended on the drunk those refusals protect. Is my meeting tied to anyone who has taken a side?

28a5ce7fe292.t: Grounded in: Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers (his last major talk, Detroit, 1948); long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565).

a5d1a7ab1ef2.t: October 20 — "Outvoted by the Budget." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Money from either side of a fight comes with the s

48964c4c8b06.t: Money from either side of a fight comes with the side attached, and A.A. named that danger early. Bill W. wrote it plainly (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 34): "Every now and then we are offered money from so-called “wet” or “dry” sources. Obviously dangerous, this. For we must stay out of that ill-starred controversy." The wets were the liquor side; the drys wanted liquor banned. Ill-starred means doomed. A gift from either would have made A.A. that side's beneficiary, and the drinker on the other side would know whose money kept the lights on. The long form names alcohol reform as a fight the groups stay out of (Big Book, p. 565), and money is the quietest way in. Nobody has to say a word; the budget says it. Today the money comes as a room, coffee and a schedule, provided by a program whose own funding depends on a law, a grant or a contract going its way. The meeting takes no position. It just can't afford for its host to lose. Test it tonight: ask who pays for your room, and what they need to win.

7e1186928b3c.t: Bill called wet and dry money dangerous because a budget can take a side without anyone saying a word. Is my room paid for by anyone with a fight to win?

e686dd040456.t: A member who ran for office on being in A.A. dragged the whole fellowship into his campaign. Bill W. (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 55): "We were next startled to learn that we had been drawn into partisan politics, this time for the benefit of a single individual. Running for public office, a member splashed his political advertising with the fact that he was an A.A. and, by inference, sober as a judge!" Partisan means taking one party's side. By inference means without saying it outright. The advertisement did not speak only for him. "A.A. being popular in his state, he thought it would help him win on election day." He was spending A.A.'s good name on one side of an election, and every voter on the other side learned that A.A. had a candidate. The long form puts politics first among the fights the groups stay out of (Big Book, p. 565). The man still drinking who votes the other way now has one more reason to think the rooms aren't for him. Today it is the campaign bio or the ad that offers recovery in A.A. as the reason to trust someone. Test it tonight: if a candidate near you runs on his A.A. membership, ask what the drinker on the other side of that election hears.

46827bc520d9.t: One member ran on being in A.A., and A.A. found itself in partisan politics for one man's benefit. Would I use my sobriety to win something?

ee7bdeece08b.t: October 22 — "Joyfully Quoted." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Nobody speaks for A.A. in a fight, and that includes the

ba456760e0cb.t: Nobody speaks for A.A. in a fight, and that includes the man who started it. Bill W. tried for years to run A.A. himself, and wrote what happened (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 39): "If I took sides in a controversy, I was joyfully quoted by some, while others murmured" — "And just who does this dictator think he is?" Joyfully quoted by some: his words became one side's weapon. The others stopped listening to him. A dictator is a ruler nobody chose. If the co-founder's opinion split the room when he gave it, no one else's opinion can stand for A.A. either. Bill put it in four words: "Personal power always failed." The long form makes it a principle for everyone (Big Book, p. 565): no group or member should express an opinion on outside fights "in such a way as to implicate A.A." Today the voice being quoted is the staff member or the addiction expert introduced as speaking from years in A.A., quoted on one side of a public argument. Half the audience cheers. The drinker in the other half hears that A.A. is against him. Test it tonight: when someone is quoted as knowing what A.A. thinks, ask who gave them the job.

a1c09998005f.t: If the co-founder's side-taking split the room, nobody else's opinion can speak for A.A. Who have I heard quoted as if they knew what A.A. thinks?

e108825d3e3c.t: October 23 — "Naturally Aggressive People." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Tradition 10 asks the most of the people who

6902fa817239.t: Tradition 10 asks the most of the people who love a fight, which is most of us, and it asks for one reason: the drunk. Bill W. did not pretend otherwise (A.A. Comes of Age): "Considering how most of us have really loved controversy, this denial of the privilege of attacking something or somebody in public is no small achievement for the naturally aggressive people that we are." Controversy means a public argument. Naturally aggressive: he meant us. Giving up the right to go after someone in public is a real sacrifice, and Bill wrote it down as one. He also wrote what it buys (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 50): "We abstain from public controversy and will not quarrel among ourselves about those things that so rip society asunder — religion, politics and reform. We have but one purpose: to carry the A.A. message to the sick alcoholic who wants it." Rip society asunder means tear it apart. The sick alcoholic who wants the message might be on either side of any of those three fights. Today the fight comes into the room through the shares: the news of the week, a politician's name, a sneer at somebody's church. Test it tonight: listen for anything said in your meeting that a newcomer from the other side would take as a door closing.

89561604d27e.t: Tradition 10 is a sacrifice made by people who love a fight, so the sick alcoholic on either side can walk in. What fight do I bring into my meeting?

b1257d148e7d.t: A group's name on a cause's list of supporters is an endorsement, whatever the group meant by it. It starts as a good night: a barbecue or a dance, the kind the group already throws for its anniversary, with a bucket by the door for a food bank or a family that lost everything. Then the cause thanks its supporters in public, and the group's name sits on a list beside organizations nobody in the group has looked into. Some of them hold positions on drinking laws, on treatment funding, on religion. A.A.'s own statement about itself, printed in pamphlet P-17 (p. 36), says A.A. "is concerned solely with the personal recovery and continued sobriety of individual alcoholics who turn to the Fellowship for help" and "does not endorse any causes". An endorsement is a public show of support. The long form gives the reason from the drunk's side (Big Book, p. 565): "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one." A name on a supporters' list is a side, and the man still drinking who is on the other one can read that list too. Today it is the sponsor board at a fundraiser, the logo wall at a recovery walk, the community partners page. Test it tonight: search your group's name online and see what list it is on.

5f49fb661c72.t: A group's name on a supporters' list takes a side without anyone saying a word. What list is my group's name on?

3771caa8f48d.t: In the Name of A.A. and Our Group

6f9ddaa26a30.t: A member who protests a law in A.A.'s name speaks for people who never agreed, and the drunk who disagrees hears that A.A. is not for him. The pamphlet P-43 draws Tradition Ten as a cartoon. A member stands up to thank A.A. for ten sober years, and then: "But before I leave" — he is "sending a telegraph in the name of A.A. and our group" to protest a bill before Congress. A telegraph here means a telegram, the fastest message of the day. His next line: "I know I speak for all of A.A." Out in the room, someone on the other side of that bill says what the whole Tradition is afraid of: "How could anyone get sober or stay sober in an outfit like that?" That is the drinker P-43 wants you to see. He came for a way out and found a political club. The long form says the groups "oppose no one" (Big Book, p. 565), and the cartoon's member opposed someone on everybody's behalf. Nothing about his ten years was false. His telegram was. Today it is the petition, the open letter or the rally sign sent from the recovery community, with A.A. meant to be read into it. Test it tonight: when anything is sent in your group's name, ask who in the room agreed to it.

1edbebb42730.t: The cartoon's member meant his thanks and his protest; only one of them was his to send in A.A.'s name. What has been sent in my group's name?

dcb72dcbd695.t: Grounded in: P-43, The Twelve Traditions Illustrated (Tradition Ten); long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565).

6115eda75ac3.t: October 26 — "They Assumed." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Two members assumed A.A. was angry on their behalf, and the

4e88c8844af9.t: Two members assumed A.A. was angry on their behalf, and the newspapers told the country it was. Bill W. told it (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 55): "A member, whose name and professional attainments are known on three continents, got hold of a letter which she thought damaged her professional reputation. She felt something should be done about this and so did her lawyer, also an A.A. They assumed that both the public and A.A. would be rightfully angry if the facts were known." They assumed. Nobody asked a group. "Forthwith, several newspapers headlined how Alcoholics Anonymous was rooting for one of its lady members — name in full, of course — to win her suit for libel." Forthwith means right away; a suit for libel is a court case over something false printed about you. A radio commentator then told the same thing to an audience Bill put at twelve million. A.A. was now one side of a lawsuit it had never heard of, and a drinker who knew the other party learned that A.A. was against him. The long form says the groups "oppose no one" (Big Book, p. 565). Today it is the statement that says what people in recovery want, written by someone nobody chose. Test it tonight: when you hear what A.A. members feel about something outside, ask who asked them.

7d1cf9b7b973.t: Two members assumed A.A. was behind them, and twelve million people heard that it was. Have I ever assumed my group agreed with me without asking?

1115217ad1d1.t: October 27 — "Into Public Controversy." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A.A.'s own parent movement was dragged into a pub

c8a5f39de0a6.t: A.A.'s own parent movement was dragged into a public fight, and Bill W. would not even thank it in public, because the drunk's chance came first. The Oxford Group, the Christian movement where Bill and Dr. Bob first found help, made the newspapers in 1936 when its leader was quoted praising a dictator; Pass It On records that "the article brought the group into public controversy." In 1940 Bill wrote to a member who asked about it (Pass It On): "unfortunately, a vast and sometimes unreasoning prejudice exists all over this country against the O.G." O.G. means the Oxford Group. He was grateful; some of its message, he wrote, had saved his life. But thanking it in public might "establish a connection between the O.G. and Alcoholics Anonymous which does not exist". So: "I had to ask myself which was the more important" — his own pleasure in paying the debt, "or that alcoholics everywhere have the best possible chance to stay alive regardless of who gets credit." A drinker who hated that fight would have taken A.A. for part of it. Today the pull is gratitude too: a church, a program or a funder that helped the group and wants its name beside A.A.'s. Test it tonight: ask whose name your meeting wears besides A.A.'s, and what fight that name is in.

15ca190942e0.t: Bill kept even his gratitude out of public view, so no drunk would think A.A. belonged to someone else's fight. Whose name does my meeting wear besides A.A.'s?

8034f2102b0f.t: October 28 — "No Basis for Contention." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. The Big Book set out to give no one a reason to a

d58c9501f94f.t: The Big Book set out to give no one a reason to argue about medicine or religion, so nobody can use A.A. to settle those fights for you. Its writers knew (Big Book, p. 19): "Of necessity there will have to be discussion of matters medical, psychiatric, social, and religious. We are aware that these matters are, from their very nature, controversial. Nothing would please us so much as to write a book which would contain no basis for contention or argument." Psychiatric means about mental illness; contention means a fight. On health, the same book sends the reader outward, to the people whose work it is (p. 133): "Do not hesitate to take your health problems to such persons." A.A. holds no view on your prescription, your diagnosis or your church for anyone to quote. The long form adds sectarian religion to the fights the groups stay out of (p. 565). The drinker this protects is the one on a medication, or of a faith, who gets told at the door that A.A. is against it and goes back out. Today it is staff, or a member, telling a newcomer what A.A. believes about his pills. Test it tonight: if someone tells a newcomer what A.A. thinks about his medication or his church, ask them for the page.

32e8d08f8e37.t: The Big Book wanted no basis for contention about medicine or religion, so A.A. has no ruling on either to hand out. Have I told a newcomer what A.A. thinks about something it never ruled on?

45e66e6fcd7a.t: October 29 — "Our Sole Aim." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Saying plainly what A.A. is has never been an outside issue;

13067ca0d435.t: Saying plainly what A.A. is has never been an outside issue; it is the one thing A.A. must say. Tradition 10 keeps A.A. out of other people's fights, not out of its own name. Bill W. drew the line in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 24): "we cannot link the A.A. name to other enterprises in the alcohol field to the extent that the public gets the impression we have abandoned our sole aim." Sole aim means only purpose. An enterprise is a business or a program. The pamphlet P-43 says it in a caption: "Ours is not a secret society" — "we carry the message anywhere we can". Saying out loud that an A.A. group charges nothing and answers to no program is not taking A.A. into a fight. It keeps A.A.'s name its own. The drinker who thinks A.A. is a program he can't afford, or a place he'll be reported from, never finds the free room down the street. Today the confusion sits on intake forms, billing sheets and websites that list twelve-step meetings as a paid service, which an A.A. group never is. Test it tonight: ask whether your meeting answers to anyone but the alcoholics in it, and say so out loud when someone asks.

33e99fedf2f5.t: Tradition 10 keeps A.A. out of other people's fights; it never asks A.A. to let others say what it is. Could a drinker tell, from what my room says about itself, that it is free and answers to no one?

71c971628943.t: October 3 — "No Views Whatever." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Read Tradition 10 in its long form before anyone tells y

0e80e0dbc7c9.t: Read Tradition 10 in its long form before anyone tells you what it means, because the words are narrower and harder than the rumour. The Big Book (p. 565): "No A.A. group or member should ever, in such a way as to implicate A.A., express any opinion on outside controversial issues—particularly those of politics, alcohol reform, or sectarian religion. The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one. Concerning such matters they can express no views whatever." Whose views? The groups', and a member's only when it drags A.A. in with him. Which fights? Outside ones: elections, liquor laws, one church against another ("sectarian" means belonging to one denomination). What it does not say is that A.A. must keep quiet about itself. What an A.A. group is (free, run by its members, answering to no one) is A.A.'s own business, not an outside issue. The reason for the silence is the drunk: a man still drinking who hears the rooms are against his party or his faith has a reason not to come. Today the words get turned around. Staff tell a client "A.A. says" something about his medication, his church or his vote. Test it tonight: when anyone says "A.A. says," ask to see where it is written.

cd25bb089b8e.t: Tradition 10 closes A.A.'s mouth on outside fights, not on what A.A. is. Have I ever repeated "A.A. says" about something A.A. has never said?

91533f98922c.t: Grounded in: Long form, Tradition 10 (Big Book, p. 565).

395a096d3d13.t: October 30 — "Practically Never." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Tradition 10 is kept first inside the room: a group tha

97ea794a2031.t: Tradition 10 is kept first inside the room: a group that never argues these fights in private will never argue them in public. Bill W. passed on what one old-timer told him (A.A. Comes of Age): "Practically never have I heard a heated religious, political, or reform argument among A.A. members. So long as we don't argue these matters privately, it's a cinch we never shall argue them publicly." A cinch means a sure thing. Akron remembered the same habit from the early 1940s; Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers sums up how Joe P. recalled the local thinking: "If you had something wrong with you, that's what you talked about; you didn't talk about sports or politics." That is not a gag. It is a room with one subject: the drinking, and the way out. And it is why Bill could say that "Our fellowship never has taken sides publicly on any question in this embattled world" — a world full of fighting. A newcomer from any side of any fight could sit down in those rooms and hear nothing that told him to leave. Today the news walks in with every phone, and the shares drift toward it. Test it tonight: count how many minutes of your meeting are about drinking and recovery, and how many are about everything else.

d106aba530fa.t: The rooms that keep this Tradition are the ones where the fights never come up, so no drinker has to hear which side the room is on. What does my meeting spend its minutes on?

0688200a34d4.t: October 31 — "We Were That Excited." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. The month ends with A.A. nearly breaking this Tradit

65763e833d5c.t: The month ends with A.A. nearly breaking this Tradition over its own name, and Bill admitting why. A film studio wrote a script about A.A.; Bill W. judged it (A.A. Comes of Age): "The proposed portrayal of A.A. seemed pretty lopsided and in rather bad taste." A portrayal is how a film shows something. "We concluded that we ought to ask for an injunction against the company for misuse of the A.A. name." An injunction is a court order to stop, so this meant going to court. It worked. Then Bill wrote the line that belongs at the end of this month: "Otherwise, we might have sued, forgetting all about A.A.'s principle of non-controversy in public." Then: "We were that excited." The people who wrote Tradition 10 nearly broke it defending A.A. itself, because defending something you love feels like it can't be wrong. A lawsuit would have put A.A. in the headlines as a fighter, and the drinker reading them would have learned the rooms had enemies. Saying what A.A. is costs nothing; going to war for it costs the drunk. Today the excitement comes the same way: someone misuses A.A.'s name, and the room wants a fight. Test it tonight: the next time you feel sure A.A. needs defending in public, ask what the drunk still out there would read about it.

98df7d66079b.t: The people who wrote Tradition 10 nearly broke it over A.A.'s own name, because they were that excited. What am I excited enough about to forget it?

754d1fd75714.t: October 4 — "Eleven to Two." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A group that votes on an outside issue now has an opinion on

6dc42b1e08db.t: A group that votes on an outside issue now has an opinion on it, and a drinker on the losing side has just been shown the door. It happens at the end of a business meeting, after the coffee money. Someone brings a petition about a local liquor law. There is no argument; the room agrees. A show of hands, just so we know where we stand. Eleven up, two down, and the secretary writes it in the minutes. No newspaper, no statement. But the group has a recorded position, and the long form's line is crossed: "in such a way as to implicate A.A." (Big Book, p. 565). Bill W. described what groups that last do instead (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 38): "The groups are willing to avoid controversy over outside issues such as political reform or religion; they stick to their single purpose of helping alcoholics to recover." Single purpose. The two who kept their hands down may stay or may drift, and the drinker who hears about that vote from them may never come at all. Today the request usually comes from outside: a campaign asking groups to "sign on." Test it tonight: ask what your group's business meeting has ever voted on, and whether every item was A.A.'s own business.

8fc7337ad5f7.t: October 5 — "Evangelist or Reformer." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. Before there were any Traditions, the Big Book's in

f1b6e2a91487.t: Before there were any Traditions, the Big Book's instructions for carrying the message already ruled out the crusade, because a crusade costs you the drunk. Chapter 7, Working With Others (Big Book, p. 89): "Don't start out as an evangelist or reformer. Unfortunately a lot of prejudice exists. You will be handicapped if you arouse it." Six pages later, sitting with the man still drinking (p. 95): "You will be most successful with alcoholics if you do not exhibit any passion for crusade or reform." A reformer, like a crusade, is out to change how everybody else lives; an evangelist is selling a faith. Either one makes the sick man pick a side before he can pick up the phone. Tradition 10 is the same instruction written for a whole group: what would handicap one member at a bedside handicaps a room in front of a town. Today the crusade comes in through a door marked "A.A. meeting" at a facility, where the program's cause is read before anyone shares: its doctrine, its position on the latest law. Test it tonight: could a drinker from either side of any argument sit down in your room and not be told what to think?

e1f5502ea477.t: The Big Book told the first A.A.s not to come to a drunk as reformers, because prejudice shuts the door. Is anything said in my room that would shut it?

b71dfb847742.t: The first member who dragged A.A. into a public fight was sure he was helping, and that is what made him dangerous. Bill W. (A.A. pamphlet P-17, pp. 52–53): "Presently an A.A. member began to publish a crusading magazine devoted to the cause of Prohibition. He thought Alcoholics Anonymous ought to help make the world bone-dry." Prohibition was the law that banned liquor outright. He told his readers he was an A.A. member. "He pointed out that he too was an “educator,” and that his brand of education was the “right kind.” As for putting A.A. into public controversy, he thought that was exactly where we should be." Now read it as the man still drinking. He picks up a magazine that says A.A. wants his bottle outlawed. He does not hear one member's opinion. He hears that the rooms are a temperance society, and he does not call. The long form names this exact fight, "alcohol reform" (Big Book, p. 565), because it is the one a drunk is surest to be on the other side of. Today the "right kind of education" comes printed in a program's brochures and campaigns about drinking, with A.A. named as if it had signed on. Test it tonight: find where your meeting is advertised, and read what else that page says.

be83269c2745.t: A sincere member put A.A.'s name on a Prohibition magazine, and every drinker who read it learned the rooms wanted his bottle. What does my room's name say to a man who is still drinking?

1d9e354a9c73.t: Radio lectures that were half A.A. and half one man's religion would have told a whole country that A.A. was his church. A member had been paid to give twelve talks about A.A. on national radio, and headquarters read the scripts first. Bill W. (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 53): "They were about 50% A.A. and 50% our friend's personal religious convictions. This could create a false public view of us. Religious prejudice against A.A. would be aroused. So we objected." Think about who would have been listening. A drinker of another faith, or of none, hears that A.A. is one man's creed, and the door he needed closes before he reaches it. The Big Book had already drawn the line for a member sitting with one drunk (p. 94): "We are dealing only with general principles common to most denominations." The long form draws it for the whole Fellowship: no opinion on "sectarian religion," meaning the teaching of any one church (p. 565). A.A. stopped the broadcast without a word in public, and the man dropped it. Today the same half-and-half turns up in a meeting run as somebody's ministry, where the host's doctrine is read from the front as if it were A.A.'s. Test it tonight: is anything read at your meeting that belongs to one faith and not to A.A.?

f481a6f9334d.t: A.A. stopped a broadcast that would have made it one man's church, because a drinker of any faith has to be able to walk in. Would a drinker of another faith, or none, be at home in my room?

34b5aa59010b.t: October 8 — "The Account Has No Face." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 10: Alcoholics Anonymous has no opinion on outside issues; hence the A.A. name ought never be drawn into public controversy. A group account cannot post as one member; every w

427ce039353b.t: A group account cannot post as one member; every word it sends out is the group's. The long form's line is not about intentions (Big Book, p. 565). It is "in such a way as to implicate A.A.," and an account with the group's name on it implicates the group every time it speaks. Bill W. saw what one member could do once he made the A.A. name his to use (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 53): "it was in the power of an A.A. to marry Alcoholics Anonymous to practically any enterprise or controversy at all, good or bad." Marry, meaning tie together for good in the public's mind. He was describing a man who had to declare his membership to the whole public to do it. Today it takes a password. A meeting starts a page so people can find the schedule, and one night the news touches drinking, or an election, and whoever holds the login shares something. It reads as the group's view, because there is nothing else it could read as. And somewhere a man still drinking, scrolling for a meeting at midnight, finds out which side the room is on before he finds out what time it starts. Test it tonight: ask who holds your group's password, and read back everything that account has posted that isn't about meetings.

2c13424987ab.t: A group account has no face, so every post is the group speaking. What would a drinker learn about my room from its page before he learned the meeting time?

da3dbedef956.t: An outside cause read out during announcements is endorsed by the chair it is read from. The email is reasonable: a campaign about drunk driving, a petition to keep a detox open, a rally about a drinking law. It is about alcohol, and two members are already involved. So the secretary reads it before the close, in the same voice as the coffee list and the anniversaries. Nobody said A.A. supports it. The slot said it. The Big Book's own Foreword records what the groups had settled on (p. xix): "And in no circumstances should we give endorsements, make alliances, or enter public controversies." In no circumstances, which includes the good ones. The long form names alcohol reform among the three fights A.A. stays out of (p. 565). Now think about the newcomer that night: maybe a man with a drunk-driving charge against him, or a job at the bar the campaign wants closed. On his first night, before anyone has shaken his hand, he has heard where this room stands and where he doesn't. Today these requests often come from the program that hosts the meeting. Test it tonight: listen to the announcements and ask, of each one, whether it is A.A.'s own business.

f6945bdfb38b.t: September 1 — "Not an Organization." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Akron, 1937. Eighteen alcoholics sat in a li

1db14edc90be.t: Akron, 1937. Eighteen alcoholics sat in a living room while Bill W. made his case: A.A. should hire paid missionaries, build a chain of hospitals that turned a profit, and publish a book. The room pushed back hard. Then it voted, and Bill won — "by the barest majority, and over the most strenuous objections," in his own account of it (A.A. Comes of Age). A.A. had just decided, democratically and in good faith, to turn itself into an organization. Nobody in that room was cynical about it. They believed structure would reach dying men faster, and they may well have been right. It never happened. Bill went east to raise the money and came back with nothing. Two years later the Big Book went to print, and page xiii carried the first thing A.A. ever said about itself in public: "We are not an organization in the conventional sense of the word." That sentence survived because a fundraising trip failed. It's also why the meeting you sat in this week has no owner, no dues, no membership committee, and nobody with the standing to put you out.

81b6dbc25749.t: Nobody in that room has the standing to put me out — not the chair, not the oldest member there, nobody. What would change for me if somebody did?

7571dc31c4d2.t: September 10 — "The Missing Clause." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. The whole safeguard in Tradition 9 is six wo

662132bfc07e.t: The whole safeguard in Tradition 9 is six words, and they are the six that get left out. The short form (Big Book, p. 562): "A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve." Service boards and committees are the offices that answer the phone, print the schedules and keep the lights on. Quote the Tradition without the ending and you have a permission slip — A.A. allows offices. Quote it whole and you have a leash: any body doing A.A.'s work answers downward, to the people it serves, or it is not doing A.A.'s work. That is the cheapest capture there is. Nobody has to lie. A sentence stops early, gets repeated, and starts to sound complete. So when a board, an office, a committee, or a program tells you it is part of A.A., ask the six-word question: who do you answer to? An A.A. service body answers to the groups, and the groups can stop paying for it tomorrow. A body that answers to owners, funders, or a head office is organized in exactly the way this Tradition says A.A. never will be. Read the Tradition to the end. The end is the point.

ff04ed07a86c.t: The safeguard is six words most people stop before. What have I accepted as settled because I only heard the first half?

b022ec394be0.t: September 11 — "Let Him Stay." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Nobody stands at the door of an A.A. meeting decid

483fc9080ec5.t: Nobody stands at the door of an A.A. meeting deciding who gets in. That was settled by the drunks who tried it. Early Cleveland had men posted for exactly that job — other members called them the "snifters," which an early member explained were "men who stood by the door, sniffing each man who came in" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers). Sniffing for liquor. Behind them stood the rules: you had to be hospitalized first, or visited by ten members, or passed by a committee. Then a man walked in with a couple of drinks in him. The snifters moved to throw him out, and somebody said: "Let him stay. Maybe something will seep in." He stayed. He got sober, "just as sober as the fellow who had been hospitalized or visited by ten members, there went another rule. In the end, pioneer A.A.'s broke so many of their own rules that there were no rules left!" That is where the open door came from. So when a programme puts an assessment, an intake, or a sign-off between you and a chair, understand what it is: the snifters, back at the door. The alcoholic still drinking is the whole reason the room exists. A.A. learned not to make him qualify for it.

fff44821c437.t: A.A. broke its own rules until none were left, because the drunk at the door was the point. Would I have got in the night I came?

c9127e7a88a9.t: September 12 — "Nobody Runs It for Life." A daily reading on A.A.'s Tradition 9: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve. Nobody runs an A.A. group for life. The

907b0bbbbb01.t: Nobody runs an A.A. group for life. The Long Form says how it is done in one short sentence (Big Book, p. 565): "Rotating leadership is the best." The drunks in Cleveland worked that out before anyone wrote it down. In October 1939 they formed A.A.'s first central committee — seven people — and built the exit into it from day one: "one man and one woman dropped off each month to be replaced by the next in line according to seniority" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers) — seniority meaning time in A.A., not rank. Bill W. admitted what everyone had assumed until then: "Up to that time, all of our affairs had been in charge of the ultra-oldtimers, and we naturally supposed it would always be that way." Naturally supposed. That is how a person becomes a position — not by a vote, but by nobody thinking to ask. Rotation is the ask, built in, so the job always comes open and never turns into a man. It is also why the chair will be open to you. Now look at any room where the same person has run "the A.A. meeting" for years and is paid to. Nobody is rotating out of a salary. That room has a manager, and A.A. groups do not.

2aa1502147a2.t: A.A. built the exit into its first committee so no job could become a person. When did the chair in my meeting last change hands?
